title: Equal physical standing for inertial frames
body:
The principle of relativity states that the laws of physics have the same form in all \cref{Inertial frames}{sr.inertial_frames}. In particular, no inertial frame is physically privileged as the true state of rest.
This allows the observers' measured numbers to differ. The requirement is that the physical laws connecting those numbers apply equally well in each frame.
statement: The laws have the same form in every inertial frame; none defines absolute rest.

title: Interchanging the two laboratories
body:
Let laboratory \(S'\) coast at velocity \(v\) along the \(x\)-axis of inertial laboratory \(S\). Both use identically calibrated rods and clocks. Since the principle of relativity gives neither laboratory a preferred claim to rest, we should be able to exchange their roles consistently.
With the same standard axis conventions, \(S'\) then describes \(S\) as moving at velocity \(-v\). This is the inverse coordinate description. Spatial isotropy adds that reversing the chosen direction cannot, on its own, introduce a new physical calibration factor.
These conditions help fix the overall scale in the \cref{Lorentz boost}{sr.lorentz_transformations.interval_condition}, after light-speed invariance has constrained its time-space mixing. Reciprocity means that the two descriptions fit together; it does not mean that both observers assign the same coordinates to every event.
statement: Identically calibrated inertial laboratories must admit reciprocal descriptions of their relative motion.

title: Law form versus measured components
body:
Equal laws do not require equal measured numbers. Two inertial observers may assign different positions, times, velocities, energies, electric fields or magnetic fields to the same situation, because they are making measurements relative to different frames.
What must survive is the physical rule relating those quantities. So coordinate disagreement is not a failure of relativity; the test is whether the observers' transformed measurements still satisfy the same law.
statement: Observers can disagree on measured components while agreeing on the physical law.

title: Sealed laboratory intuition
body:
Imagine a sealed laboratory in a train moving smoothly at constant velocity along a straight track. You can drop balls, stretch springs, operate clocks or send light pulses, but you cannot look outside.
According to the relativity principle, these experiments do not reveal a special state of uniform motion. They obey the same laws as they would in another ideal inertial laboratory. To say how fast the train is moving, you must compare it with something outside: uniform motion alone leaves no distinctive internal signature.
statement: Uniform motion alone cannot be detected by experiments wholly inside an ideal inertial laboratory.

title: From Galileo to Einstein
body:
Galileo's ship argument already captured the idea that uniform motion cannot be detected by experiments confined to the moving system. The difficulty in nineteenth-century electrodynamics was that Maxwell's equations did not keep their form under the Galilean frame changes used in mechanics.
Lorentz and Poincaré developed much of the mathematics needed to address that difficulty. Einstein's 1905 step was to apply relativity without exception to both mechanics and electrodynamics, while abandoning any observable ether rest frame. Rather than treating electromagnetism as an exception, he revised the coordinate relations between inertial frames.
statement: Einstein extended inertial-frame equivalence to electrodynamics as well as mechanics.

title: Keeping relativity while replacing absolute time
body:
Relativity of uniform motion did not begin with Einstein. In Newtonian mechanics, the inertial-frame change \(x'=x-vt,\ t'=t\) leaves acceleration unchanged, so the same free-motion and Newtonian force laws can apply in both frames.
The difficulty comes when we also require \cref{invariant vacuum light speed}{sr.constancy_of_speed_of_light}. That requirement conflicts with the Galilean rule for time. SR resolves the conflict by retaining equal physical standing for inertial frames and replacing their coordinate transformation, rather than choosing a true ether rest frame.
Finding that replacement still needs explicit assumptions such as homogeneity, isotropy and common calibration. The relativity postulate alone does not determine the value of \(c\) or every coefficient of the transformation.
statement: Relativity of uniform motion survives when Galilean coordinate changes are replaced by Lorentz transformations.

title: The later mathematical symmetry
body:
The relativity postulate is a physical statement: inertial laboratories have equal standing. Once their allowed \cref{frame changes}{sr.lorentz_transformations} have been established, we can ask whether a proposed law respects that equivalence.
The mathematical test is \cref{Lorentz symmetry}{sr.lorentz_invariance}. Coordinates and tensor components may change, but the complete law must retain its physical content when transformed consistently.
So Lorentz symmetry implements the postulate mathematically after the frame changes are known. We should not reverse the reasoning and claim to prove the physical postulate merely by assuming that symmetry in advance.
statement: Lorentz covariance expresses inertial-frame equivalence using the frame changes appropriate to SR.

title: The vacuum light-speed postulate
body:
The light-speed postulate says that every \cref{inertial frame}{sr.inertial_frames} assigns a vacuum light pulse the same speed \(c\), independently of the source's uniform motion. Each frame uses its own standard network of Einstein-synchronised clocks to make that measurement.
This is a physical claim about light and inertial measurements. It is worth separating it from the SI convention that fixes the numerical value exactly:
\[c\overset{\text{SI definition}}{=}299\,792\,458\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}.\]
The convention tells us how the metre is defined in terms of the second and light speed. It does not, by itself, prove that the relativistic postulate describes nature.
statement: Every inertial frame assigns vacuum light the same speed \(c\), independently of the source's motion.

title: Invariance, not a large speed
body:
The surprising claim is not simply that light travels very fast. If that were all, we could still expect a moving observer to measure a slightly different speed, just as they would for a thrown ball.
Instead, different inertial observers moving uniformly relative to one another measure the same vacuum speed for the same pulse. It is this agreement despite relative motion—not the large number alone—that forces us to rethink the relation between space and time.
statement: The postulate concerns agreement between moving observers, not just light being fast.

title: Why Galilean velocity addition fails
body:
Let frame \(S'\) move at speed \(v\) along the \(x\)-axis of inertial frame \(S\). Our familiar Galilean rule subtracts the frame's displacement while leaving time unchanged:
\[x'=x-vt,\qquad t'=t.\]
Now apply it to a vacuum light pulse with \(dx/dt=c\). The rule predicts \(dx'/dt'=c-v\), because the moving frame appears to chase the light. But the light-speed postulate requires the speed to be \(c\) in \(S'\) as well.
So we cannot keep both this spatial rule and a time coordinate shared unchanged by the frames. Time must enter the transformation differently too. This identifies the difficulty with the Galilean assumptions; further reasoning is still needed to determine the \cref{Lorentz coefficients}{sr.lorentz_transformations.interval_condition}.
statement: A common vacuum light speed is incompatible with Galilean velocity addition.

title: A flash described in each inertial frame
body:
Choose a flash's emission event as the origin of an inertial frame with Einstein-synchronised clocks. At time \(t>0\), the vacuum flash has spread to a spherical surface of radius \(r=ct\). If we draw only one spatial dimension, its two rays satisfy
\[x=\pm ct.\]
A second inertial frame assigns its own time and position coordinates to the emission and the later wavefront events. It too measures speed \(c\). How can both descriptions work? The frames need not agree about which distant events occurred at the same time. Each can therefore assemble its own simultaneous spherical shell without assigning the same time labels to every point on the other's shell.
Requiring the two light-ray directions to agree physically constrains how time and space mix. It does not yet fix the whole coordinate rule: the full argument must also determine an overall scale factor.
statement: With Einstein-synchronised clocks, a vacuum flash expands at speed \(c\) in every inertial frame.

title: Light in vacuum and in matter
body:
Light travels more slowly in glass, water and many other material media than it does in vacuum. Its measured speed in a medium can also depend on the state of that medium, so the qualification vacuum matters.
The invariant speed \(c\) refers to vacuum light and, more generally, to the limiting speed built into SR's spacetime structure. A slower light pulse in glass is therefore not a counterexample to the postulate: it is a different physical situation, involving the interaction of light with matter.
statement: The invariant speed is the vacuum value; propagation in a material medium can be slower.

title: Light without an ether frame
body:
Maxwell's theory described light as an electromagnetic wave with a definite speed. Under Galilean kinematics, however, a moving observer would generally measure a different wave speed. This raised the question: relative to what was Maxwell's speed specified?
Ether models supplied a proposed answer, but ether-drift experiments—most famously Michelson and Morley's 1887 null result—undermined simple accounts of motion through a stationary ether. No single experiment logically produced special relativity. Einstein's 1905 formulation instead made the same vacuum light speed for every inertial observer a postulate, dispensing with an observable ether rest frame.
statement: Einstein made invariant vacuum light speed a postulate rather than an ether-drift correction.

title: Light speed constrains coordinate changes
body:
Consider two standard inertial frames using rods and clocks with the same calibration. The \cref{relativity postulate}{sr.principle_of_relativity} says that neither frame is privileged, so their descriptions must be reciprocal. The light-speed postulate adds a second constraint: each description must give vacuum light the same speed.
With homogeneity and spatial isotropy also stated, these requirements lead to the standard \cref{Lorentz boost}{sr.lorentz_transformations.interval_condition}. Notice the direction of the argument: the postulates are inputs used to find the transformation, rather than conclusions obtained by assuming its final formula.
Once the rule has been found, we can check algebraically that it preserves the spacetime interval. That check reveals the geometric structure behind the coordinate changes.
statement: Together with inertial-frame equivalence and spacetime symmetry assumptions, invariant \(c\) leads to Lorentz boosts.

title: Free motion defines the inertial class
body:
An inertial frame is a reference frame in which a free particle moves in a straight line at constant velocity. Here free means that interactions affecting its motion can be neglected: we are using unforced motion to test the frame.
In one spatial dimension, this motion has the form \(x(t)=x_0+vt\), where \(x_0\) is the starting position and \(v\) is constant. In three spatial dimensions, the same rule is \(\mathbf x(t)=\mathbf x_0+\mathbf v t\). So equal time intervals give equal displacement vectors.
statement: Free particles move at constant velocity in an inertial frame.

title: A grid and a clock convention
body:
To describe when and where an event occurs, a reference frame needs more than an observer at one position. It supplies a spatial coordinate grid, clocks at rest throughout that grid, and a convention for synchronising them. The event's coordinate time is then the reading of the clock at its location—not the later time at which a distant spectator receives its light.
Standard SR coordinates use Cartesian spatial axes and Einstein synchronisation: a reflected light signal is assigned equal outward and return travel times. This tells us how to set the clocks when comparing frames. The physical claim that vacuum light has the same speed in all inertial frames is a separate postulate; the clock convention alone does not prove it.
With this equipment in place, a frame can label a detector click by one time and three positions. Another coasting laboratory can use its own grid and clocks to describe the very same click.
statement: A frame supplies spatial labels and a synchronised time coordinate.

title: Testing a frame with free particles
body:
Choose a laboratory grid and its clock coordinate \(t\), then follow several test particles whose interactions can be neglected. If the frame is inertial, their tracks have the form
\[\mathbf x(t)=\mathbf x_0+\mathbf v t,\]
with constant \(\mathbf v\). The important qualification is free motion. A particle that is pushed, pulled or constrained can accelerate even in a perfectly inertial frame, so its acceleration alone does not disqualify the frame.
Now consider a rotating grid. It generally makes free tracks appear curved; an accelerating grid makes their coordinate velocities change. This is why free particles help us identify an inertial description. Identifying which motions count as free and which frames count as inertial is part of the empirical setup of mechanics, rather than something proved later from the Lorentz formulae.
statement: Unforced motion tests the frame; acceleration caused by an interaction does not disqualify it.

title: Approximating a nonaccelerating laboratory
statement: A real laboratory is inertial only to the accuracy with which rotation, acceleration and gravity can be neglected.

title: The observers compared by SR
body:
Special relativity compares the reports made in different \cref{inertial frames}{sr.inertial_frames}. Two physical postulates constrain how those reports can differ. The \cref{principle of relativity}{sr.principle_of_relativity} gives the frames equal physical standing, while \cref{vacuum light-speed invariance}{sr.constancy_of_speed_of_light} supplies a common signal speed \(c\).
To construct a particular coordinate transformation, we also assume homogeneous space and time, spatial isotropy (no preferred spatial direction), and commonly calibrated rods and clocks. These assumptions help turn the postulates into a definite boost formula.
Thus the inertial-frame definition tells us which observers we are comparing. Calling a frame inertial does not, by itself, establish either physical postulate.
statement: The relativity and light-speed postulates apply to the same class of inertial frames.

title: Different reports of one experiment
body:
Suppose two inertial laboratories coast past one another. Each can describe its own grid as stationary, so their coordinates and measured velocity components need not match. Their reports are not arbitrary, however: a definite frame-change rule must connect them.
For example, a particle at rest in one laboratory has zero spatial velocity there, but nonzero velocity in the other. There is no contradiction, because velocity is measured relative to a chosen grid. The \cref{Lorentz transformations}{sr.lorentz_transformations} tell us how to relate these different reports in SR.
The same distinction applies to \cref{event coordinates}{sr.spacetime_event} and to quantities such as the \cref{electric field}{sr.electric_field}: changing the frame can change the reported numbers without changing which physical situation is being described.
statement: Frame-dependent measurements remain constrained by common physical laws.

title: One occurrence, with place and time labels
body:
A spacetime event is a single occurrence at a definite place and time—for example, one detector click. In an \cref{Inertial frame}{sr.inertial_frames}, we label it by coordinates such as \((ct,x,y,z)\) or \((t,x,y,z)\), depending on the convention.
The occurrence is the event; the coordinate tuple is the frame's way of identifying where and when it happened.
statement: An event is one spacetime occurrence; its coordinates depend on the chosen frame.

title: The occurrence and its labels
body:
Consider one local detector click. The laboratory grid identifies its position, and the clock at that location assigns its coordinate time. Another inertial laboratory can assign a different position and time to the very same click, because its grid and clock network are different.
The physical occurrence is therefore not identical to its coordinate tuple. Changing the labels neither creates another click nor moves the original event. Keeping this distinction in mind lets us compare frame-dependent measurements without confusing them with a disagreement about what happened.
statement: Two frames can assign different coordinates to the same detector click.

title: A pointlike idealisation
body:
An event is a pointlike idealisation in spacetime. A bulb flashing at one place and one time can be represented by an event; the bulb's whole journey cannot, because it occupies many places and times.
A journey, orbit, wave pulse or extended experiment must therefore be described by many events arranged into a history. The distinction is useful even though real flashes and detector responses have a small, finite extent.
statement: A history comprises many events; one event does not represent an extended process.

title: Putting the time label in length units
body:
It is often convenient to multiply the time coordinate by \(c\) and write \(ct\). Since speed multiplied by time has units of length, all four spacetime coordinates then use the same units. With only one spatial dimension shown, an event can be plotted as \((ct,x)\).
This makes equations and diagrams easier to compare. It does not make time geometrically identical to space: their different roles still appear in the signs of the spacetime metric.
statement: Using \(x^0=ct\) gives time and space coordinates common units without making their geometric roles identical.

title: Coordinate disagreement without physical disagreement
body:
Different observers can disagree about an event's coordinates while agreeing on which occurrence took place. Think of two grid systems labelling the same point; in relativity, the time label can change as well as the spatial ones.
So a new coordinate value should not be interpreted as a new physical event. The label depends on the frame, while the occurrence being labelled does not.
statement: Relabelling an event changes its coordinates, not which occurrence took place.

title: Building histories and separations from events
body:
An event represents one occurrence. To describe a separation, we need two events: subtracting their coordinate tuples gives a displacement, from which we can calculate the \cref{spacetime interval}{sr.spacetime_interval}. To describe a particle's history, we instead follow a sequence of events forming its worldline.
A \cref{Minkowski diagram}{sr.minkowski_diagram} plots selected coordinates of those events. Once an origin and frame are chosen, an origin-relative \cref{position four-vector}{sr.position_four_vector} can also package an event's labels.
These constructions serve different purposes, but begin with the same underlying occurrences. None makes one particular coordinate grid part of the event itself.
statement: Intervals compare event pairs, diagrams display events, and worldlines assemble them into histories.

title: Laws built from local quantities
body:
A local differential law relates field values and a finite set of their derivatives at the same \cref{spacetime event}{sr.spacetime_event}. The derivatives describe how the field varies through neighbouring events, taken in a limit. They do not insert a separate instantaneous value from a remote point.
This tells us what information the law uses locally. It does not yet tell us how quickly a disturbance spreads. A relativistic causal theory must additionally have dynamics and admissible data that respect the light-cone limit; a local differential equation alone does not guarantee finite-speed propagation.
statement: A local law uses fields and derivatives at an event; causal propagation is a further requirement.

title: What enters a local differential law
body:
In a local field equation, quantities such as a field \(\phi(x)\), a source \(j(x)\) and a derivative \(\partial_\mu\phi(x)\) are all evaluated at the same event \(x\). A derivative still carries information about variation, but it does so through the limiting behaviour of arbitrarily close neighbours.
So an equation can constrain how a field changes without directly inserting a distant field value at the same coordinate time. To find a particular solution, we will generally still need initial and boundary conditions.
The distinction is between the information entering the law and the behaviour of its solutions. How far a disturbance can spread in a given time depends on the particular equation; it does not follow from the word differential alone.
statement: Derivatives describe nearby variation without requiring a separate value at a distant simultaneous point.

title: Fields as local variables
body:
A field assigns a variable to each spacetime event. This gives us a natural way to write a local law: relate the field value, its derivatives and any sources at that event, then require the same equation to hold point by point.
For example, a wave equation can describe a disturbance propagating from initial data or a source. Its mathematical structure determines the propagation cone (the directions along which changes can travel). Other local differential equations can have quite different propagation properties.
Fields therefore provide the variables for a local description, but do not by themselves settle causality. We must also choose dynamics whose propagation properties meet the causal requirements of the relativistic model.
statement: Field equations constrain quantities point by point; their propagation properties depend on the equations.

title: Distant influence through intermediate events
body:
Locality does not mean that distant systems can never influence one another. If one charge is disturbed, another can respond later because a disturbance has travelled through the intervening electromagnetic field.
In this description, the response is built from local field interactions and the time needed for propagation. There is no instantaneous instruction sent directly from one separated charge to the other.
The qualifications matter: local dependence says which quantities enter the equation at an event, while the additional causal condition limits how changes can affect distant events. Together they allow distant effects without requiring instantaneous action at a distance.
statement: Local causal theories allow distant effects mediated through fields rather than instantaneous distant commands.

title: Local dependence versus causal propagation
body:
In a relativistic causal theory, a physical signal emitted at an event must remain inside or on that event's future \cref{light cone}{sr.light_cone}. The invariant speed \cref{\(c\)}{sr.constancy_of_speed_of_light} sets the boundary: light follows it, while slower signals remain inside.
It is tempting to infer this restriction just because an equation is local, but a further check is needed. A local differential expression can have solutions in which a disturbance immediately develops a distant tail. The classical diffusion equation is a familiar mathematical example: it uses local derivatives, yet its solutions can spread instantaneously.
Electromagnetic wave propagation meets the appropriate finite-speed condition because of its dynamics and admissible physical solutions. So causality is a property we establish for the theory, not something obtained from locality alone.
statement: Relativistic causal dynamics restricts signals to the light cone; locality alone does not establish that restriction.

title: From action at a distance to fields
body:
Newtonian gravity was successfully described as action at a distance: a body's gravitational force depended directly on other bodies' positions. Faraday's lines of force and Maxwell's field equations offered a different, physically productive picture for electromagnetism. Changes could be carried through the field, region by neighbouring region, at finite speed.
Special relativity sharpened the reason to take this distinction seriously. An instantaneous distant influence would require agreement about what happened at the same time in separated places, whereas SR does not supply a frame-independent distant simultaneity. Field mediation made it possible to describe influence without relying on that agreement.
statement: Faraday and Maxwell made local field mediation central to electromagnetic physics.

title: Locality in actions and conservation laws
body:
A local \cref{field Lagrangian}{sr.field_lagrangian} is built from fields and derivatives at one event. When an appropriate field action is varied, it gives local \cref{field equations}{sr.field_equations}: relations that must hold throughout spacetime, event by event.
A local balance law also tells us more than a statement about a total quantity. For example, \cref{charge continuity}{sr.charge_conservation} relates the density change in a small region to charge flowing through its boundary. It explains how the balance is maintained locally, rather than merely asserting that the universe's total charge stays fixed.
These are uses of pointwise organisation. Any claims about symmetry, conservation or causal propagation still need their own argument or physical input; locality is not a substitute for those steps.
statement: Local densities and differential balance laws express field dynamics and transport event by event.

title: Changing the coordinates, preserving the physics
body:
Lorentz transformations translate the spacetime coordinates of an event from one inertial frame to another. They take the place of the familiar Galilean rules when we require both the \cref{Constancy of the speed of light}{sr.constancy_of_speed_of_light} and the \cref{Principle of relativity}{sr.principle_of_relativity}.
The key change is that time can no longer be shared unchanged by the frames. Time and position must transform together so that both observers measure the same vacuum light speed, despite their relative motion.
statement: Lorentz transformations reconcile inertial-frame equivalence with a common vacuum light speed.

title: Coordinate changes between inertial frames
body:
A Lorentz transformation is a linear change between standard inertial spacetime coordinates, using a common origin event and the same rod-and-clock calibration. It can include a spatial rotation, a boost (a change of relative velocity), or their combination. If we also shift the origin, the resulting affine change is called a Poincaré transformation.
For the usual continuous frame changes that preserve the direction of time, the boost coefficients follow from the \cref{relativity postulate}{sr.principle_of_relativity} and \cref{invariant vacuum light speed}{sr.constancy_of_speed_of_light}, together with homogeneity and spatial isotropy.
The resulting matrices preserve the \cref{Minkowski metric}{sr.metric_tensor} and \cref{interval}{sr.spacetime_interval}. This provides another, geometric way to characterise the transformations. In the construction used here, however, interval preservation is checked after deriving the boost from the postulates; it is not assumed at the start.
statement: Lorentz transformations relate inertial coordinates while preserving the Minkowski quadratic form.

title: Standard boost setup
body:
To isolate a change of velocity from other coordinate choices, consider a standard boost. Let inertial frame \(S'\) move at signed velocity \(v\) along the \(x\)-axis of \(S\), with \(\lvert v\rvert<c\). Both frames use identically calibrated Cartesian rods and Einstein-synchronised clocks, and their spatial axes are parallel, without relative rotation.
Choose the origin events to coincide at \(t=t'=0\). It is convenient to define
\[\beta\coloneqq v/c,\qquad
 \gamma\coloneqq(1-\beta^2)^{-1/2}.\]
Thus \(\beta\) expresses the relative velocity as a fraction of light speed, while \(\gamma\) is the Lorentz factor.
The moving origin follows \(x=vt\) in \(S\). For this arrangement, the boost mixes only \(ct\) and \(x\), leaving \(y'=y\) and \(z'=z\). Shifting the origins or rotating the axes would add coordinate changes that these standard-boost equations are not intended to include.
statement: The standard \(x\)-boost compares parallel, commonly calibrated frames with relative speed \(v\) and coincident origin events.

title: Why the inertial coordinate rule is linear
body:
Suppose two inertial observers describe the same experiment using their own position grids and synchronised clocks. We want a rule that converts one set of coordinates into the other.
We assume homogeneous space and time: no place or instant is distinguished. So the same event displacement should be converted in the same way wherever or whenever it occurs. With continuity (small input changes produce small output changes), this gives an affine coordinate rule. Affine means a linear combination of the coordinates, possibly with a constant offset.
The offset allows for different choices of origin. By choosing the same origin event, we remove it, leaving a linear transformation. Its coefficients depend on relative velocity, not on where the event happens. The new time coordinate can therefore contain both old time and old position terms; we have not yet fixed their coefficients.
The physical postulates do the remaining work. Light-speed invariance constrains the mixing, while the \cref{relativity postulate}{sr.principle_of_relativity.no_preferred_frame} requires a consistent inverse description. Spatial isotropy and common rod-and-clock calibration also enter when fixing the coefficients. These ingredients explain why the final rule is more than a formula chosen merely to preserve light rays.
statement: Homogeneity gives an affine coordinate rule; a shared origin removes its translation.

title: Deriving the boost from the postulates
body:
Take inertial frames \(S,S'\) with common units, shared origin and parallel axes, and let \(S'\) move along \(+x\) with signed velocity \(v\), \(\lvert v\rvert<c\). Put \(\beta=v/c\). Assume homogeneous space/time, spatial isotropy and Einstein-synchronised clocks.
We first use linearity to narrow down the possible coordinate rule. Since the moving origin must obey the condition \(x'=0\) when \(x=vt\), we can write
\[\begin{aligned}
x'&=a(x-\beta ct),\\
ct'&=b\,ct+d\,x.
\end{aligned}\]
The unknown coefficients depend on \(v\). We can constrain them by considering light travelling in each direction. By the \cref{light-speed postulate}{sr.constancy_of_speed_of_light.definition}, the rays \(x=ct\) and \(x=-ct\) remain the respective forward/backward rays \(x'=ct'\) and \(x'=-ct'\), on the continuous branch through the identity (the one reached without reversing the axes or time). Substituting these two rays into the coordinate rule gives
\[\begin{aligned}
b+d&=a(1-\beta),\\
b-d&=a(1+\beta),
\end{aligned}\]
Adding the two equations gives \(b=a\); subtracting them gives \(d=-a\beta\). So the mixing is fixed, but the common scale \(a\) remains unknown.
To determine that scale, now use \cref{inertial-frame equivalence}{sr.principle_of_relativity.no_preferred_frame}. Exchanging the laboratories gives the inverse boost with velocity \(-v\). Spatial isotropy and common calibration give the same scale for \(v\) and \(-v\). Applying the forward rule followed by its inverse must restore the starting coordinates. After substituting and simplifying, this requires
\[a^2(1-\beta^2)=1.\]
There are two algebraic signs to consider. At zero relative velocity the frames coincide, so \(a(0)=1\). Requiring a continuous change from that case, without reversing time or the axis, selects
\[a=\gamma=(1-\beta^2)^{-1/2}.\]
Substituting the coefficients back into our starting rule therefore gives
\[\begin{aligned}
ct'&=\gamma(ct-\beta x),\\
x'&=\gamma(x-\beta ct).
\end{aligned}\]
Notice what each input has contributed. Light-speed invariance fixed the mixing, while reciprocity and isotropy supplied the remaining normalisation. We have therefore derived the coefficients without first assuming the invariant interval.
\explanation{transverse}{Why are the transverse coordinates unchanged?}{The transverse directions also need checking. Linearity and symmetry about the boost axis allow a common scale \(y'=k(v)y,\ z'=k(v)z\). Applying the forward and inverse transformations must undo this scaling, so reciprocity requires \(k(v)k(-v)=1\). Spatial isotropy makes \(k(-v)=k(v)\), and hence \(k^2=1\). Since \(k(0)=1\), continuity selects \(k=1\). This is why the transverse coordinates remain unchanged.}
statement: Light-speed invariance fixes the mixing; reciprocity and isotropy fix the Lorentz factor.

title: The standard \(x\)-directed boost
body:
For standard inertial frames with parallel axes, common calibration and coincident origin events, let \(S'\) move at velocity \(v\) along \(x\). Set \(\beta=v/c\), \(\lvert\beta\rvert<1\), and \(\gamma=(1-\beta^2)^{-1/2}\).
With these conventions, the same event receives coordinates related by
\[\begin{aligned}
ct'&=\gamma(ct-\beta x),\\
x'&=\gamma(x-\beta ct),\\
y'&=y,\qquad z'=z.
\end{aligned}\]
To convert back, use the same formulae with \(v\) replaced by \(-v\). At \(v=0\), the coordinates agree, as they should. At low relative speed its leading spatial rule is the Galilean \(x'\simeq x-vt\), but the relativity-of-simultaneity term \(t'=\gamma(t-vx/c^2)\) cannot in general be discarded when comparing distant events. It is what allows simultaneity to differ between the frames.
statement: For \(\beta=v/c\), \(ct'=\gamma(ct-\beta x)\) and \(x'=\gamma(x-\beta ct)\).

title: Checking the invariant quadratic form
body:
Let \(S'\) be a standard \(x\)-boost of \(S\), with \(\beta=v/c\) and \(\gamma=(1-\beta^2)^{-1/2}\). Choose any two events. Since the coordinate rule is linear, subtracting their transformed coordinates gives
\[\begin{aligned}
c\Delta t'&=\gamma(c\Delta t-\beta\Delta x),\\
\Delta x'&=\gamma(\Delta x-\beta c\Delta t).
\end{aligned}\]
Now square these expressions and subtract them. The mixed time-space terms cancel, and collecting the remaining terms gives:
\[\begin{aligned}
c^2\Delta t'^2-\Delta x'^2
 &=\gamma^2(1-\beta^2)\\
 &\quad{}\times(c^2\Delta t^2-\Delta x^2)\\
 &=c^2\Delta t^2-\Delta x^2.
\end{aligned}\]
For the final equality, recall that \(\gamma^2(1-\beta^2)=1\), by the definition of \(\gamma\). Since \(\Delta y'=\Delta y\) and \(\Delta z'=\Delta z\), the full four-dimensional quadratic form is preserved.
So the derived boost preserves more than the two light-ray directions: it preserves this quadratic form for non-null separations too. Here that is a consequence we have checked, rather than a premise used to normalise the \cref{postulate-based derivation}{sr.lorentz_transformations.interval_condition}.
statement: Substituting the derived boost preserves \(c^2\Delta t^2-\Delta x^2\), not just the light rays.

title: A linear map preserving the metric
body:
In Cartesian inertial coordinates write \(x^\mu=(ct,x,y,z)\), with \(\mu=0,1,2,3\). Since a common-origin Lorentz frame change is linear, we can collect its coefficients in a matrix:
\[x'^\mu=\Lambda^\mu{}_\nu x^\nu.\]
The repeated upper/lower index is summed, so the formula says that each new coordinate is a linear combination of the old ones. The Minkowski matrix in the \(+---\) convention is \(\eta=\mathrm{diag}(1,-1,-1,-1)\). The condition that this measuring rule gives the same result after the transformation is
\[\Lambda^T\eta\Lambda=\eta.\]
The superscript \(T\) denotes matrix transpose. If we write the same condition with explicit indices, it becomes
\[\eta_{\alpha\beta}
 \Lambda^\alpha{}_\mu\Lambda^\beta{}_\nu
 =\eta_{\mu\nu}.\]
The matrix condition holds for rotations as well as boosts. If we also translate the origin, event coordinates acquire a constant offset. That offset cancels when subtracting two events, so their displacement still transforms by \(\Lambda\).
statement: A Lorentz matrix satisfies \(\Lambda^T\eta\Lambda=\eta\).

title: Relabelling rather than moving an event
body:
A passive Lorentz transformation changes the coordinate description of an event, not the event itself. We keep the physical occurrence fixed and ask which labels another inertial frame assigns to it.
In a \cref{Minkowski diagram}{sr.minkowski_diagram}, this looks like tilted axes being used to describe the same point. The event has not been dragged elsewhere in reality; its coordinates differ because the axes and the associated clock convention differ.
statement: A passive Lorentz transformation assigns new coordinates to the same spacetime occurrence.

title: Why simultaneity, clock rates and lengths change
body:
Our intuition suggests that events simultaneous for one observer should also be simultaneous for another. A Lorentz boost changes that picture, because it mixes time with the coordinate along the relative motion:
\[\Delta t'=\gamma\left(\Delta t-\frac{v\Delta x}{c^2}\right).\]
If two separated events are simultaneous in the first frame, \(\Delta t=0\). Their position difference \(\Delta x\) can still be nonzero, so the second frame generally assigns a nonzero time difference. This is relativity of simultaneity.
Clock rates and lengths involve particular event choices. For \cref{time dilation}{sr.time_dilation.lorentz_derivation}, choose two ticks on one moving clock: in its rest frame they occur at the same position. For \cref{length contraction}{sr.length_contraction}, choose events at the rod's two ends that are simultaneous in the measuring frame. Putting the appropriate condition into the same boost gives each result.
Thus the effects use different measurement conditions, not different transformation laws. Neither implies an abnormal clock in its own rest frame or a rod mechanically crushed by changing the observer's frame.
statement: Mixing time and space changes frame-dependent measurements while preserving their physical relationships.

title: Agreement about a fixed pair of events
body:
Choose two \cref{Spacetime events}{sr.spacetime_event} and ask how far apart they are in space and time. Different inertial observers generally assign different coordinate distances and elapsed times, so neither number alone provides their common answer.
The spacetime interval combines those measurements using the metric. For the same fixed pair of events, all inertial observers obtain the same interval square. It is this combination—not each individual coordinate difference—that they agree on.
statement: All inertial observers agree on the interval square for the same two events.

title: The metric square of a separation
body:
Using the \(+---\) convention, define the spacetime interval square between two events by
\[\begin{aligned}
\Delta s^2&\coloneqq c^2\Delta t^2-\Delta x^2\\
 &\quad{}-\Delta y^2-\Delta z^2.
\end{aligned}\]
Each \(\Delta\) is the second event's coordinate minus the first event's coordinate in the chosen frame. Thus the time difference contributes positively and the three spatial differences negatively.
The same definition can be written compactly using the \cref{Metric tensor}{sr.metric_tensor}:
\[\Delta s^2\equiv\eta_{\mu\nu}\Delta x^\mu\Delta x^\nu.\]
Here \(\Delta x^0=c\Delta t\), and the repeated indices are summed. The compact expression and the expanded formula perform the same calculation.
statement: With signature \(+---\), \(\Delta s^2=c^2\Delta t^2-\lvert\Delta\mathbf x\rvert^2\).

title: Removing the coordinate origin
body:
The interval describes the separation of two events, rather than the coordinates of one event by itself. If their coordinate tuples are \(x_1^\mu\) and \(x_2^\mu\), first subtract them:
\[\Delta x^\mu\coloneqq x_2^\mu-x_1^\mu.\]
Why take a difference? Moving the coordinate origin adds the same offset to both tuples, so that offset cancels in the subtraction. What remains is the displacement between the events, used in the \cref{interval calculation}{sr.spacetime_interval.metric_derivation}.
statement: Subtracting two event coordinate tuples gives the displacement used in the interval.

title: Evaluating the metric on an event separation
body:
Take two \cref{events}{sr.spacetime_event} with coordinate tuples \(x_1^\mu\) and \(x_2^\mu\), using \(x^0=ct\). First subtract the tuples, so that we describe their separation rather than either event relative to an arbitrary origin:
\[\Delta x^\mu\coloneqq x_2^\mu-x_1^\mu.\]
The \cref{Minkowski metric}{sr.metric_tensor.interval_contraction} in the \(+---\) convention is \(\eta=\mathrm{diag}(1,-1,-1,-1)\). We obtain the interval square by applying that measuring rule twice to the same displacement. In index notation, this contraction is
\[\Delta s^2\coloneqq
 \eta_{\mu\nu}\Delta x^\mu\Delta x^\nu.\]
Because the matrix is diagonal, only terms with matching indices survive. Its entries then give
\[\begin{aligned}
\Delta s^2
 &=c^2\Delta t^2-\Delta x^2\\
 &\quad{}-\Delta y^2-\Delta z^2.
\end{aligned}\]
There are two inputs to this calculation: the event pair supplies the displacement, and the metric supplies the combining rule. Since Lorentz transformations preserve the metric, all inertial descriptions of that same pair yield the same interval. We are using the metric to calculate a separation, not deriving the metric again from the resulting formula.
\optional_details{Expanding the repeated indices}{The repeated indices normally instruct us to sum over every pair of index values. Since the metric is diagonal in standard inertial coordinates, the off-diagonal terms vanish and only four terms remain: \(\eta_{00}(c\Delta t)^2+\eta_{11}\Delta x^2+\eta_{22}\Delta y^2+\eta_{33}\Delta z^2\). Substituting \(1,-1,-1,-1\) gives the interval formula.}
statement: Contracting an event displacement twice with the Minkowski metric gives its invariant square.

title: Timelike, null and spacelike separations
body:
For a fixed pair of distinct events, calculate
\[\Delta s^2=c^2\Delta t^2-\lvert\Delta\mathbf x\rvert^2\]
using the \(+---\) convention. The sign tells us how the time available compares with the spatial separation.
If \(\Delta s^2>0\), the pair is timelike: there is enough time for a slower-than-light connection. If \(\Delta s^2=0\), it is null or lightlike, as for events joined by a vacuum light ray. If \(\Delta s^2<0\), it is spacelike: a connecting signal would have to exceed \(c\).
Because the interval is invariant, changing inertial frame cannot change this classification. To distinguish future from past for a timelike or null separation, we also choose a time orientation; ordinary physical frame changes preserve it.
statement: Positive, zero and negative interval squares distinguish timelike, null and spacelike separation in \(+---\) signature.

title: Invariant does not mean conserved
body:
The word invariant compares different observers' descriptions of the same event pair. A Lorentz boost can change the time and spatial components they report, while leaving
\[\Delta s^2=c^2\Delta t^2-\lvert\Delta\mathbf x\rvert^2\]
unchanged. It does not make \(\Delta t\) or the spatial distance separately invariant, nor does it give every pair of events the same interval.
Invariant also differs from conserved. Conservation concerns what stays constant as a physical system evolves. Here we are holding the events fixed and changing the frame used to describe them.
An ordinary rotation preserving Euclidean squared length is a useful analogy: the components change while their combination does not. The essential difference is that Minkowski time and space enter with opposite signs.
statement: Invariance compares observers for a fixed event pair; it does not make all time or distance components equal.

title: Null light paths and clock readings
body:
For a vacuum light segment, spatial distance equals \(c\) times elapsed coordinate time:
\[\lvert\Delta\mathbf x\rvert=c\lvert\Delta t\rvert.\]
So the two contributions cancel in the \(+---\) interval formula, leaving zero interval square. These null directions form the \cref{light cone}{sr.light_cone}.
Now choose two events on one inertial clock. In its rest frame, both occur at the same position, so there is no spatial term. The interval square is therefore \(c^2\Delta t_{\rm rest}^2\). The clock's elapsed reading is called proper time for this straight history.
For a non-inertial timelike history, the clock follows a different path through spacetime, and we accumulate infinitesimal proper-time elements along it. The general \cref{proper-time construction}{sr.proper_time} matters because the accumulated clock reading need not be determined by the endpoint interval alone.
statement: Null segments have zero interval; a clock's timelike history accumulates proper time.

title: From separation to clock and causal geometry
body:
The interval gives inertial observers a common scalar for a fixed event pair, even though their separate time and distance measurements differ. Its sign identifies the causal type of the separation, its timelike infinitesimal form underlies clock time, and the same metric rule also contracts relativistic vectors.
These uses share a geometric structure, but do not make the interval a complete description of every situation. Different displacements can have the same square, just as different spatial arrows can have the same length. Also, an arbitrary curved clock history generally accumulates a proper time different from that obtained from its finite endpoint separation alone.
statement: The same metric square supports causal classification, clock time and relativistic vector norms.

title: A bilinear measuring rule
body:
Different inertial observers assign different time and space components to the same displacement. The metric tensor tells us how to combine those components into a quantity they can agree on.
It therefore acts as a spacetime measuring rule, especially for the \cref{Spacetime interval}{sr.spacetime_interval} and scalar products of \cref{Four-vectors}{sr.four_vectors}. Unlike an ordinary Euclidean ruler, however, it combines time and space with opposite signs. That difference is essential to its physical meaning.
statement: The Minkowski metric combines time and space components into Lorentz-invariant scalar products.

title: The Minkowski bilinear form
body:
The Minkowski metric is a symmetric, nondegenerate bilinear form on flat spacetime displacements. Bilinear means that it is linear in each of its two vector inputs; nondegenerate means that no nonzero vector has zero product with every vector.
In Cartesian inertial coordinates \(x^\mu=(ct,x,y,z)\), this atlas uses
\[\eta_{\mu\nu}\coloneqq\mathrm{diag}(1,-1,-1,-1).\]
Here the indices range over \(0,1,2,3\), and a repeated upper/lower index is summed. Thus, for displacements with components \(X^\mu,Y^\nu\), their scalar product is \(\eta_{\mu\nu}X^\mu Y^\nu\).
This form is preserved by \cref{Lorentz frame changes}{sr.lorentz_transformations}. The overall \(+---\) convention can be reversed if all related formulae are changed consistently; that is a different convention, not a different physical theory. Also, these constant diagonal entries belong to Cartesian inertial coordinates, rather than to every possible coordinate chart.
statement: In Cartesian inertial coordinates \(x^0=ct\), this atlas uses \(\eta_{\mu\nu}=\mathrm{diag}(1,-1,-1,-1)\).

title: Why time and space have opposite signs
body:
For a displacement with components \(X^\mu=(c\Delta t,\Delta x,\Delta y,\Delta z)\), the \(+---\) metric gives
\[Q(X)=(c\Delta t)^2-\lvert\Delta\mathbf x\rvert^2.\]
The minus sign makes an important difference. A displacement \((5,3,0,0)\), with components measured in metres, has \(Q=25-9=16\,\mathrm{m^2}\). But the nonzero displacement \((3,3,0,0)\) has \(Q=0\), because its time and space contributions cancel.
That cancellation cannot occur for a sum of four positive Euclidean squares. It allows null directions and the causal distinctions represented by the \cref{light cone}{sr.light_cone}.
The metric supplies the combining rule. Because Lorentz transformations preserve it, observers can report different components while obtaining the same scalar result.
statement: Opposite signs allow nonzero null directions and distinguish timelike from spacelike separations.

title: Constructing the invariant bilinear form
body:
Write an event displacement in Cartesian inertial coordinates as \(X=(c\Delta t,\Delta x,\Delta y,\Delta z)\), with components \(X^\mu\). We want a symmetric quadratic form \(Q(X)\) that all the derived \cref{Lorentz boosts}{sr.lorentz_transformations.boost_formula} preserve.
Spatial isotropy means that no spatial direction is preferred. So the three spatial squares must have the same coefficient, giving the form
\[Q(X)=a(X^0)^2+b\sum_{i=1}^3(X^i)^2.\]
The same symmetry rules out time-space cross terms, since such terms would pick out a direction in space. For an \(x\)-boost, write \(\beta=v/c\) and \(\gamma=(1-\beta^2)^{-1/2}\):
\[\begin{aligned}
X'^0&=\gamma(X^0-\beta X^1),\\
X'^1&=\gamma(X^1-\beta X^0).
\end{aligned}\]
After substituting these expressions into \(Q\) and expanding the squares, we find a mixed term
\[-2\gamma^2\beta(a+b)X^0X^1.\]
There is no such mixed term in the original form, so its coefficient must vanish for every displacement and boost speed. It follows that \(b=-a\): time and space must enter with opposite signs. The remaining terms agree because \(\gamma^2(1-\beta^2)=1\), with transverse components unchanged.
The invariance condition has fixed the relative signs, but leaves an overall scale. Choose \(a=1\), giving the \(+---\) convention. Then
\[Q(X)=\eta_{\mu\nu}X^\mu X^\nu,\]
with \(\eta=\mathrm{diag}(1,-1,-1,-1)\). The corresponding symmetric bilinear form uses these same coefficients for its two inputs. Thus we have obtained the metric signs from boost invariance and isotropy. We have not assumed an interval formula first and then used it to justify the metric that produces that formula.
\optional_details{Expanding the contraction}{Write \(\Delta x^\mu\coloneqq(c\Delta t,\Delta x,\Delta y,\Delta z)\). Since \(\eta_{\mu\nu}\) is diagonal in these coordinates, the off-diagonal terms vanish. The contraction therefore reduces to \(\eta_{00}(c\Delta t)^2+\eta_{11}\Delta x^2+\eta_{22}\Delta y^2+\eta_{33}\Delta z^2\). Substituting \(1,-1,-1,-1\) gives the usual interval formula.}
statement: Spatial isotropy and Lorentz boosts fix the Minkowski form up to an overall scale.

title: Changing index position with the metric
body:
The metric also lets us change the index position of vector components. This is called lowering an index. Starting with \(V^\mu\coloneqq(V^0,V^1,V^2,V^3)\), multiply by the metric and sum over the repeated index:
\[V_\mu\coloneqq\eta_{\mu\nu}V^\nu
 \overset{+---}{=}(V^0,-V^1,-V^2,-V^3).\]
So, in these coordinates and this sign convention, lowering leaves the time component unchanged and reverses the three spatial signs. The metric has mapped the original vector to an \cref{associated covector}{math.cotangent_space.metric_warning}. This is not a change of observer: the raised and lowered components have different transformation roles, related by the chosen metric.
Contracting the lowered and raised components then gives
\[\begin{aligned}
V_\mu V^\mu
 &\overset{\text{metric}}{=}(V^0)^2-(V^1)^2\\
 &\quad{}-(V^2)^2-(V^3)^2.
\end{aligned}\]
This is how the opposite time and space signs enter the scalar product through index notation.
statement: With signature \(+---\), lowering a four-vector index reverses the three spatial component signs.

title: An indefinite metric
body:
It is easy to read a four-component scalar product as though it were an ordinary Euclidean dot product with one extra coordinate. The Minkowski metric does not work that way: its time and space terms have opposite signs.
Consequently, a nonzero separation can have positive, zero or negative interval square. These are the timelike, lightlike and spacelike cases. In particular, zero Minkowski square does not imply that the displacement itself is zero; its nonzero contributions may cancel.
statement: A nonzero vector can have zero Minkowski square; the metric is not a positive Euclidean ruler.

title: How component changes preserve a scalar
body:
Write a displacement as a column \(X\). Another inertial frame describes that same displacement by \(X'=\Lambda X\). In \(+---\) inertial coordinates the measuring matrix is \(\eta=\mathrm{diag}(1,-1,-1,-1)\).
To calculate its square in the new frame, substitute \(X'=\Lambda X\) into the metric expression. Since the \cref{Lorentz matrix}{sr.lorentz_transformations.matrix_form} obeys \(\Lambda^T\eta\Lambda=\eta\), the factors simplify:
\[\begin{aligned}
X'^T\eta X'
 &=X^T\Lambda^T\eta\Lambda X\\
 &=X^T\eta X.
\end{aligned}\]
The middle line contains the changed components through the two factors of \(\Lambda\). The metric-preservation identity removes those factors, leaving the original result. So \(X^0,X^1,\ldots\) can change while their metric combination stays the same. Applying the same calculation to two different vectors preserves \(X^T\eta Y\).
The comparison must keep the geometric inputs fixed: we are describing the same displacement in two frames. We are not claiming that different displacements, or vectors changing during a process, all have the same scalar product.
statement: The identity \(\Lambda^T\eta\Lambda=\eta\) makes contractions agree between Lorentz-related inertial frames.

title: Minkowski geometry and Einstein's extension
body:
Minkowski's 1908 spacetime formulation made the invariant quadratic form central to relativity's geometry. In SR, Cartesian inertial coordinates express that fixed, flat geometry using \(\eta_{\mu\nu}\).
General relativity goes further: the metric \(g_{\mu\nu}(x)\) becomes a dynamical geometric field. It still determines intervals, causal directions and scalar products, but spacetime geometry is no longer fixed in advance to be Minkowski geometry.
One distinction is worth keeping in mind. Metric components can depend on position even in flat spacetime if we choose non-inertial coordinates. So variable entries alone do not demonstrate curvature. The GR advance is that geometry itself participates in the dynamics, not simply that a matrix has acquired position-dependent entries.
statement: GR makes spacetime geometry dynamical rather than fixing it as Minkowski geometry.

title: A causal map centred on one event
body:
Choose one spacetime event and ask which other events could be causally connected to it. The light cone organises the answer: its boundary marks events joined by light, while its interior allows slower-than-light matter or signals.
Events outside are spacelike separated from the starting event. There is not enough time, relative to their spatial separation, for a signal travelling at or below \(c\) to connect them. Thus the cone is a map of causal possibilities, not simply a picture of nearby and distant places.
statement: A light cone separates possible causal connections from spacelike-separated events.

title: The null boundary through an event
body:
Fix a vertex event \(O\) in flat spacetime. The light-cone boundary is the set of events \(P\) whose displacement from \(O\) has zero \cref{interval square}{sr.spacetime_interval}. The vertex itself is included as the zero-displacement case.
Once we choose which direction in time counts as future, positive time separation gives the future boundary and negative separation gives the past boundary. Timelike displacements lie inside the cones; spacelike displacements lie outside.
The word cone is sometimes used informally to include the causal interior too. Here, when we say cone boundary, we mean the null surface itself, so that lightlike and timelike possibilities remain distinct.
statement: The light-cone boundary consists of zero-interval directions from the chosen event.

title: Constructing the null surface
body:
Choose a vertex event and displacement components \((c\Delta t,\Delta\mathbf x)\). In the \(+---\) convention, the \cref{interval}{sr.spacetime_interval.definition} gives
\[\Delta s^2=c^2\Delta t^2-\lvert\Delta\mathbf x\rvert^2.\]
To find the light-cone boundary, set \(\Delta s^2=0\). The two squared contributions must then be equal. Taking the nonnegative spatial magnitude gives
\[\lvert\Delta\mathbf x\rvert=c\lvert\Delta t\rvert.\]
For \(\Delta t>0\) this is the spherical lightfront emitted from the vertex; \(\Delta t<0\) gives events that could send light to it. At each chosen time separation we obtain one spherical surface. As that time varies, these surfaces sweep out the full null boundary.
The chosen event tells us where to centre the construction; the interval tells us which separations to include. Notice that zero interval does not require zero coordinate separation: nonzero space and time contributions can cancel.
statement: Setting \(\Delta s^2=0\) gives \(\lvert\Delta\mathbf x\rvert=c\lvert\Delta t\rvert\).

title: Two halves of the null surface
body:
Fix an event \(O\) and choose the ordinary future time direction. Its future null boundary contains events with \(\Delta t>0\) and \(\lvert\Delta\mathbf x\rvert=c\Delta t\). A light pulse emitted at \(O\) can reach them.
The past null boundary instead has \(\Delta t<0\) and \(\lvert\Delta\mathbf x\rvert=-c\Delta t\). Light from one of those events can arrive at \(O\). The minus sign makes the spatial distance positive even though the time difference is negative.
Events in the timelike interior have a spatial separation strictly smaller than \(c\lvert\Delta t\rvert\). So there are two distinctions to keep separate: future versus past tells us the time direction, while boundary versus interior distinguishes lightlike from slower-than-light causal possibilities.
statement: The future and past cone boundaries have positive and negative time separation from the vertex.

title: Reading the causal regions
body:
For an event displacement, form
\[\Delta s^2=c^2\Delta t^2-\lvert\Delta\mathbf x\rvert^2\]
in the \(+---\) convention. If the result is positive, \(\Delta s^2>0\), then \(\lvert\Delta\mathbf x\rvert<c\lvert\Delta t\rvert\): the event is timelike-separated and lies inside a cone. If it is in the future, there is enough time for an appropriate slower-than-light history to reach it.
If the result is zero, the event lies on the null boundary. If it is negative, the spatial separation is too large for the available time: the event is spacelike-separated, outside both cones. A connecting signal would have to exceed \(c\).
These are statements about what is possible. An event inside the cone is not necessarily the result of an actual signal from the vertex; the geometry only says that such a causal connection is allowed.
statement: Timelike events lie inside the cone, null events on its boundary, and spacelike events outside.

title: Observer agreement about causal type
body:
The \cref{interval}{sr.spacetime_interval.metric_derivation} for a fixed event pair has the same value in every Lorentz-related inertial frame. So a positive, zero or negative value cannot change simply because a different observer describes the pair.
It follows that all these observers share the null boundary and the timelike/spacelike classification. Ordinary time-orientation-preserving boosts also keep future-directed timelike and null separations future-directed: a possible causal arrival cannot become its own earlier cause by changing frame.
A spacelike pair is different. Its temporal order can reverse between frames, but its interval remains spacelike. Changing the order of its time labels therefore does not create a possible slower-than-light causal connection.
statement: Lorentz-related frames agree on the sign of the interval and on the light-cone boundary.

title: Elapsed time matters as much as distance
body:
Outside the light cone does not simply mean far away. An event only a short distance away can be outside if too little time has elapsed for light to reach it. Conversely, a very distant event can be inside the future cone if enough time is available.
The relevant comparison is therefore spatial separation against elapsed time multiplied by \(c\). Distance and time must be considered together before deciding whether a causal connection is possible.
statement: Being outside the cone means insufficient time for a causal signal, not simply a large distance.

title: Why the boundary is drawn as a cone
body:
In one spatial dimension the null condition becomes
\[\Delta x=\pm c\Delta t.\]
Plot \(x\) horizontally and \(ct\) vertically with equal length scales. Each unit of \(ct\) then matches one unit of \(x\), so the two null lines make \(45^\circ\) angles on the page. If we stretch one axis relative to the other, the drawn angles change. The paths are still null; only the picture has been rescaled.
Now imagine allowing light to travel in a second spatial direction too. At each time its front is a circle, so stacking the circles gives a cone surface in a three-dimensional drawing. In full three-space-plus-time, each positive time slice of the future null surface is a sphere. We cannot draw all four dimensions on a page, but stacking those spherical lightfronts is the same construction in one higher dimension.
statement: Equal-scale \(x,ct\) plots show null directions at \(45^\circ\); extra spatial dimensions give the cone picture.

title: A working plot of spacetime
body:
A Minkowski diagram places events and histories on spacetime axes, letting us reason visually about light propagation, simultaneity and changing inertial frames.
It brings together the algebra of \cref{Lorentz transformations}{sr.lorentz_transformations} and the geometry of the \cref{Light cone}{sr.light_cone}. The picture is particularly useful for choosing the right events for a calculation, provided we remember that ordinary lengths and angles on the page are not themselves spacetime intervals.
statement: A Minkowski diagram displays histories and simultaneity choices in a reduced spacetime picture.

title: Events and worldlines on spacetime axes
body:
A Minkowski diagram is a spacetime plot showing \cref{Spacetime events}{sr.spacetime_event}, worldlines, light cones and, when needed, Lorentz-transformed axes. Usually we show only one spatial coordinate \(x\) and the time coordinate \(ct\).
Suppressing the other spatial directions makes the diagram drawable on a page. A point then represents an event and a curve represents a history through events, rather than a shape traced in space at one instant.
statement: A Minkowski diagram usually plots one spatial coordinate against \(ct\).

title: Axis scales and null slopes
body:
The vertical axis is usually \(ct\), rather than \(t\), so that both axes have units of length. If x and ct also use equal scales on the page, light rays satisfy
\[x\overset{\text{light}}{=}\pm ct\]
and appear as 45-degree lines.
This convention makes the causal structure easy to recognise without recalculating the interval every time. If the axis scales differ, however, the drawn light-ray angles differ too. The 45 degrees belongs to the plotting convention, not to a frame-independent Euclidean angle in spacetime.
statement: Light rays appear at \(45^\circ\) only when the \(x\) and \(ct\) axes have equal length scales.

title: Reading points, histories and speeds
body:
Use equal length scales, with \(x\) horizontal and \(ct\) vertical. A point marks one event. To follow a particle or clock through time, join its successive events into a \cref{worldline}{math.worldline.curves_and_coordinates}.
A vertical worldline has constant \(x\), so the object is at rest in this frame. A sloping straight worldline represents constant velocity. For a segment with finite \(\Delta t\), the spatial velocity is \(\Delta x/\Delta t\). Since time is plotted vertically, slower-than-light timelike lines are closer to vertical than the 45-degree null directions.
These visual rules use the chosen coordinates and scales. Another frame can change the coordinate slopes, and stretching the drawing can change their appearance, without changing which physical events make up the history.
statement: A point represents an event; a curve represents a history through events.

title: Constructing the moving-frame axes
body:
We can locate the moving axes by asking which events belong to each one. Use equal length scales on a plot of \(x\) versus \(ct\). Let \(S'\) move at signed velocity \(v\) along the \(x\)-axis of \(S\), with shared origin, \(\beta=v/c\) and \(\gamma=(1-\beta^2)^{-1/2}\).
The \cref{standard boost}{sr.lorentz_transformations.boost_formula} is
\[\begin{aligned}
x'&=\gamma(x-\beta ct),\\
ct'&=\gamma(ct-\beta x).
\end{aligned}\]
The \(ct'\)-axis is the history of the primed origin, so \(x'=0\). Its plotted line is \(x=\beta ct=vt\). The \(x'\)-axis is the set of events simultaneous with the origin according to \(S'\), so \(ct'=0\), giving \(ct=\beta x\).
The conditions follow from the meanings of the axes: points on a time axis have zero spatial coordinate, while points on a space axis have zero time coordinate. Once we choose the appropriate zero, the boost locates that axis on the unprimed plot. Marking ticks needs a further caution. Their calibration follows the Lorentz coordinates; equal Euclidean lengths along the tilted axes need not represent equal coordinate intervals.
\optional_details{Deriving the tilted axes}{For \(x'\overset{\text{boost}}{=}\gamma(x-vt)\), setting \(x'=0\) gives \(x=vt\), the \(ct'\)-axis. For \(ct'\overset{\text{boost}}{=}\gamma(ct-\beta x)\), setting \(ct'=0\) gives \(ct=\beta x\), the \(x'\)-axis. Thus each axis is found by setting the other primed coordinate to zero. In the usual equal-scale diagram, the axes tilt symmetrically toward the light cone.}
statement: The moving origin gives the \(ct'\)-axis; moving-frame simultaneity gives the \(x'\)-axis.

title: Euclidean page distance is not interval
body:
A Minkowski diagram uses ordinary graph paper, but its spacetime measuring rule is not the ordinary Euclidean rule. Page lengths and angles can therefore suggest comparisons that are physically wrong.
For instance, a drawn light-ray segment has nonzero page length but zero spacetime interval square. To calculate an invariant separation, use the metric and the event coordinates. The diagram helps organise causal relationships and coordinate choices; it does not replace that calculation with a ruler measurement.
statement: Ordinary lengths and angles on the page do not measure the Minkowski interval.

title: Different simultaneity slices
body:
The \(ct'\)-axis follows the moving frame's spatial origin. Lines parallel to its \(x'\)-axis collect events that this frame calls simultaneous. Since another inertial frame generally uses differently tilted axes, it also uses a different set of simultaneous slices through the same spacetime.
This helps us organise measurements before doing the algebra. A \cref{length measurement}{sr.length_contraction.measurement} selects endpoint events from one simultaneous slice. A \cref{clock-rate comparison}{sr.time_dilation.measurement} instead follows two ticks on one clock's history. The diagram shows why these are different choices, even when both calculations use the same boost.
We should read coordinate and causal relationships from the picture, then use the metric for quantitative spacetime measurements. Ordinary page lengths and angles do not supply that measuring rule.
statement: Tilted axes show how observers assign different space and time coordinates to the same events.

title: Read the stated plotting conventions
body:
Before reading numbers from a Minkowski diagram, check its units, scales and axis calibration. Unless these are stated carefully, the picture is most reliable as a qualitative guide: apparent Euclidean lengths and angles can mislead.
Useful questions are: which points are the events, which curves are worldlines, where are the lightlike directions, and which axes belong to each frame? Answering these first helps us choose the right coordinate conditions for a calculation, instead of trying to infer a spacetime distance directly from the page.
statement: Reliable quantitative reading needs explicit units, axis calibration and the metric rule.

title: Time carried by a clock
body:
Imagine carrying a reliable clock from one event to another. Its elapsed reading is called proper time. It belongs to the particular journey the clock makes, rather than to a distant observer's coordinate system.
An inertial frame also assigns a coordinate time to each event, using a network of synchronised clocks. These two descriptions agree for a clock at rest in that frame. For a moving clock, we need the spacetime interval to relate them.
statement: A travelling clock measures proper time along its own worldline.

title: Timelike length measured in seconds
body:
Proper time \(\tau\) is the time accumulated along a future-directed timelike \cref{worldline}{math.worldline.definition}. With signature \(+---\), the infinitesimal \cref{spacetime interval}{sr.spacetime_interval.definition} on such a path is positive. Define
\[ d\tau\coloneqq\frac{\sqrt{ds^2}}{c},\qquad \Delta\tau\coloneqq\int_A^B d\tau. \]
The integral follows the specified path from event \(A\) to event \(B\). An ideal clock travelling along that path records \(\Delta\tau\). Relating this geometrical quantity to an actual clock is a physical clock idealisation; it is not a claim that every real clock is immune to disturbance.
statement: Along a timelike worldline, \(d\tau=\sqrt{ds^2}/c\); elapsed proper time is \(\int d\tau\).

title: Coordinate time versus clock time
body:
An inertial frame measures coordinate time \(t\) with clocks synchronised throughout that frame. A moving clock passes different members of this network, so comparing its reading with \(t\) compares one clock with a coordinated collection of clocks.
Proper time instead follows that one clock. If it stays at rest in the chosen frame, successive ticks occur at the same spatial coordinates and \(d\tau=dt\). If it moves, the spatial separation between ticks contributes to the interval and \(d\tau<dt\). The usual \cref{time-dilation comparison}{sr.time_dilation.measurement} is the constant-speed case.
statement: Coordinate time belongs to a frame; proper time is accumulated by one travelling clock.

title: Deriving the clock rate along a path
body:
Take two neighbouring events on the clock's timelike worldline. The \cref{interval rule}{sr.spacetime_interval.metric_derivation} gives
\[ ds^2=c^2dt^2-|d\mathbf x|^2. \]
Write \(\mathbf v\coloneqq d\mathbf x/dt\) and \(v=|\mathbf v|\). Substituting \(|d\mathbf x|^2=v^2dt^2\) and the definition \(ds^2=c^2d\tau^2\) gives
\[ \begin{aligned}c^2d\tau^2&=(c^2-v^2)dt^2,\\ d\tau&=dt\sqrt{1-v^2/c^2}=\frac{dt}{\gamma},\\ \gamma&\coloneqq(1-v^2/c^2)^{-1/2}.\end{aligned} \]
We choose the positive root because both times increase along the future-directed path. This is a local relation: \(v\) may change as the clock accelerates. Only when its speed is constant can we take \(\gamma\) outside the integral and write \(\Delta\tau=\Delta t/\gamma\).
statement: For instantaneous speed \(v<c\), \(d\tau=dt/\gamma\); constant speed gives \(\Delta\tau=\Delta t/\gamma\).

title: Different journeys can accumulate different times
body:
Suppose two clocks leave together at event \(A\) and meet again at event \(B\). Each accumulates
\[ \Delta\tau=\int_{t_A}^{t_B}\sqrt{1-v(t)^2/c^2}\,dt \]
along its own path, with \(v(t)\) measured in one fixed inertial frame. Different speed histories can therefore give different elapsed readings, even though the departure and reunion events are shared.
This does not contradict invariance. All inertial observers agree on the proper time for each specified path; they need not assign equal proper times to two different paths. For example, a clock at rest in this frame accumulates \(t_B-t_A\), while one that travels away and returns accumulates less. Acceleration permits the reunion but is not an extra term in this proper-time integral.
statement: The elapsed proper time depends on the worldline, not just its endpoint events.

title: Not an observation delay
body:
A distant clock may look slow or fast because signals take time to reach us. That is a separate issue from the time the clock actually accumulates.
When two travelling clocks reunite, their readings can be compared side by side at the same event. No signal-delay correction can remove a difference that remains there. Proper time describes those accumulated readings, not the arrival rate of images or radio messages.
statement: Clock differences at reunion remain after correcting for light-travel delays.

title: No clock rides with light
body:
For a lightlike path, \(ds^2=0\). We can therefore say that its proper-time interval is zero as a limiting geometrical statement. We cannot use that zero as a clock parameter: dividing by \(d\tau\) would fail.
There is no inertial frame moving at \(c\), so a photon has no rest frame in which a little clock could be inspected. Proper time as an elapsed clock reading applies to timelike paths. This distinction becomes important when constructing four-velocity and treating massless particles.
statement: A null path has zero interval, but light has no inertial rest frame or travelling clock.

title: A frame-independent parameter for motion
body:
To describe motion geometrically, we need both a path and a parameter telling us how far along it the particle has progressed. Coordinate time would make that parameter depend on our chosen observer.
Proper time provides the alternative: every observer agrees on the clock's reading at each event of its path. Differentiating position with respect to this shared parameter gives \cref{four-velocity}{sr.velocity_four_vector.components}. The same invariant clock measure also makes worldline integrals useful in relativistic action principles.
statement: Differentiating position by proper time produces four-velocity without privileging a frame.

title: Clock time becomes geometry
body:
Einstein's 1905 analysis connected time measurements with clocks carried by observers and with explicit synchronisation procedures. It replaced the assumption that every observer merely reads a copy of one universal time.
Minkowski's spacetime formulation then gave elapsed clock time a geometrical interpretation: it is the timelike length of the clock's worldline, expressed in seconds. This brought clock-rate comparisons and the later clock paradox into a common framework, in which we compare paths through spacetime.
statement: Einstein connected time to physical clocks; Minkowski expressed elapsed time as worldline length.

title: Whose clock and which two events?
body:
A clock coasts through a laboratory. Choose two ticks on that clock and compare the elapsed times: the lab assigns a longer coordinate-time interval than the travelling clock records. This is time dilation.
Neither clock is faulty. The comparison uses different ways of timing the same two events: the travelling clock's \cref{Proper time}{sr.proper_time}, and the time assigned by the lab's synchronised network. Fixing the events first helps us keep those readings distinct. A light clock gives a geometric way to understand why \cref{Lorentz transformations}{sr.lorentz_transformations} require this difference.
statement: A moving clock records less time between its ticks than the lab clock network assigns.

title: The uniform-motion clock-rate relation
body:
Choose two ticks on one clock moving at constant speed \(v\), \(\lvert v\rvert<c\), through an inertial laboratory. Let \(\Delta\tau\) be the clock's own elapsed reading and \(\Delta t\) the time difference assigned by the lab's synchronised clock network.
For this fixed pair of clock events, the uniform-motion relation is
\[\Delta t=\gamma\Delta\tau,\qquad
 \gamma\coloneqq(1-v^2/c^2)^{-1/2}.\]
At nonzero relative speed, \(\gamma>1\), so \(\Delta\tau\) is smaller than \(\Delta t\). This is the sense in which the lab calls the moving clock slow. In its own rest frame, however, the clock still measures seconds normally; there is no local change in the definition of a second.
statement: For constant speed \(v<c\), lab time and moving-clock time obey \(\Delta t=\gamma\Delta\tau\).

title: One travelling clock and a lab clock network
body:
Let \(S\) be an inertial laboratory and \(S'\) the rest frame of a clock moving along the lab's \(x\)-axis at speed \(v<c\). Choose ticks A and B on that same clock.
In \(S'\), the clock is stationary, so the ticks occur at the same position. Its own elapsed reading is therefore \(\Delta\tau=\Delta t'\). In the lab, by contrast, the clock has moved between ticks, so A and B occur at different positions.
To time both locally, the lab uses one clock near A and another near B, synchronised in \(S\). Subtracting their readings gives \(\Delta t\). So the experiment compares one travelling clock with a coordinate-time network. It does not compare photographs of distant clocks, which would also involve the light-travel time to the camera.
statement: Two ticks on one moving clock are timed by different synchronised lab clocks.

title: A clock made from a returning light pulse
body:
A clock carries two mirrors separated by rest distance \(L\) perpendicular to its uniform motion. In the clock's rest frame \(S'\), a vacuum pulse leaves the lower mirror, reflects from the upper mirror and returns to the same lower mirror. Count one full outward-and-return journey as the interval between ticks.
Since the pulse travels a total rest-frame distance \(2L\), the \cref{light-speed postulate}{sr.constancy_of_speed_of_light} gives
\[\Delta\tau=\Delta t'=\frac{2L}{c}.\]
Here \(\Delta\tau\) is simply the elapsed reading of the resting clock. We have calibrated the clock before using any time-dilation formula.
In the standard boost to a lab \(S\), transverse coordinates are unchanged, so the mirror separation is still \(L\). As the apparatus moves horizontally through the lab, the pulse must follow diagonal paths to meet the mirrors. The unchanged transverse separation is an input from the standard boost; we do not need to assume longitudinal length contraction to set up this clock.
statement: A transverse light clock has rest-frame round-trip time \(2L/c\).

title: A diagonal path at the same speed
body:
In the lab, the whole light clock moves sideways while the pulse travels. The pulse must therefore reach the upper mirror's new position, rather than the position where that mirror was when the pulse left. On the return trip it must similarly meet the lower mirror at its later position.
The lab describes two equal diagonal paths, each longer than the mirror separation \(L\). If the full lab return time is \(\Delta t\), the clock moves horizontally by \(v\Delta t/2\) during each half-trip, while the light travels \(c\Delta t/2\).
