The key point is that light still has speed \(c\) in both frames. Since it takes a longer path in the lab, it must take more lab time. These diagonals describe the pulse inside the moving apparatus, not a signal travelling from the clock to a distant spectator.
statement: The moving mirrors make the lab light path longer while the pulse still travels at \(c\).

title: The transverse light-clock calculation
body:
Consider a light clock with transverse mirror separation \(L\), moving at uniform speed \(v<c\) through an inertial lab. Its rest-frame return time is \(\Delta\tau=2L/c\). In the standard boost the transverse separation stays \(L\), and the vacuum pulse still has speed \(c\).
Let \(\Delta t\) be its full return time in the lab. During either equal half-trip the apparatus moves \(v\Delta t/2\), while the pulse travels \(c\Delta t/2\). These distances form a right triangle: \(L\) is its vertical side, the mirror displacement is its horizontal side, and the light path is the hypotenuse. So Pythagoras gives
\[\left(\frac{c\Delta t}{2}\right)^2
 =L^2+\left(\frac{v\Delta t}{2}\right)^2.\]
The resting clock told us that \(L=c\Delta\tau/2\). Substitute this expression, multiply by four, and collect the \(\Delta t^2\) terms:
\[(c^2-v^2)\Delta t^2=c^2\Delta\tau^2.\]
Dividing by \(c^2-v^2\) and taking the positive square root (elapsed times are positive) gives
\[\begin{aligned}
\Delta t&=\gamma\Delta\tau,\\
\gamma&\coloneqq(1-v^2/c^2)^{-1/2}.
\end{aligned}\]
We have combined three inputs: the rest-clock calibration, the unchanged transverse separation and the common light speed. The whole path is inside the apparatus, so no signal-travel delay to a distant spectator enters this calculation.
As a check, \(v=0\) gives \(\gamma=1\), so the readings agree. For \(0<v<c\), \(\gamma>1\), and the moving clock records less elapsed time than the lab network.
statement: Using the same \(c\) in both frames gives \(\Delta t=\Delta\tau/\sqrt{1-v^2/c^2}\).

title: Why the comparison applies to ideal clocks
body:
A light clock is a useful model, but we want to know whether the result applies to other clocks too. An ideal clock measures elapsed time along its own history. Different ideal mechanisms resting together in an isolated inertial laboratory are assumed to agree once calibrated.
For uniform inertial motion, we can transform the two tick events without specifying the clock mechanism. The Lorentz rule therefore gives the same rate relation for any such clock. If a particular mechanism fails to keep time, that is an imperfection to model rather than a different SR transformation.
The idealisation still matters. Real clocks respond to temperature, forces and other environmental conditions. Accelerated histories also need the appropriate proper-time model; the uniform-motion argument alone does not analyse every physical clock under every condition.
statement: Ideal clocks at rest together agree on elapsed time; uniform motion does not privilege one clock mechanism.

title: Ten lab seconds and eight clock seconds
body:
A clock coasts at \(v=0.6c\). The lab assigns \(\Delta t=10\,\mathrm s\) between two ticks on its worldline. First calculate the Lorentz factor, then divide the lab interval by it to find the travelling-clock interval:
\[ \begin{aligned}\gamma&=\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-0.6^2}}=1.25,\\ \Delta\tau&=\frac{10}{1.25}\,\mathrm s=8\,\mathrm s.\end{aligned} \] The travelling clock records eight seconds while the lab clock network assigns ten. Conversely, an eight-second interval on that moving clock occupies ten lab seconds. Since \(\gamma\) is a ratio, it has no units. The difference in elapsed readings does not mean that a second has changed its local definition or that the travelling observer experiences their own clock as defective.
statement: At \(v=0.6c\), ten lab seconds correspond to eight seconds on the moving clock.

title: Clock rates from the inverse boost
body:
Let \(S'\) be the rest frame of a clock moving at constant velocity \(v\) along the \(x\)-axis of inertial lab \(S\). Use Einstein-synchronised clocks, and write the Lorentz factor as \(\gamma=(1-v^2/c^2)^{-1/2}\).
To make a definite clock-rate comparison, choose two ticks on that one clock. Because it is at rest in \(S'\), they satisfy \(\Delta x'=0\), and its own elapsed reading is \(\Delta\tau=\Delta t'\).
The inverse \cref{standard boost}{sr.lorentz_transformations.boost_formula} gives
\[\Delta t=\gamma\left(
 \Delta t'+\frac{v\Delta x'}{c^2}\right).\]
Since both ticks occur at the same primed position, the position term vanishes. Replacing \(\Delta t'\) by the clock reading \(\Delta\tau\) then gives:
\[\Delta t\overset{\Delta x'=0}{=}
 \gamma\Delta t'=\gamma\Delta\tau.\]
Notice the two parts of the reasoning: the boost supplies the frame relation, while the choice of events tells us which position difference is zero. Setting the unprimed rather than primed position difference to zero would select a clock at rest in the other frame, and hence a different comparison.
statement: The same-clock condition \(\Delta x'=0\) reduces the inverse boost to \(\Delta t=\gamma\Delta\tau\).

title: An alternative interval calculation
body:
We can obtain the same result from interval invariance, as an alternative to substituting directly in the inverse boost. Choose two ticks on one clock moving uniformly at speed \(v<c\) along \(x\) in an inertial lab \(S\).
In its rest frame the ticks have no spatial separation, so their interval square is \(c^2\Delta\tau^2\), where \(\Delta\tau\) is that clock's elapsed reading. In \(S\), their displacement satisfies \(\Delta x=v\Delta t\). The \cref{interval}{sr.spacetime_interval} must agree for this same pair of events in both frames. Equating the rest-frame and lab expressions therefore gives
\[\begin{aligned}
c^2\Delta\tau^2
 &=c^2\Delta t^2-\Delta x^2\\
 &=(c^2-v^2)\Delta t^2.
\end{aligned}\]
Factor out \(c^2\) and take the positive square root. Since we are comparing positive elapsed times, the result is
\[\Delta\tau=\frac{\Delta t}{\gamma},\qquad
 \gamma=(1-v^2/c^2)^{-1/2}.\]
This argument combines interval invariance with the chosen clock history. It reaches the result by another route, rather than adding a premise required by the boost proof. The finite endpoint relation here assumes a straight inertial history. If the speed varies instead, \cref{proper time}{sr.proper_time} is accumulated along the actual path.
statement: For the same inertial clock history, interval invariance also gives \(\Delta\tau=\Delta t/\gamma\).

title: How can each call the other's clock slow?
body:
Let \(S\) be an inertial lab and \(S'\) the rest frame of a clock coasting through it at velocity \(v\). The lab compares two ticks on that one moving clock with coordinate time assigned by its own synchronised clock network.
To reverse the comparison, we perform a different experiment: follow one clock at rest in \(S\) and compares its ticks with the network synchronised in \(S'\). We have now chosen two ticks on a different clock, so these are different event pairs.
There is a further reason not to combine the two comparisons as though they used one time standard: clocks synchronised in one network are not mutually synchronised according to the other. For the standard boost, with \(\gamma=(1-v^2/c^2)^{-1/2}\),
\[\Delta t'=\gamma\left(
 \Delta t-\frac{v\Delta x}{c^2}\right).\]
For two separated lab events simultaneous in \(S\), put \(\Delta t=0\). The expression becomes
\[\Delta t'=-\gamma\frac{v\Delta x}{c^2},\]
which is generally nonzero. So the frames disagree about the synchronisation of separated clocks, not about the result of one identical procedure. This relativity of simultaneity is what makes the reciprocal rate comparisons consistent.
statement: The reciprocal clock comparisons use different synchronised clock networks and different event pairs.

title: Clock time versus signal-arrival time
body:
A camera records when light arrives, whereas a synchronised coordinate-time network records when the clock events occur. The distinction matters: arrival rates can include Doppler effects as well as time dilation.
Correcting for the signal's travel time therefore does not remove the SR clock-rate difference. It removes an additional effect that would otherwise obscure the comparison.
Clocks that separate and later reunite can also compare their accumulated readings locally, without any remote signal delay. Such a reunion involves different worldlines, however, so one unchanging relative inertial frame cannot describe the entire trip. We must calculate the proper time along each clock's path.
statement: Correcting light-travel delay does not remove time dilation.

title: A length depends on the measuring frame
body:
Length contraction compares an object's rest length with the length measured in an inertial frame where it is moving. The measurements differ because each frame chooses its own simultaneous endpoint events.
Like time dilation, the effect follows from the \cref{Lorentz transformations}{sr.lorentz_transformations}. We do not need an additional rule that mechanically compresses the object; we need to specify carefully how each frame measures its length.
statement: A moving rod's measured length differs from its rest length because simultaneity differs between frames.

title: Rest length and moving-frame length
body:
Take a rod at rest in inertial frame \(S'\), aligned along \(x'\). Its endpoints have constant separation \(L_0\), the rest length. Frame \(S\) sees the rod move at uniform speed \(v<c\) along its length.
To measure the moving rod in \(S\), record both endpoint positions at the same \(S\)-time. Otherwise the rod would move between the two position measurements. The separation \(L\) obtained this way obeys
\[L=\frac{L_0}{\gamma},\qquad
 \gamma=(1-v^2/c^2)^{-1/2}.\]
Since \(\gamma>1\) at nonzero speed, the moving-frame length is smaller. Only the dimension along the standard boost is contracted; transverse coordinate separations remain unchanged. This formula describes a simultaneous-coordinate measurement, so it need not equal the apparent length in a photograph.
statement: For inertial motion along the rod, \(L=L_0/\gamma\); transverse dimensions are unchanged.

title: Choosing simultaneous endpoint events
body:
To measure a moving object's length in a given frame, we must record both endpoint positions at the same coordinate time. Measuring the back now and the front later would mix the length with the distance travelled between those measurements.
Suppose the rod rests in \(S'\), so its endpoints have fixed primed coordinates. The moving-frame observer in \(S\) chooses one event on each endpoint history, with \(\Delta t=0\). Because simultaneity differs between frames, those same two events need not satisfy \(\Delta t'=0\).
The \cref{Lorentz boost}{sr.lorentz_transformations} converts their coordinates, and a \cref{Minkowski diagram}{sr.minkowski_diagram} shows the different simultaneity slices. The length difference comes from choosing these different slices through the rod's history, rather than from deforming it in its rest frame.
statement: A frame measures length using the two endpoint positions at the same coordinate time.

title: Combining a boost with simultaneity
body:
Let a rod rest in inertial \(S'\) with constant endpoint separation \(L_0\) along \(x'\). In inertial \(S\) it moves at velocity \(v\) along \(x\), with \(\gamma=(1-v^2/c^2)^{-1/2}\).
To measure the length in \(S\), choose one event at each endpoint, simultaneous in that frame: \(\Delta t=0\). Let their unprimed separation be \(L=\Delta x\). Since the rod's endpoints have fixed primed positions, their primed spatial difference is \(L_0\), even though the events need not be simultaneous in \(S'\).
The \cref{boost}{sr.lorentz_transformations.boost_formula} gives
\[\Delta x'=\gamma(\Delta x-v\Delta t).\]
Now substitute \(\Delta t=0\), \(\Delta x=L\) and the fixed rest-frame endpoint separation \(\Delta x'=L_0\). These three measurement conditions give
\[L_0=\gamma L,\qquad L=\frac{L_0}{\gamma}.\]
At zero relative speed, \(\gamma=1\), and the lengths agree. At nonzero speed, \(L<L_0\). The difference follows from the event choices and the boost; we have not compared two photographs or assumed a mechanical squeezing of the rod.
statement: Putting \(\Delta t=0\) into the boost gives \(L_0=\gamma L\).

title: Different slices of one rod history
body:
A rod does not become physically crushed merely because an observer changes frame. In its own rest frame, its rest length remains \(L_0\).
The moving-frame measurement uses a different pair of endpoint events: the pair simultaneous according to that frame's clocks. Since simultaneity is frame-dependent, the resulting spatial separation can be shorter without any deformation of the rod in its rest frame.
statement: Length contraction compares frame-dependent endpoint events, rather than a physical crushing of the rod.

title: One object, four linked components
body:
A boost changes both the time and the spatial description of an event. Four-vectors extend this pattern to other quantities: their four components change together according to the same Lorentz rule.
The useful idea is that different component lists can describe the same object. This is similar to describing one arrow using rotated spatial axes, except that boosts mix time and space components as well. Counting four entries is not enough; their transformation behaviour is what matters.
statement: A four-vector has observer-dependent components linked by one Lorentz transformation law.

title: The Lorentz transformation rule
body:
A contravariant four-vector is a spacetime vector whose components transform between inertial frames as
\[ V'^\mu=\Lambda^\mu{}_\nu V^\nu. \]
Here \(\Lambda\) is the \cref{Lorentz transformation}{sr.lorentz_transformations.definition} for that frame change, \(\mu,\nu=0,1,2,3\), and a repeated index is summed. The zeroth component is the time component; the other three are spatial components.
The components may represent a displacement, a velocity or a momentum, with appropriate units. The physical quantity changes from example to example, but the transformation rule is shared.
statement: A contravariant four-vector obeys \(V'^\mu=\Lambda^\mu{}_\nu V^\nu\).

title: Spacetime displacement supplies the pattern
body:
Take two events and subtract their coordinates:
\[ \Delta x^\mu\coloneqq(c\Delta t,\Delta x,\Delta y,\Delta z). \]
An inertial coordinate change may include a translation as well as a Lorentz transformation: \(x'^\mu=\Lambda^\mu{}_\nu x^\nu+a^\mu\). On subtracting the coordinates of the two events, the same translation cancels:
\[ \Delta x'^\mu=\Lambda^\mu{}_\nu\Delta x^\nu. \]
Thus the displacement has a transformation law independent of the chosen origin. Other quantities earn the name four-vector when their components obey this same rule. This example motivates the definition; it does not require all four-vectors to have dimensions of length.
statement: Event differences transform homogeneously, even when the coordinate origins differ.

title: The transformation law is the test
body:
Suppose we write down four measured numbers in one laboratory. That tells us their values, but not how another observer should obtain their own four numbers. To call the list a four-vector, we must establish that the new values are given by the Lorentz transformation.
A useful test is to ask what happens under a particular boost. Time and the component parallel to the boost mix with the required factors; transverse components follow the same transformation as a displacement. A list of four unrelated temperatures would not acquire this behaviour merely by being written in a column.
statement: Four-vector status is a rule across frames, not a property of one four-entry list.

title: Why the scalar product is invariant
body:
The \cref{Minkowski metric}{sr.metric_tensor.definition}, with signature \(+---\), defines
\[ V\cdot W\coloneqq\eta_{\mu\nu}V^\mu W^\nu = V^0W^0-\sum_{i=1}^3V^iW^i. \]
Both vectors transform by \(\Lambda\). Substituting their transformation laws into the contraction gives
\[ \begin{aligned}V'\cdot W'&=\eta_{\mu\nu}\Lambda^\mu{}_\alpha\Lambda^\nu{}_\beta V^\alpha W^\beta\\ &=\eta_{\alpha\beta}V^\alpha W^\beta=V\cdot W.\end{aligned} \]
The second line uses \cref{metric preservation}{sr.metric_tensor.lorentz_preservation}: \(\Lambda^T\eta\Lambda=\eta\). So the invariance follows from two inputs together, the vectors' transformation laws and the metric that Lorentz transformations preserve. It is not a Euclidean sum of four squared components.
statement: If \(V\) and \(W\) are four-vectors, \(\eta_{\mu\nu}V^\mu W^\nu\) is frame-independent.

title: The metric associates a covector
body:
A vector and a covector have different transformation roles. Given a vector \(V^\mu\), the metric associates a covector by
\[ V_\mu\coloneqq\eta_{\mu\nu}V^\nu. \]
In standard inertial coordinates with signature \(+---\), this reads
\[ (V_0,V_1,V_2,V_3)=(V^0,-V^1,-V^2,-V^3). \]
This is not a boost or a new observer's component list. It is a metric-dependent correspondence between a vector and a \cref{dual-space readout}{math.cotangent_space.metric_warning}. Applied to another vector \(W\), that readout produces the Minkowski scalar \(V_\mu W^\mu\). The minus signs encode the measuring rule, rather than being decorative changes of notation.
statement: With \(+---\), lowering a vector index reverses the three spatial signs.

title: Not any four numbers
body:
Four numbers can always be placed in a column. The notation alone does not make them components of a spacetime vector.
For example, three spatial velocity components together with the constant \(c\) give the list \((c,\mathbf v)\), but that list does not obey the four-vector boost rule. Proper-time differentiation introduces an extra factor \(\gamma\), giving the actual four-velocity \(U^\mu=\gamma(c,\mathbf v)\). Always ask for the transformation argument, rather than relying on the appearance of the formula.
statement: A four-entry column is a four-vector only if it transforms correctly.

title: Displacement, velocity and momentum
body:
A \cref{position displacement}{sr.position_four_vector.displacements} describes separation between events. \cref{Four-velocity}{sr.velocity_four_vector.definition} describes a timelike tangent per unit proper time, and \cref{four-momentum}{sr.momentum_four_vector.definition} packages energy and spatial momentum.
Their components have different dimensions and meanings, so these are not interchangeable objects. What they share is the Lorentz transformation rule. That common structure lets the same contraction and frame-change methods be used in each case. Four-current and the electromagnetic four-potential provide later field-theory examples.
statement: Different physical quantities can share the four-vector transformation rule.

title: Writing equations that survive a change of frame
body:
If two four-vectors are equal in one inertial frame, applying the same Lorentz matrix to both sides preserves their equality in every other inertial frame. Likewise, an equation between invariant contractions does not depend on which components we used to calculate them.
This is why four-vector notation is useful: it makes the frame behaviour of an equation visible. It does not by itself prove a proposed physical law. That law still needs a physical argument or experimental support; covariance tells us how to express it consistently across frames.
statement: Equations between four-vectors transform together; invariant contractions give scalar relations.

title: Event coordinates relative to an origin
body:
A spacetime event specifies both where and when something happens. After choosing an origin event, we can package the four coordinates as \((ct,x,y,z)\).
The chosen origin matters: an event is a point of spacetime, while its position vector points from the origin to that point. Differences between event positions remove this origin choice and provide the displacements used in relativistic geometry.
statement: Choosing an origin lets us represent an event by a spacetime position vector.

title: Position relative to an origin event
body:
Choose an origin event \(O\) and inertial coordinates whose four values vanish there. The position vector of another \cref{event}{sr.spacetime_event.definition} relative to \(O\) has components
\[ x^\mu\coloneqq(ct,x,y,z). \]
For frame changes that keep this same origin event, these components obey the \cref{four-vector transformation rule}{sr.four_vectors.definition}. If the origin changes as well, the event coordinates acquire an additional translation. It is therefore important to distinguish the event itself from its origin-relative vector representation.
statement: Relative to an origin \(O\), an event has position components \(x^\mu=(ct,x,y,z)\).

title: Why the time component is \(ct\)
body:
The three spatial coordinates are lengths, whereas \(t\) is a time. Multiplying it by the constant light speed \(c\) gives a length \(ct\), so all four components have the same units.
This convention also puts the light cone in a simple form. For light travelling along the \(x\)-axis from the origin, \(x=\pm ct\). It does not make time physically identical to space: the Minkowski interval still gives the time component a different sign from the spatial components.
statement: Multiplying time by \(c\) gives all four position components dimensions of length.

title: What changes when the origin changes
body:
Suppose event \(P\) has position vector \(x^\mu\) relative to \(O\). If we choose a new origin \(O_1\), at position \(b^\mu\) in the same axes, its new components are \(x^\mu-b^\mu\).
Nothing happened to the event: we changed the reference from which we measure its position. This is the affine character of spacetime (points have no preferred zero). A separation between two events is unchanged by this translation, although its components can still change if we boost or rotate the axes. The invariant interval is a further contraction of that displacement, not the displacement component list itself.
statement: Changing the origin changes a position vector, while leaving the event and event differences intact.

title: Boosting positions with a shared origin
body:
Let frames \(S\) and \(S'\) assign zero coordinates to the same event. For \(S'\) moving at speed \(v\) along \(S\)'s \(x\)-axis, the \cref{boost equations}{sr.lorentz_transformations.boost_formula} give
\[ \begin{aligned}ct'&=\gamma(ct-\beta x),\\ x'&=\gamma(x-\beta ct),\\ y'&=y,\qquad z'=z,\qquad \beta=v/c.\end{aligned} \]
These are precisely the components of \(x'^\mu=\Lambda^\mu{}_\nu x^\nu\). The shared-origin condition removes a translation term; it is not an extra physical postulate. If the origins differ, the event-coordinate law is affine, but subtracting two such laws still gives the homogeneous four-vector rule for \(\Delta x^\mu\).
statement: With a shared origin, \(x'^\mu=\Lambda^\mu{}_\nu x^\nu\); translations cancel from differences.

title: Subtracting events removes the origin choice
body:
Given events \(A\) and \(B\), define their displacement by
\[ \Delta x^\mu\coloneqq x_B^\mu-x_A^\mu. \]
Under \(x'^\mu=\Lambda^\mu{}_
u x^
u+a^\mu\), the same translation \(a^\mu\) occurs for both events and cancels in the subtraction. Therefore \(\Delta x'^\mu=\Lambda^\mu{}_
u\Delta x^
u\), even when the frames use different origins.
This makes a displacement a natural input to measurements of separation. With the Minkowski metric, \(\Delta s^2=\eta_{\mu
u}\Delta x^\mu\Delta x^
u\) gives the \cref{invariant interval}{sr.spacetime_interval.definition}. The displacement is an object with frame-dependent components; its interval is an observer-independent scalar.
statement: \(\Delta x^\mu=x_B^\mu-x_A^\mu\) transforms as a four-vector independently of translations.

title: Position includes the time of the event
body:
Ordinary position answers “where?”. A spacetime position also answers “when?”. Two flashes at the same lamp but at different times therefore have different position four-vectors.
Likewise, two flashes simultaneous in one frame but at different lamps differ in their spatial components. A boost generally mixes those time and space differences, which is why a three-dimensional position vector alone cannot describe an event's relativistic transformation.
statement: Events at the same spatial position can still have different position four-vectors.

title: A nanosecond expressed as a distance
body:
Relative to a specified origin event, suppose a flash occurs at \(t=2\,\mathrm{ns}\) and \((x,y,z)=(0.30\,\mathrm m,0,0)\). Using \(c\simeq3.0\times10^8\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\),
\[ ct\simeq(3.0\times10^8)(2\times10^{-9})\,\mathrm m=0.60\,\mathrm m. \]
Its position components are therefore approximately \((0.60\,\mathrm m,0.30\,\mathrm m,0,0)\). The first entry records the time, converted to length units; it is not a fourth spatial coordinate. Changing the origin changes these numbers without changing the flash.
statement: At \(t=2\,\mathrm{ns}\), \(ct\simeq0.60\,\mathrm m\).

title: From event positions to particle motion
body:
Position components connect event descriptions with the rest of relativistic mechanics. Subtract two positions to obtain a displacement, then contract it with the metric to find an interval.
Along a particle's worldline, take the derivative of position with respect to its proper time. This produces \cref{four-velocity}{sr.velocity_four_vector.components}: an object whose definition combines the geometry of the path with the clock carried along it. The arbitrary constant origin drops out of this derivative.
statement: Event differences give displacements; proper-time derivatives give four-velocity.

title: A worldline tangent measured by its own clock
body:
A particle's worldline tells us which events it visits. To describe its motion at one event, we take a tangent to that curve and specify how it is parameterised.
For a massive particle, proper time supplies a parameter that all inertial observers agree on. Four-velocity is position change per unit of that clock time. Its spatial part is consequently related to ordinary velocity, but is not identical to it.
statement: Four-velocity describes a massive particle's tangent per unit proper time.

title: Position change per unit proper time
body:
Let \(x^\mu(\tau)\) describe a massive particle's timelike \cref{worldline}{math.worldline.definition}. Its four-velocity is
\[ U^\mu\coloneqq\frac{dx^\mu}{d\tau}, \]
where \(\tau\) is the particle's \cref{proper time}{sr.proper_time.definition}. Because a Lorentz frame change is linear on position differences and leaves \(d\tau\) invariant, it gives \(U'^\mu=\Lambda^\mu{}_\nu U^\nu\).
This definition applies locally whether the particle is coasting or accelerating. It requires a timelike path; a lightlike path has no nonzero proper-time increment by which to divide.
statement: For a timelike worldline, \(U^\mu\coloneqq dx^\mu/d\tau\).

title: Why coordinate time gives the wrong parameter
body:
Ordinary velocity divides a spatial displacement by coordinate time: \(\mathbf v=d\mathbf x/dt\). But a boost changes \(dt\) as well as \(d\mathbf x\), so the resulting components obey velocity addition, not a linear four-vector rule.
Proper time avoids this problem. Every observer uses the same \(d	au\) for the same short piece of the worldline. Differentiating \(x'^\mu=\Lambda^\mu{}_
u x^
u+a^\mu\), with constant \(\Lambda\) and \(a\), therefore gives
\[  rac{dx'^\mu}{d	au}=\Lambda^\mu{}_
u rac{dx^
u}{d	au}. \]
The translation differentiates to zero. This combines the position transformation and the invariant clock parameter into exactly the required four-vector transformation.
statement: Proper time is shared across frames, whereas coordinate time changes under a boost.

title: Combining position and the clock-rate relation
body:
Take the \cref{position components}{sr.position_four_vector.definition} \(x^\mu=(ct,\mathbf x)\) along a timelike worldline. The \cref{proper-time rate}{sr.proper_time.rate} supplies \(dt/d\tau=\gamma\), where \(\gamma=(1-v^2/c^2)^{-1/2}\) and \(\mathbf v=d\mathbf x/dt\).
Now differentiate the position and apply the chain rule:
\[ \begin{aligned}U^\mu&=\left(c\frac{dt}{d\tau},\frac{d\mathbf x}{dt}\frac{dt}{d\tau}\right)\\ &=\gamma(c,\mathbf v).\end{aligned} \]
Both ingredients matter: the worldline supplies the position derivative, while proper time supplies its common scaling. If the speed changes, \(\gamma\) changes too; the expression is still valid at each event.
statement: Using \(dt/d\tau=\gamma\) gives \(U^\mu=\gamma(c,\mathbf v)\).

title: Why every timelike four-velocity has norm \(c\)
body:
Use \(U^\mu=\gamma(c,\mathbf v)\) and the \(+---\) Minkowski metric. Their contraction is
\[ \begin{aligned}U_\mu U^\mu&=\gamma^2(c^2-v^2)\\ &=\frac{c^2-v^2}{1-v^2/c^2}=c^2.\end{aligned} \]
The cancellation is not a statement that ordinary speed stays fixed. Proper time normalises the tangent: from \(ds^2=c^2d\tau^2\), dividing by \(d\tau^2\) gives the same result directly.
As an accelerating particle's tangent changes, its time and spatial components change together while maintaining this norm. “Magnitude \(c\)” is a Minkowski-norm statement, not motion at light speed through ordinary space.
statement: With signature \(+---\), \(U_\mu U^\mu=c^2\), independently of the particle's speed.

title: Following the direction of a worldline
body:
Imagine marking a particle's worldline with ticks from its own clock. A short arrow between neighbouring ticks shows both a direction in spacetime and a change per unit proper time. Taking closer ticks gives the local tangent, four-velocity.
For a particle at rest in the chosen frame, that arrow points along the time axis. Motion tilts it towards the spatial direction of travel. Acceleration changes the tilt along the path. This picture is helpful, provided the norm is measured with the Minkowski metric rather than with the ruler used to draw the page.
statement: Four-velocity is the future-directed tangent with a scale fixed by the travelling clock.

title: Why \((c,\mathbf v)\) is missing a factor
body:
Differentiating position by coordinate time gives \(dx^\mu/dt=(c,\mathbf v)\). That looks like a four-vector, but its denominator is tied to one frame.
Changing the parameter to proper time multiplies every component by \(dt/d\tau=\gamma\). Thus the actual four-velocity is \(\gamma(c,\mathbf v)\). The factor is required by the transformation argument, not added merely to make the formula resemble relativistic momentum.
statement: Four-velocity is \(\gamma(c,\mathbf v)\), not \((c,\mathbf v)\).

title: At rest, the worldline still advances in time
body:
For a particle at rest in the chosen inertial frame, \(\mathbf v=0\), so \(\gamma=1\) and
\[ U^\mu=(c,0,0,0). \]
The spatial components vanish because the particle stays at one place, while the time component records its clock's advance. In this frame \(dt=d\tau\).
A boosted observer assigns nonzero spatial components to the same four-velocity, but still obtains \(U_\mu U^\mu=c^2\). Being at rest is frame-dependent; the normalisation is not.
statement: A particle at rest in an inertial frame has \(U^\mu=(c,0,0,0)\).

title: The kinematic input to four-momentum
body:
Four-velocity describes how a worldline is traversed, without yet specifying which forces or conservation laws govern the motion. Multiplying by a Lorentz-scalar mass gives \(p^\mu=mU^\mu\), the \cref{massive-particle four-momentum}{sr.momentum_four_vector.components}.
The transformation property follows from geometry. Identifying its components with physical energy and momentum, and conserving their total in interactions, adds dynamical input. Keeping those roles distinct helps explain both the usefulness and the limits of a purely kinematic derivation.
statement: Multiplying four-velocity by invariant mass gives the massive-particle momentum candidate.

title: Energy and momentum transform together
body:
Observers moving relative to one another assign different energies and momenta to the same particle. Four-momentum tells us how those measurements fit together.
For a massive particle, the construction starts with four-velocity and a scalar mass. To use the resulting object in physics, we also identify its components with measured momentum and energy transfer, and require conservation of total four-momentum in an isolated interaction. The mathematics and the physical identification are both needed.
statement: Four-momentum combines energy and three-momentum into one conserved relativistic quantity.

title: The energy–momentum four-vector
body:
For a massive particle of invariant mass \(m\), define
\[ p^\mu\coloneqq mU^\mu=(E/c,\mathbf p), \]
where \(U^\mu\) is its \cref{four-velocity}{sr.velocity_four_vector.definition}. Since \(m\) is a Lorentz scalar, \(p^\mu\) transforms as a four-vector. Its components are interpreted as energy divided by \(c\) and ordinary spatial momentum.
Here invariant means that observers agree on \(m\) for the same particle state. It does not say that a composite body's mass cannot change when its internal energy changes. The construction \(mU\) requires a timelike worldline; massless four-momentum is treated separately.
statement: For a massive particle, \(p^\mu=mU^\mu=(E/c,\mathbf p)\).

title: From four-velocity to momentum components
body:
The \cref{four-velocity construction}{sr.velocity_four_vector.components} gives \(U^\mu=\gamma(c,\mathbf v)\). Multiplying by invariant mass gives
\[ \begin{aligned}p^\mu&=mU^\mu=(\gamma mc,\gamma m\mathbf v),\\ \mathbf p&=\gamma m\mathbf v,\qquad E=\gamma mc^2.\end{aligned} \]
At low speed, \(\gamma\simeq1\), so the spatial part approaches \(m\mathbf v\). This calibrates \(m\) against ordinary inertial mass.
The time component has the right units for \(E/c\), but units alone do not establish that it is physical energy. The work–energy calculation verifies energy changes; conservation in interactions supplies the further physical identification.
statement: For a massive particle, \(\mathbf p=\gamma m\mathbf v\) and \(E=\gamma mc^2\).

title: Why the time component tracks work
body:
For a particle whose invariant mass stays fixed, use \(\mathbf p=\gamma m\mathbf v\), three-force \(\mathbf F\coloneqq d\mathbf p/dt\), and the mechanical work rate \(\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf v\). These are dynamical inputs, not consequences of coordinate transformations alone.
Let \(\mathbf a=d\mathbf v/dt\). Differentiating \(\gamma=(1-v^2/c^2)^{-1/2}\) gives \(d\gamma/dt=\gamma^3\mathbf v\cdot\mathbf a/c^2\).
\optional_details{Differentiating the Lorentz factor}{The speed may change with time. Write \(\gamma=(1-v^2/c^2)^{-1/2}\), where \(v^2=\mathbf v\cdot\mathbf v\). The product rule gives \(d(v^2)/dt=2\mathbf v\cdot\mathbf a\). Apply the chain rule: \[ \begin{aligned}\frac{d\gamma}{dt}&=-\frac12\left(1-\frac{v^2}{c^2}\right)^{-3/2}\left(-\frac{2\mathbf v\cdot\mathbf a}{c^2}\right)\\ &=\gamma^3\frac{\mathbf v\cdot\mathbf a}{c^2}.\end{aligned} \] The two minus signs cancel, and \((1-v^2/c^2)^{-3/2}=\gamma^3\). Thus speed increasing along the acceleration increases \(\gamma\); an acceleration perpendicular to velocity changes direction but not \(\gamma\) at that instant.}
Now differentiate the momentum and take its scalar product with velocity:
\[ \begin{aligned}\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf v&=\gamma m\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf v+mv^2\frac{d\gamma}{dt}\\ &=mc^2\frac{d\gamma}{dt}=\frac{d(\gamma mc^2)}{dt}.\end{aligned} \]
The simplification uses \(\gamma+\gamma^3v^2/c^2=\gamma^3\).
\optional_details{Simplifying the work rate}{Substitute the derivative just obtained and factor out \(m\mathbf v\cdot\mathbf a\): \[ \mathbf F\cdot\mathbf v=m\left(\gamma+\gamma^3\frac{v^2}{c^2}\right)\mathbf v\cdot\mathbf a. \] From \(\gamma^2(1-v^2/c^2)=1\), we have \(1+\gamma^2v^2/c^2=\gamma^2\). Multiplying by \(\gamma\) gives \(\gamma+\gamma^3v^2/c^2=\gamma^3\). Therefore \[ \mathbf F\cdot\mathbf v=m\gamma^3\mathbf v\cdot\mathbf a=mc^2\frac{d\gamma}{dt}. \] Since \(m\) and \(c\) are constant here, the last expression is \(d(\gamma mc^2)/dt\).}
So changes in \(\gamma mc^2\) equal the energy delivered by mechanical work. This establishes the changing part of the energy, while leaving an additive constant to be addressed separately. It must not be applied unchanged to heating a body, because then its invariant mass can change.
statement: For fixed mass, \(\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf v=d(\gamma mc^2)/dt\).

title: Recovering Newtonian kinetic energy
body:
Given the fixed-mass work relation \(dE=d(\gamma mc^2)\), integrate from rest to speed \(v\). The energy supplied in the acceleration is
\[ K\coloneqq E(v)-E(0)=(\gamma-1)mc^2. \]
For \(v\ll c\), expand \(\gamma\simeq1+v^2/(2c^2)\). It follows that
\[ K\simeq\frac12mv^2. \]
This is an important check: relativistic dynamics reproduces the familiar work required to accelerate a slowly moving mass. The subtraction also shows why the check alone does not determine rest energy. Any common energy constant cancels between \(E(v)\) and \(E(0)\).
statement: \(K=(\gamma-1)mc^2\simeq\tfrac12mv^2\) for \(v\ll c\).

title: What work alone leaves undetermined
body:
The work calculation fixes how much energy acceleration transfers to a fixed-mass particle. By itself, it permits \(E=\gamma mc^2+C\): differentiating would remove any constant \(C\).
Relativistic dynamics makes a stronger physical identification. It uses \(p^\mu=mU^\mu\), with mass calibrated by low-speed momentum, and conserves total four-momentum in isolated interactions. The time component then identifies the conserved energy as \(E=cp^0=\gamma mc^2\); the spatial components identify momentum. Radiation and fields must be included where they carry energy or momentum.
A separate arbitrary rest-energy offset cannot simply be inserted in the time component while leaving the spatial components unchanged: that altered list would not obey the same Lorentz transformation rule. The conservation law and this physical identification are tested dynamical structure, not a proof from the two kinematic SR postulates alone. A convention for the empty reference state is also understood when specifying total energy.
statement: Work fixes energy differences; conserved four-momentum supplies the relativistic energy identification.

title: Combining the metric and four-velocity normalisation
body:
The \cref{four-velocity norm}{sr.velocity_four_vector.fixed_norm} gives \(U_\mu U^\mu=c^2\). With \(p^\mu=mU^\mu\), both factors in a contraction acquire \(m\), so
\[ p_\mu p^\mu=m^2U_\mu U^\mu=m^2c^2. \]
Now expand the same contraction with the \cref{\(+---\) metric}{sr.metric_tensor.interval_contraction} and \(p^\mu=(E/c,\mathbf p)\):
\[ \frac{E^2}{c^2}-|\mathbf p|^2=m^2c^2. \]
This equation joins two inputs: the proper-time normalisation fixes the norm, and the metric tells us how energy and momentum enter it. Both energy and momentum change under a boost, but this particular combination does not. The fixed-norm condition is often called the mass-shell relation.
statement: \(p_\mu p^\mu=m^2c^2\) follows from \(p=mU\) and \(U_\mu U^\mu=c^2\).

title: The mass-shell relation in energy units
body:
The invariant-norm result is \(E^2/c^2-|\mathbf p|^2=m^2c^2\). Multiplying by \(c^2\) and rearranging gives
\[ E^2=c^2|\mathbf p|^2+m^2c^4. \]
All terms now have dimensions of energy squared. For positive-energy particles, \(E=\sqrt{c^2|\mathbf p|^2+m^2c^4}\). Setting momentum to zero gives the rest-energy case; setting mass to zero gives the massless relation \(E=c|\mathbf p|\).
This is often more useful than writing energy in terms of speed, because experiments and collision calculations naturally supply energy and momentum. It also avoids treating mass as something that grows merely because an observer chooses a different frame.
statement: \(E^2=c^2|\mathbf p|^2+m^2c^4\) connects measured energy, momentum and invariant mass.

title: Different energies describe the same state
body:
A particle at rest in one frame has zero spatial momentum there. An observer moving relative to it measures nonzero momentum and a larger energy. Both descriptions can be correct because energy and momentum are components, not Lorentz scalars.
The invariant relation \(E^2-c^2|\mathbf p|^2=m^2c^4\) ensures that both observers infer the same \(m\). Increasing energy by changing observer is therefore different from supplying internal energy to a body. In the first case only the description changes; in the second the physical state changes and its invariant mass may change too.
statement: A boost changes energy and momentum together while preserving invariant mass.

title: A nonzero time component at rest
body:
In a massive particle's rest frame, \(\mathbf v=0\) and \(\gamma=1\). Substitution into \(p^\mu=m\gamma(c,\mathbf v)\) gives
\[ p^\mu=(mc,\mathbf0),\qquad E_0=cp^0=mc^2. \]
The particle has no bulk kinetic energy in this frame, yet its energy component is nonzero. This is the rest energy, whose physical meaning is developed in \cref{mass–energy equivalence}{sr.mass_energy_equivalence.definition}.
The conclusion uses the identification of four-momentum with physical energy and momentum, not just the fact that a four-vector can have a nonzero time component.
statement: At rest, \(p^\mu=(mc,\mathbf0)\) and the energy component gives \(E_0=mc^2\).

title: Momentum needs the Lorentz factor
body:
Writing Newtonian momentum \(m\mathbf v\) beside a number called energy does not produce a four-vector. The entries must transform together under boosts.
For a massive particle they are \((\gamma mc,\gamma m\mathbf v)\). The factor \(\gamma\) is essential at high speed; at low speed it tends to one, recovering Newtonian momentum. We keep \(m\) for invariant mass rather than hiding this factor inside an observer-dependent “relativistic mass”. This leaves the distinction between changing frame and changing a body's internal state explicit.
statement: Relativistic spatial momentum is \(\gamma m\mathbf v\), with \(m\) invariant.

title: Light has momentum without a rest frame
body:
The expression \(p^\mu=mU^\mu\) uses proper time along a timelike worldline. A massless particle has no such clock parameter, so inserting \(m=0\) into that construction is not a valid way to find its momentum.
Instead, massless energy–momentum is a future-directed null four-vector, satisfying
\[ p_\mu p^\mu=0,\qquad E=c|\mathbf p|. \]
For a light pulse, electrodynamics supplies the same energy–momentum relation and its physical interpretation. Its energy can be nonzero even though invariant mass is zero. The pulse has momentum in its direction of travel and has no inertial rest frame.
statement: A massless particle has \(E=c|\mathbf p|\), but its four-momentum cannot be constructed as \(mU\).

title: One conservation law for energy and momentum
body:
For an isolated interaction, add the four-momenta of all participating particles and fields. The physical conservation law states that this total is the same before and after.
Its time component expresses energy conservation; its three spatial components express momentum conservation. Because the total transforms as a four-vector, the same equality holds in every inertial frame. This is the practical bridge from spacetime geometry to collision calculations and, through the invariant norm, to rest energy.
statement: Conservation of total four-momentum expresses energy and momentum conservation in every inertial frame.

title: Why should a resting body have energy?
body:
A resting body has no kinetic energy as a whole, but it can still contain thermal motion, strained material, chemical energy or trapped radiation. Rest energy is the energy of that whole state when its total momentum is zero.
Mass–energy equivalence says \(E_0=Mc^2\). Here \(M\) is invariant mass: all inertial observers agree on it for the same physical state. Invariant does not mean constant or conserved. Supplying internal energy changes the state and can change its mass.
There are two useful questions to ask. How does the result follow from the physical energy–momentum four-vector? And why should energy retained inside a body contribute to its inertia? The first has a compact mathematical answer; the equal-light-pulse experiment helps make the second less mysterious.
statement: A body can store and release energy without moving as a whole; its rest mass measures that energy.

title: Rest energy is not kinetic energy
body:
For a massive particle, or a complete body considered in uniform bulk motion, write the rest energy as \(E_0\), the energy in the chosen frame as \(E\), and their difference as the bulk kinetic energy \(K\):
\[ \begin{aligned}E_0&=mc^2,\\ E&=\gamma mc^2,\\ K&=E-E_0=(\gamma-1)mc^2.\end{aligned} \]
Here \(v\) is the speed of the particle or the body's centre of momentum, and \(\gamma=(1-v^2/c^2)^{-1/2}\). At rest, \(K=0\), but \(E=E_0\) need not be zero.
Changing observer changes the bulk kinetic energy, not the mass of that same physical state. Heating a body is different: it changes internal energy, so even an observer in its rest frame measures a different \(E_0\). The particles inside need not be individually at rest when the body as a whole is.
statement: \(E=E_0+K\), with \(E_0=mc^2\) and \(K=(\gamma-1)mc^2\).

title: Rest energy and invariant mass
body:
Mass–energy equivalence relates a system's invariant mass \(M\) to its energy \(E_0\) in the frame where its total spatial momentum vanishes:
\[ E_0=Mc^2. \]
For a single massive particle, write \(m\) instead of \(M\). For a composite body, include the energy of its contents, motion, fields and interactions within the specified system. Rest energy is the total energy in this frame, not just energy available for extraction.
In any inertial frame, the equivalent energy–momentum relation is
\[ E^2-c^2|\mathbf P|^2=M^2c^4. \]
A system with null total four-momentum, such as a single light pulse in vacuum, has no rest frame. It is therefore not an example of a body sitting at rest with zero energy.
statement: A system with a rest frame has \(E_0=Mc^2\), where \(M\) is its invariant mass.

title: From the physical four-momentum to rest energy
body:
Use the \cref{physical energy–momentum identification}{sr.momentum_four_vector.energy_physical_input}: \(P^\mu=(E/c,\mathbf P)\), with total four-momentum conserved for an isolated system. Its time component is physical energy, not merely a fourth number appended to momentum.
For a massive particle, \(p^\mu=mU^\mu\) and \(U_\mu U^\mu=c^2\). For a system with timelike total four-momentum, define its invariant mass \(M>0\) through the corresponding \cref{norm relation}{sr.momentum_four_vector.invariant_norm}. With signature \(+---\),
\[ \begin{aligned}P_\mu P^\mu&=\frac{E^2}{c^2}-|\mathbf P|^2=M^2c^2,\\ E^2&=c^2|\mathbf P|^2+M^2c^4.\end{aligned} \]
Now choose the system's centre-of-momentum frame, where \(\mathbf P=0\). The same equation becomes \(E_0^2=M^2c^4\). Taking the positive-energy branch gives
\[ E_0=Mc^2. \]
Thus the result combines the physical meaning of four-momentum, its invariant norm and a definite rest-frame condition. The symbol \(M\) agrees with inertial mass: for the same complete system in a slowly moving frame, \(\mathbf P\simeq M\mathbf v\). Geometry organises these inputs; it does not replace the conservation law.
statement: The invariant norm of conserved four-momentum gives \(E_0=Mc^2\) when total momentum is zero.

title: Light leaves without a kick
body:
Imagine a resting body sending out two equal light pulses in opposite directions. Each carries energy \(L/2\). Their momenta cancel, so the body does not recoil: it is still at rest after losing energy \(L\). Nothing in this frame looks like a loss of bulk kinetic energy.
Now watch the same experiment from a frame in which the body moves. The two pulses have different Doppler shifts. One loses energy and the other gains it, but the gains and losses do not cancel exactly: together they carry \(\gamma L\), which is larger than \(L\).
The moving observer therefore assigns a larger energy loss to the body. The extra part, \((\gamma-1)L\), is a loss of its kinetic energy. Its speed is unchanged, so the natural explanation is that the body's inertia has decreased. Comparing the slow-speed kinetic energies makes that inference quantitative without first assuming \(E_0=Mc^2\).
\optional_details{Why the light carries gamma times L}{Choose a boost along the pulse axis with speed \(v\), and \(\beta=v/c\). The \cref{energy transformation}{sr.momentum_four_vector.energy_transformation} is \(E'=\gamma(E-vp_x)\). Each pulse has \(p_x=\pm L/(2c)\), so
\[ \begin{aligned}L'_+&=\frac{\gamma L}{2}(1-\beta),\\ L'_-&=\frac{\gamma L}{2}(1+\beta),\\ L'_++L'_-&=\gamma L.\end{aligned} \]
The signs depend on which pulse we label plus; the sum does not. The light-energy rule can also be obtained from relativistic electrodynamics. In either form it is physical input about radiation, not an assumption of the emitting body's rest-energy formula.}
statement: Symmetric light emission leaves a body at rest, yet another observer sees a loss of kinetic energy.

title: Inferring inertia from two energy balances
body:
A body emits two equal, opposite light pulses with total energy \(L\) in its rest frame. It does not recoil. In a frame moving at speed \(v\) along the pulse axis, the \cref{light energy transformation}{sr.momentum_four_vector.energy_transformation} gives the combined pulse energy \(\gamma L\), where \(\gamma=(1-v^2/c^2)^{-1/2}\).
Call the body's rest-frame energies before and after \(E_{\rm b},E_{\rm a}\), and its energies in the moving frame \(H_{\rm b},H_{\rm a}\). Conservation of energy applied to body plus radiation in each frame gives
\[ \begin{aligned}E_{\rm b}-E_{\rm a}&=L,\\ H_{\rm b}-H_{\rm a}&=\gamma L.\end{aligned} \]
Subtract the first balance from the second. Since moving energy minus rest energy is kinetic energy, the result is
\[ K_{\rm b}-K_{\rm a}=(\gamma-1)L. \]
\optional_details{Why subtracting isolates kinetic energy}{Within a consistent energy convention, \(H-E\) is the work needed to bring that body's state from rest to speed \(v\), namely its kinetic energy. A common offset \(C\) between conventions cancels:
\[ \begin{aligned}&(H_{\rm b}-E_{\rm b})-(H_{\rm a}-E_{\rm a})\\ &\quad=(K_{\rm b}+C)-(K_{\rm a}+C)\\ &\quad=K_{\rm b}-K_{\rm a}.\end{aligned} \]
The same convention must be used before and after emission. Assigning a new arbitrary energy zero to each state would invalidate the comparison.}
Now use a slow relative speed. Inertial mass is measured by \(K\simeq\tfrac12Mv^2\), while \(\gamma-1\simeq v^2/(2c^2)\). Comparing the leading coefficients gives
\[ \begin{aligned}\tfrac12(M_{\rm b}-M_{\rm a})v^2&\simeq\frac{L}{2c^2}v^2,\\ M_{\rm b}-M_{\rm a}&=\frac{L}{c^2}.\end{aligned} \]
The approximation is used to identify the low-speed inertia coefficient; the inferred coefficient is \(L/c^2\). This route establishes a change in mass from a change in rest energy. Its inputs are radiation's energy transformation, energy conservation and the Newtonian limit. It does not alone fix an absolute rest-energy zero; the full four-momentum identification supplies the relation \(E_0=Mc^2\).
statement: Equal light pulses carrying energy \(L\) reduce the emitter's inertial mass by \(L/c^2\).

title: Why zero momentum leaves nonzero energy
body:
Given the physical energy–momentum relation
\[ E^2=c^2|\mathbf P|^2+M^2c^4, \]
choose the system's rest frame. Its total momentum is zero, so the momentum term vanishes:
\[ \begin{aligned}E_0^2&=M^2c^4,\\ E_0&=Mc^2\qquad\text{(positive-energy branch).}\end{aligned} \]
What vanishes is bulk momentum, not the invariant norm of four-momentum. The nonzero time component remains. This is why “at rest” cannot be read as “has no energy”.
For a composite body, total momentum can be zero while constituents move inside it. Their internal energies are included in \(E_0\), rather than being removed by choosing the body's rest frame.
statement: Setting \(\mathbf P=0\) in the mass-shell relation gives the positive root \(E_0=Mc^2\).

title: The mass belongs to the whole system
body:
Choose exactly what belongs to the system, and let its total energy and momentum be \(E_{\rm tot}\) and \(\mathbf P_{\rm tot}\). Its invariant mass satisfies
\[ M^2c^4=E_{\rm tot}^2-c^2|\mathbf P_{\rm tot}|^2. \]
In the centre-of-momentum frame, opposite internal momenta can cancel while their energies add. Thermal motion and trapped radiation therefore contribute to \(M\), even though the system has no bulk momentum. Interaction energies matter too: a bound state can have less mass than its separated constituents when formation releases energy to the surroundings.
Consequently \(M\) is not generally the sum of the constituents' individual rest masses. Include containers, stresses and interaction fields when they are needed for a complete body. For the complete isolated system, conserved total four-momentum means conserved invariant mass; energy exchange can change the mass of a chosen subsystem.
statement: Internal motion, fields and binding contribute to system mass; constituent masses need not add.

title: A heated sealed box
body:
Choose the box, its walls and contents as the system. Supply energy, for example by absorbing equal light pulses from opposite directions, then seal it and let it settle. Compare states at rest, with no net momentum added and no matter entering or leaving.
Would the warmer box resist acceleration more strongly? No new particles need have entered. What changed is their internal motion and the energy stored within the walls and contents. The box is a useful way to pose the puzzle, but temperature alone does not prove the answer.
The \cref{two-pulse inertia argument}{sr.mass_energy_equivalence.light_inertia} supplies the missing reasoning: reversing the emission experiment shows why retained energy adds inertia. Once that relation is established, energy \(Q\) retained by the box increases its mass by \(Q/c^2\). If any energy escapes, use the net retained amount. Accelerating the whole box is a different operation: that changes its bulk kinetic energy, not its rest energy.
statement: Energy retained inside a resting box contributes to its inertia, even when no matter is added.

title: How much mass does stored energy add?
body:
Suppose a box starts and ends at rest and retains \(Q=90\,\mathrm{kJ}=9.0\times10^4\,\mathrm J\), with no matter added. Once the rest-energy relation is established, apply it to the change of state:
\[ \begin{aligned}\Delta M&=\frac{Q}{c^2}\\ &\simeq\frac{9.0\times10^4}{(3.0\times10^8)^2}\,\mathrm{kg}\\ &=1.0\times10^{-12}\,\mathrm{kg}.\end{aligned} \]
This is one nanogram, a tiny mass change for an everyday amount of heating. Its small size comes from dividing by the enormous factor \(c^2\), not from the relation being only approximate in principle.
If the box later radiates away that energy and returns to its original state, it loses the corresponding mass. For the larger isolated system containing both box and escaped radiation, total energy–momentum remains conserved.
statement: Retaining \(90\,\mathrm{kJ}\) increases a resting box's mass by about one nanogram.

title: Not a magic substance conversion
body:
“Mass turns into energy” can be convenient shorthand for a reaction that releases rest energy. Taken literally, it suggests two different substances being exchanged, which is misleading.
Mass characterises the energy–momentum of a specified system. If a nucleus forms a more tightly bound state and radiation escapes, the remaining nucleus has lower mass. If the system includes that radiation as well, total energy–momentum is still conserved. The useful questions are therefore what system we mean, which state it is in, and where the released energy goes.
A body's entire rest energy is not necessarily available to extract. The accessible amount depends on which physical transitions and final states are possible.
statement: Mass measures a system's rest energy; it is not a separate substance transformed into energy.

title: Energy loss and mass change have the same sign
body:
Compare two states of the same chosen system, each in its centre-of-momentum frame. Define changes as final minus initial. Since \(E_0=Mc^2\) for each state,
\[ \Delta M=\frac{\Delta E_0}{c^2}. \]
If the body loses rest energy, \(\Delta E_0<0\), so its mass decreases. If it retains supplied energy, both changes are positive. Nothing here requires an unchanged particle count to imply unchanged mass.
For example, a charged capacitor includes the stored electric field energy in its total rest energy. Compare the complete capacitor before and after charging, including its mechanical supports and any other changed energies. The mass increase is the net retained energy divided by \(c^2\).
statement: For states compared at rest, \(\Delta M=\Delta E_0/c^2\).

title: Rest energy is not every observer's total energy
body:
The famous expression \(Mc^2\) gives rest energy. A frame in which the body moves assigns \(E=\gamma Mc^2\), and the excess is its bulk kinetic energy.
Do not infer that \(M\) increased merely because this observer measures more energy. For the same state, the observer also measures momentum, and the combination
\[ E^2-c^2|\mathbf P|^2=M^2c^4 \]
stays fixed. Supplying internal energy, by contrast, changes the physical state and its rest mass. For a single massless particle, \(E=c|\mathbf p|\); there is no rest frame in which to apply a massive-body rest-energy formula.
statement: A moving massive body has \(E=\gamma Mc^2\); \(Mc^2\) is its rest energy.

title: Einstein's 1905 light-emission argument
body:
In September 1905, Einstein considered a body emitting equal light pulses in opposite directions. He used the transformation of light energy from his earlier relativity paper and compared energy conservation in the body's rest frame with conservation in a moving frame.
The difference between those balances gave a change in kinetic energy. Its low-speed behaviour implied that emitting energy \(L\) reduces inertial mass by \(L/c^2\). This was a physical argument about radiation and inertia, not simply an algebraic substitution into an already assumed rest-energy formula.
The later four-momentum formulation expresses the broader relation compactly and extends the bookkeeping to complete systems. It is useful to distinguish that modern formulation from the specific argument in the 1905 note.
statement: Einstein inferred a change in inertia from radiation loss, using energy balances in two frames.

title: Why reaction masses do not simply add
body:
In a reaction, the sum of the final particles' rest masses can differ from the sum of the initial rest masses. The difference is accounted for by kinetic energy, radiation and interaction energy; it is not a failure of energy conservation.
For a complete isolated system, total four-momentum is conserved and so is its invariant mass. What often changes is how that total is distributed among subsystems and their relative motion. This distinction makes mass–energy equivalence useful for understanding binding-energy mass defects, nuclear reactions and particle production, without treating rest mass as a separately conserved substance.
statement: Binding, heating and radiation transfer change subsystem masses while total four-momentum is conserved.

title: Choosing a whole history
body:
Imagine drawing many trial paths between two specified events. A Lagrangian assigns an action to each path. The action principle says that the physical one has no first-order change in action when we perturb it in any allowed direction.
This is a mathematical way of specifying dynamics, not a claim that a particle previews its future and chooses a route. Once expressed as differential equations, the same dynamics can be solved from suitable initial data.
statement: The physical history is stationary under small allowed changes of the whole path.

title: Stationarity with stated boundary conditions
body:
Given a \cref{Lagrangian}{sr.lagrangian.definition}, form
\[ S[q]=\int_{t_1}^{t_2}L(q,\dot q,t)\,dt. \]
The action principle requires the first variation \(\delta S\) to vanish for every allowed infinitesimal variation of the path. In the standard mechanical problem, the endpoint times and positions are fixed, but the interior of the trial path is free to change.
Stationarity is the dynamical postulate. Differentiating and integrating by parts turn it into local equations; they do not prove that this postulate describes a given physical system.
statement: Given an action \(S[q]\), physical paths satisfy \(\delta S=0\) for all allowed variations.

title: Compare nearby histories
body:
A useful picture is to draw one candidate trajectory and gently push a short section sideways, leaving its endpoints alone. Re-evaluate the action for this slightly changed curve.
For a stationary path, the change has no term linear in the size of that push, whichever smooth allowed push we choose. Quadratic and higher-order changes may remain. This is the path version of a function having zero slope, with many possible directions of variation instead of just one.
statement: Nearby trial histories compare actions; they are not alternative journeys actually made.

title: Stationary is not always smallest
body:
At the bottom of a bowl, the slope vanishes. It also vanishes at the top of a hill and at a saddle. First derivatives alone do not distinguish these cases.
The same warning applies to action. Requiring its first variation to vanish says nothing by itself about the sign of its second variation. “Least action” is a familiar historical name, but “stationary action” states the requirement without incorrectly promising a minimum.
statement: \(\delta S=0\) specifies stationarity, not necessarily a minimum of the action.

title: What is held fixed at the endpoints
body:
The standard trial paths all begin at the same \(q(t_1)\) and end at the same \(q(t_2)\), with \(t_1,t_2\) fixed. Therefore
\[ \delta q(t_1)=\delta q(t_2)=0. \]
This does not mean that their velocities agree there. It is their position variations that vanish. When the action variation is integrated by parts, the boundary contribution is proportional to \(\delta q\), so it disappears.
Different boundary conditions lead to different boundary requirements. The fixed-endpoint assumption is a definite mathematical setup, not a rule that every physical experiment must literally fix its future endpoint.
statement: Fixed endpoint positions make their variations zero, removing the usual boundary term.

title: Turning a path variation into a derivative
body:
Choose any smooth function \(\eta(t)\) vanishing at \(t_1,t_2\), and define a family of paths
\[ q_a(t)\coloneqq q(t)+a\eta(t). \]
The number \(a\) controls the size of the change, while \(\eta\) specifies its shape. Substitution into the action gives an ordinary function \(S(a)\). The first variation is its derivative at zero:
\[ \delta S[\eta]\coloneqq\left.\frac{dS(a)}{da}\right|_{a=0}. \]
Stationarity requires this derivative to vanish for every allowed shape \(\eta\), not merely for one selected family. This is how a statement about whole paths can impose an equation at every interior time.
statement: For \(q_a=q+a\eta\), stationarity means \(dS[q_a]/da|_{a=0}=0\) for every allowed \(\eta\).

title: Relativistic actions
body:
If observers agree on the action assigned to each physical trial history, they also agree on which history is stationary. This motivates Lorentz-scalar actions in relativistic physics.
For a massive free particle, \(S=-mc^2\int d\tau\) uses the proper time along its path. For fields, contracting tensor indices and using the invariant flat-spacetime measure provides another route. These are examples of implementing relativistic symmetry. The general stationary-action principle is broader and does not require the SR postulates as prerequisites.
statement: A relativistic action gives the same number to a physical history in every inertial frame.

title: Why a whole-path principle gives a local equation
body:
For an action depending on \(q\) and \(\dot q\) at each time, the first variation contains terms proportional to \(\delta q\) and its derivative. Integration by parts collects them into a coefficient multiplying \(\delta q\).
Because that variation may be chosen freely in a small interior region, its coefficient must vanish there. This is the central reasoning behind the \cref{Euler–Lagrange argument}{sr.euler_lagrange_equations.arbitrary_variation}. A global comparison of paths therefore yields a local differential equation.
statement: Local dependence of the Lagrangian turns stationarity into local equations of motion.

title: From least to stationary action
body: Maupertuis and Euler developed eighteenth-century “least action” principles, Lagrange placed mechanics into a systematic variational form, and Hamilton formulated the time-integral principle closest to modern usage. The historical name can mislead: the physical path need only make the first variation vanish and may be a minimum, maximum or saddle point. “Stationary action” states the mathematics more accurately.
statement: The modern condition is stationary action, despite the historical name “least action”.

title: The local rule inside an action
body:
To predict motion, we first choose variables describing the system and a function called the Lagrangian. Evaluating it at successive times gives contributions that can be added into one number, the action.
The useful division of labour is between the model and the method. The chosen Lagrangian contains the physics of the particular system. Stationarity of its action supplies a common procedure for obtaining equations of motion. A compact formula can therefore describe a complicated history, but its physical ingredients still have to be justified.
statement: A Lagrangian assigns a local contribution to each part of a trial history.

title: The function integrated along a path
body:
A mechanical Lagrangian is a function \(L(q,\dot q,t)\) of generalised coordinates \(q\), their velocities \(\dot q\), and possibly time. Generalised coordinates are the variables chosen to describe the configuration; an angle can be as useful as a Cartesian position.
The action of a trial path is
\[ S[q]\coloneqq\int_{t_1}^{t_2}L(q(t),\dot q(t),t)\,dt. \]
This defines a number for each path, not an equation of motion by itself. The \cref{action principle}{sr.action_principle.definition} is the additional dynamical requirement that its first variation vanish.
statement: In mechanics, \(L(q,\dot q,t)\) defines the action \(S[q]=\int L\,dt\).

title: How a local rule describes a whole history
body:
At one instant, a first-order Lagrangian uses the coordinate and velocity at that instant. It does not need a separate input listing the whole future path. Integrating those local values nevertheless gives a number depending on the entire trial history.
When we vary that history, the velocity changes as well as the position. The dependence on both is what eventually produces a differential equation involving acceleration. The action is global in this sense, while the resulting equation can still be local in time.
statement: The local function is evaluated along a path; the action adds its contributions.

title: Not unique
body:
Consider \(\widetilde L=L+dF(q,t)/dt\). Its action differs from the original by
\[ \widetilde S-S=F(q(t_2),t_2)-F(q(t_1),t_1). \]
If the endpoint positions and times are fixed, this difference has zero variation. Both actions therefore give the same interior Euler–Lagrange equations. The endpoint qualification matters: changing boundary conditions can change the role of such terms.
Consequently the appearance of a Lagrangian is not unique. This freedom also cautions us against identifying every term in it directly with a separately measurable energy.
statement: Adding a total derivative changes only endpoint contributions to the action.

title: A particle in a potential
body:
For a nonrelativistic particle moving along one coordinate \(x\), a useful model is
\[ L\coloneqq\frac12m\dot x^2-V(x). \]
Here the first term is kinetic energy and \(V\) is the potential energy. Applying the stationary-action procedure gives \(m\ddot x=-dV/dx\), the familiar force law.
The pattern \(T-V\) is therefore a valuable starting example, not the definition of every Lagrangian. Relativistic kinetic terms and velocity-dependent interactions require other expressions. A proposed model must reproduce the intended physical equations in its range of validity.
statement: For a slow particle in a velocity-independent potential, \(L=\tfrac12m\dot x^2-V(x)\).

title: Constructing a relativistic free-particle model
body:
For a free massive particle, choose an invariant action proportional to the elapsed proper time:
\[ S\coloneqq-mc^2\int d\tau. \]
The \cref{proper-time rate}{sr.proper_time.rate} gives \(d\tau=dt\sqrt{1-v^2/c^2}\). Substitution constructs its coordinate-time Lagrangian:
\[ L=-mc^2\sqrt{1-v^2/c^2}. \]
The proportionality and sign are the physical free-particle model, calibrated to the Newtonian limit; they are not forced by the word “Lagrangian”. More generally, \cref{four-vector contractions}{sr.four_vectors.scalar_products} supply invariant ingredients. In a relativistic theory it is the action that must have an observer-independent meaning, even if a particular expression for \(L\) uses coordinate time.
statement: The free-particle choice \(S=-mc^2\int d\tau\) gives \(L=-mc^2\sqrt{1-v^2/c^2}\).

title: Chosen, not mechanically discovered
body:
There is no universal rule that discovers the correct Lagrangian without physical input. We choose the variables, interactions, symmetries and approximations that are appropriate to the system.
The variational method then tells us what those choices imply. Agreement with experiments, known limiting behaviour and other physical constraints tests the model. An elegant invariant expression is a candidate, not a guarantee that nature follows it.
statement: Choosing a Lagrangian supplies a physical model; variation does not choose that model for us.

title: Extending the method to fields
body:
A particle model has finitely many coordinates. A field model assigns variables throughout space, so its local contribution is a Lagrangian density integrated over space and time.
The same separation remains useful: choose the density, then vary the field configuration. Symmetries of that action also become a systematic route to conserved quantities through \cref{Noether’s theorem}{sr.noether_theorem}. The framework links dynamics and symmetry without identifying them as the same assumption.
statement: A field density extends the same model-and-variation method to variables at every event.

title: Lagrange's analytical mechanics
body: Lagrange's 1788 Mécanique analytique recast mechanics in generalized coordinates and famously avoided geometric diagrams. The reformulation replaced separate constructions for each machine or orbit with one analytic method. Later field theory gave the Lagrangian a still wider role: a compact local expression could encode dynamics, symmetry and relativistic covariance together.
statement: Lagrange made generalised coordinates and one analytic procedure central to mechanics.

title: Stationary action as an equation
body:
Once a Lagrangian has been chosen, we need a practical way to find its stationary histories. The Euler–Lagrange equation is that reusable procedure.
Its derivation combines the first variation of the action, the fixed endpoint condition and the freedom to vary the interior path. Each input has a job: the Lagrangian supplies the derivatives, the boundary condition removes an endpoint term, and arbitrary interior variations turn an integral statement into a local equation.
statement: The Euler–Lagrange equation is stationary action expressed locally.

title: The local stationary-action equation
body:
For a first-order action \(S[q]=\int L(q,\dot q,t)dt\) with fixed endpoint variations, the Euler–Lagrange equations are
\[ \frac{d}{dt}\frac{\partial L}{\partial\dot q_i}-\frac{\partial L}{\partial q_i}=0. \]
There is one equation for every independently varied coordinate \(q_i\). The partial derivatives treat the arguments \(q\) and \(\dot q\) of the function \(L\) independently; the total time derivative then follows the actual path.
These equations follow from the \cref{action principle}{sr.action_principle.definition} applied to the specified Lagrangian. Their physical content depends on that model, not on the symbols alone.
statement: For each coordinate, \(d(\partial L/\partial\dot q_i)/dt=\partial L/\partial q_i\).

title: Position and velocity vary together
body:
For one coordinate, take \(q_a=q+a\eta\), where the endpoint values of \(\eta\) vanish. Differentiating with respect to time gives \(\dot q_a=\dot q+a\dot\eta\).
Thus the position variation and velocity variation cannot be chosen independently along the path: \(\delta\dot q=d(\delta q)/dt\). Treating the arguments of \(L\) as independent when taking partial derivatives is compatible with this fact. The former differentiates a function; the latter describes which changes come from a genuine varied path.
statement: Changing the path changes its velocity too, with \(\delta\dot q=d(\delta q)/dt\).

title: First variation
body:
Start with the \cref{action}{sr.lagrangian.definition} \(S[q]=\int_{t_1}^{t_2}L(q,\dot q,t)dt\) and vary a smooth path while fixing its endpoints. The chain rule applied to \(L(q+a\eta,\dot q+a\dot\eta,t)\) gives
\[ \delta S=\int_{t_1}^{t_2}\left(\frac{\partial L}{\partial q}\delta q+\frac{\partial L}{\partial\dot q}\delta\dot q\right)dt. \]
Both terms are needed because varying a path changes its position and its velocity. Stationarity requires the sum to vanish for all allowed variations; it does not require the two terms to vanish separately. To exploit arbitrary \(\delta q\), we must first remove the derivative on the second variation.
statement: The chain rule gives \(\delta S=\int(L_q\delta q+L_{\dot q}\delta\dot q)dt\).

title: Integration by parts
body:
Given the first variation \(\delta S=\int(L_q\delta q+L_{\dot q}\delta\dot q)dt\), write \(p=\partial L/\partial\dot q\). Since \(\delta\dot q=d(\delta q)/dt\), integration by parts gives
\[ \begin{aligned}\int_{t_1}^{t_2}p\,\delta\dot q\,dt&=[p\delta q]_{t_1}^{t_2}\\ &\quad-\int_{t_1}^{t_2}\dot p\,\delta q\,dt.\end{aligned} \]
The \cref{fixed-endpoint condition}{sr.action_principle.fixed_endpoints} makes the bracket zero. Consequently
\[ \delta S=\int_{t_1}^{t_2}(L_q-\dot p)\delta q\,dt. \]
This step does not set \(p\) to zero or assume constant momentum. It moves a derivative so that every interior term multiplies the same freely chosen position variation.
statement: Integration by parts moves the derivative off the variation; fixed endpoints remove its boundary term.

title: Why the coefficient must vanish everywhere
body:
After integration by parts and fixed endpoint conditions, stationarity takes the form
\[ 0=\int_{t_1}^{t_2}\left(\frac{\partial L}{\partial q}-\frac{d}{dt}\frac{\partial L}{\partial\dot q}\right)\delta q\,dt. \]
Why must the bracket vanish at every time? If it were positive in a small region, choose a smooth positive variation supported there and zero elsewhere. The integral would be positive, contradicting stationarity. The same reasoning excludes a negative region, under the usual continuity assumptions.
Therefore the bracket is zero. Repeating this argument for each independent coordinate gives the Euler–Lagrange equations. It is the freedom of the variation, not merely one zero integral, that permits this conclusion.
statement: A smooth coefficient integrating to zero against every interior variation must vanish pointwise.

title: Several coordinates and the independence requirement
body:
For \(L(q_1,\ldots,q_n,\dot q_1,\ldots,\dot q_n,t)\), hold all variations but \(\delta q_i\) at zero in turn. The same stationary-action argument yields
\[ \frac{d}{dt}\frac{\partial L}{\partial\dot q_i}=\frac{\partial L}{\partial q_i},\qquad i=1,\ldots,n. \]
The coordinates may be lengths, angles or other convenient configuration variables. We are not adding a new force law for each notation; we are expressing the chosen model in that coordinate system.
Constraints need care. Independent generalised coordinates can incorporate some constraints, while others require multipliers or a constrained variational treatment. The formula should not be applied as if dependent variations were freely independent.
statement: One Euler–Lagrange equation applies to every independently varied coordinate.

title: Recovering Newton's equation
body:
Choose the nonrelativistic model \(L=\tfrac12m\dot x^2-V(x)\), with constant mass. Its derivatives are
\[ \frac{\partial L}{\partial\dot x}=m\dot x,\qquad \frac{\partial L}{\partial x}=-V'(x). \]
The Euler–Lagrange equation therefore reads \(d(m\dot x)/dt=-V'(x)\), or \(m\ddot x=-V'(x)\).
For a spring with \(V=\tfrac12kx^2\), this becomes \(m\ddot x=-kx\). The force law came from our choice of potential; the same variational machinery would work with a different \(V\).
statement: For \(L=\tfrac12m\dot x^2-V(x)\), the variational equation gives \(m\ddot x=-V'(x)\).

title: Not an extra force law
body:
The Euler–Lagrange equation is not a second physical requirement imposed after stationary action. It is the local form of that requirement for the specified differentiable, first-order action and allowed variations.
The real modelling choice was the Lagrangian and its domain of applicability. Writing down a different Lagrangian can change the motion even though the same Euler–Lagrange formula is used. Boundary conditions, constraints and regularity assumptions are also part of the problem.
statement: The variational equation and stationary action describe the same dynamics for the stated setup.

title: Euler, Lagrange and the calculus of variations
body: Euler developed a differential equation for extrema of integrals, and Lagrange introduced the variation notation and extended the method into mechanics. Their work separated a problem-specific function from a reusable variational procedure. The modern Euler-Lagrange equation preserves exactly that division: choose \(L\), then apply the same machinery to derive the motion.
statement: Euler and Lagrange separated a reusable variational method from the problem-specific function.

title: Dynamics in phase space
body:
A second-order equation for position needs both position and velocity as initial information. Hamiltonian mechanics reorganises that information into coordinates and their conjugate momenta.
The result is a pair of first-order evolution equations for each coordinate. This does not add a new physical force law. When the change of variables is regular, it describes the same motion as the Lagrangian equations, but exposes a useful geometry of states and their flow.
statement: Hamiltonian mechanics evolves coordinates and momenta together in phase space.

title: The Hamiltonian as a change of variables
body:
Given a Lagrangian, introduce \cref{canonical momenta}{sr.canonical_momentum.definition} \(p_i=\partial L/\partial\dot q_i\). Suppose these relations can be solved locally for \(\dot q_i(q,p,t)\). Define
\[ H(q,p,t)\coloneqq\sum_i p_i\dot q_i-L(q,\dot q,t). \]
Every velocity on the right must then be replaced by that solution. The independent variables of \(H\) are \(q,p,t\), not \(q,\dot q,t\). Together with the stationary-action dynamics, this Legendre transform gives Hamilton's equations. Singular momentum maps need a constrained treatment beyond this definition.
