statement: For an invertible momentum map, \(H(q,p,t)=\sum_i p_i\dot q_i-L\), with velocities eliminated.

title: Why the Legendre subtraction is useful
body:
Why use \(p\dot q-L\), rather than simply replacing the symbol \(\dot q\) in \(L\)? For one coordinate, differentiating this combination produces \(p\,d\dot q\), which cancels the velocity term \(L_{\dot q}d\dot q\) because \(p=L_{\dot q}\).
The remaining differential involves \(dp\), \(dq\) and \(dt\). This cancellation is the point of the Legendre transform: it changes which quantities are independent. Solving for \(\dot q(q,p,t)\) is essential; otherwise a formula still containing an independent velocity is not yet a Hamiltonian on phase space.
statement: The subtraction cancels velocity differentials, making momentum an independent argument.

title: Phase space
body:
Position alone does not tell us where a moving system will go next. A phase-space point records the coordinates \(q_i\) and momenta \(p_i\), supplying the state needed for the first-order Hamilton equations.
As time advances, that point traces a curve in this larger space. For one oscillator, configuration space is a line of possible positions, while phase space is a plane of position and momentum. A closed orbit there records successive states of an oscillation; it is not the particle's literal path through physical space.
statement: A phase-space point records both configuration and conjugate momentum.

title: The paired evolution equations
body:
For a regular Legendre transform of a Lagrangian system, Hamilton's equations are
\[ \dot q_i=\frac{\partial H}{\partial p_i},\qquad \dot p_i=-\frac{\partial H}{\partial q_i}. \]
The first equation recovers the velocity from the momentum description. The second states how that momentum changes. Together they are equivalent to the \cref{Euler–Lagrange dynamics}{sr.euler_lagrange_equations.definition} under the assumptions of the transform.
They also apply when \(H\) depends explicitly on time; time independence is needed for conservation of \(H\), not for the existence of these equations. Constraints can modify the canonical formulation and cannot be ignored.
statement: \(\dot q_i=\partial H/\partial p_i\) and \(\dot p_i=-\partial H/\partial q_i\) evolve the state.

title: Deriving Hamilton’s equations, including time dependence
body:
For one coordinate, let \(H=p\dot q-L\), with velocity eliminated by \(p=L_{\dot q}\). Keeping explicit time dependence, its differential is
\[ \begin{aligned}dH&=\dot q\,dp+p\,d\dot q\\ &\quad-L_q\,dq-L_{\dot q}\,d\dot q-L_t\,dt\\ &=\dot q\,dp-L_q\,dq-L_t\,dt.\end{aligned} \]
The velocity differentials cancel by the definition of canonical momentum. The \cref{Euler–Lagrange equation}{sr.euler_lagrange_equations.definition} supplies \(L_q=\dot p\), so
\[ dH=\dot q\,dp-\dot p\,dq-L_t\,dt. \]
Compare this with \(dH=H_qdq+H_pdp+H_tdt\), treating \(q,p,t\) independently. Matching coefficients gives \(H_p=\dot q\), \(H_q=-\dot p\), and \(H_t=-L_t\).
The transform supplies the variable change; Euler–Lagrange supplies the dynamics. Neither ingredient can be omitted from this argument.
statement: The Legendre transform and Euler–Lagrange equation together produce Hamilton’s equations.

title: Hamiltonian is not merely a synonym for energy
body:
For familiar particles in time-independent conservative potentials, \(H\) is the total energy. That is a useful example, not its most general definition.
Along Hamiltonian motion, the coordinate and momentum terms in \(dH/dt\) cancel, leaving \(dH/dt=\partial H/\partial t\). Therefore no explicit time dependence implies a conserved Hamiltonian. Whether this is the physical energy being measured also depends on the chosen time coordinate, interactions and possible constraints. Time-dependent coordinate changes and gauge systems are reasons to state the interpretation rather than assume it.
statement: The Hamiltonian generates time evolution; its energy interpretation depends on the model and coordinates.

title: A particle in a potential, including the free limit
body:
The momentum of \(L=\tfrac12m\dot x^2-V(x)\) is \(p=m\dot x\), so the inverse relation is \(\dot x=p/m\). Substitute it into the Legendre transform:
\[ \begin{aligned}H&=p\frac{p}{m}-\left(\frac{p^2}{2m}-V(x)\right)\\ &=\frac{p^2}{2m}+V(x).\end{aligned} \]
Hamilton's equations now give \(\dot x=p/m\) and \(\dot p=-V'(x)\). Combining them recovers \(m\ddot x=-V'(x)\). This example checks both the change of variables and its dynamical equivalence. The free-particle case is \(V=0\); a nonconstant potential is not a free particle.
statement: For \(L=\tfrac12m\dot x^2-V(x)\), eliminating velocity gives \(H=p^2/(2m)+V(x)\).

title: Why phase space is useful
body:
Hamiltonian mechanics puts the full instantaneous state in one space and turns dynamics into a flow there. This makes it possible to study changes of canonical variables without repeatedly returning to a particular force diagram.
Poisson brackets express that evolution algebraically, and conserved quantities constrain the flow. These structures are useful in statistical mechanics and provide a bridge to quantum mechanics. They do not require us to discard the Lagrangian description; the two viewpoints answer different practical questions about the same regular system.
statement: Phase-space evolution makes canonical transformations, conservation and later quantisation accessible.

title: Hamilton between optics and mechanics
body: Hamilton's work grew from an analogy between geometrical optics and particle mechanics. His canonical equations recast second-order motion as coupled first-order evolution in coordinates and momenta. This did not supersede Lagrange's equations; it exposed a phase-space structure that later proved fundamental to statistical mechanics, canonical transformations and quantum theory.
statement: Hamilton’s first-order phase-space equations exposed a structure shared by optics and mechanics.

title: A coordinate's dynamical partner
body:
In Newtonian examples, “momentum” usually means mass times velocity. The canonical definition asks a different question: how strongly does the Lagrangian change when a chosen coordinate's velocity changes?
The answer supplies a momentum conjugate to that coordinate. It often agrees with mechanical momentum, but velocity-dependent interactions can make the two differ. This definition also identifies the variable needed when we rewrite the dynamics in phase space.
statement: Canonical momentum is the coordinate partner defined by velocity dependence in the Lagrangian.

title: Momentum conjugate to a coordinate
body:
Given a \cref{Lagrangian}{sr.lagrangian.definition} and independently chosen coordinates \(q_i\), define
\[ p_i\coloneqq\frac{\partial L}{\partial\dot q_i}. \]
When taking this partial derivative, hold the other arguments of \(L\) fixed. There is a separate conjugate momentum for each coordinate. Its dimensions depend on that coordinate: the partner of an angle has angular-momentum units, not linear-momentum units.
The definition does not by itself state conservation. A coordinate absent explicitly from \(L\) has a conserved conjugate momentum on solutions of the Euler–Lagrange equations.
statement: The momentum conjugate to \(q_i\) is \(p_i\coloneqq\partial L/\partial\dot q_i\).

title: Where it appears in the variation
body:
For \(S=\int L(q,\dot q,t)dt\), vary the coordinates and integrate the velocity-variation terms by parts. Before imposing endpoint conditions, the boundary contribution is
\[ \delta S\big|_{\rm boundary}=\left[\sum_i\frac{\partial L}{\partial\dot q_i}\delta q_i\right]_{t_1}^{t_2}. \]
Its coefficient of each endpoint displacement is exactly \(p_i=\partial L/\partial\dot q_i\). This explains why that velocity derivative is paired with the coordinate, rather than being an arbitrary momentum-like definition.
The fixed-endpoint problem sets this contribution to zero by setting \(\delta q_i=0\). We can still inspect the coefficient before doing so. This argument interprets the canonical construction; it does not assert that canonical momentum must equal mechanical momentum.
statement: The endpoint coefficient in \(\delta S\) is \(p_i\delta q_i\), identifying the conjugate partner.

title: When canonical and mechanical momentum agree
body:
For \(L=\tfrac12m\dot x^2-V(x)\), hold \(x\) fixed while differentiating with respect to \(\dot x\):
\[ p=\frac{\partial L}{\partial\dot x}=m\dot x. \]
The potential contributes nothing because it has no velocity argument. In this model the canonical momentum is the ordinary mechanical momentum. That agreement follows from the form of \(L\), not from a general identity between the two concepts.
statement: A quadratic kinetic term with no velocity-dependent potential gives \(p=m\dot x\).

title: Velocity-dependent interactions
body:
Consider the nonrelativistic charged-particle model
\[ L=\tfrac12m\mathbf v^2+e\mathbf A\cdot\mathbf v-e\phi. \]
The signed charge is \(e\), and the potentials are evaluated at the particle's position and time. Differentiating by velocity gives
\[ \mathbf p_{\rm can}=m\mathbf v+e\mathbf A. \]
The \cref{vector potential}{sr.vector_potential} contributes because its interaction term is velocity-dependent. Mechanical momentum remains \(m\mathbf v\) in this approximation. This is an illustration of the canonical definition, not a derivation of electromagnetism from mechanics. Under a gauge change the canonical expression can change while the physical trajectory and mechanical momentum do not.
statement: For electromagnetic coupling, \(\mathbf p_{\rm can}=m\mathbf v+e\mathbf A\) in the slow-particle model.

title: Role in Hamiltonian mechanics
body:
After computing \(p_i=\partial L/\partial\dot q_i\), ask whether these equations can be solved for all velocities in terms of \(q,p,t\). If so, velocities can be traded for momenta in the \cref{Hamiltonian construction}{sr.hamiltonian_formalism.definition}.
For a regular Lagrangian this is locally possible when the velocity Hessian, \(\partial^2L/\partial\dot q_i\partial\dot q_j\), is nonsingular. If it is singular, constraints may relate the momenta and the simple unconstrained construction is insufficient. The familiar quadratic kinetic example is regular; gauge field theories require more care.
statement: A locally invertible velocity–momentum relation permits the Hamiltonian change of variables.

title: Not automatically four-momentum
body:
Canonical momentum is tied to a chosen coordinate and Lagrangian. A \cref{physical four-momentum}{sr.momentum_four_vector.definition} instead packages energy and spatial momentum with a Lorentz transformation law.
For a relativistic free particle, the spatial canonical momentum of the usual coordinate-time Lagrangian agrees with \(\gamma m\mathbf v\). Coupling to a vector potential changes the canonical expression. Thus the relationship can be close and useful, but cannot be inferred merely because both quantities are denoted by \(p\).
statement: A coordinate-conjugate momentum is not automatically a relativistic four-momentum.

title: Notation overload
body:
The symbol \(p\) may denote Newtonian momentum, relativistic three-momentum, a four-vector component or a canonical momentum. These uses are related but not interchangeable.
Check which coordinate is conjugate, which derivative defines the quantity and whether a potential term is included. For angular coordinates, the conjugate momentum may be angular momentum. Keeping these definitions visible prevents mistakes when moving between mechanics, relativity and gauge coupling.
statement: The meaning of \(p\) comes from its definition, not from the letter.

title: Three connected roles of the same derivative
body:
The same quantity appears in three places: as a velocity derivative of \(L\), as the coefficient of an endpoint variation, and as the variable paired with a coordinate in Hamiltonian mechanics.
These are connected roles, not three unrelated definitions. They explain why canonical momentum is useful for symmetry arguments and changes of description, while leaving open whether it coincides with a particular mechanical momentum.
statement: Canonical momentum links the Lagrangian derivative, endpoint variation and phase-space variables.

title: Symmetry becomes conservation
body:
A conservation law can look like a separate fact to memorise. Noether's theorem explains a common pattern behind many such facts: a continuous symmetry of an action produces a current whose divergence vanishes when the equations of motion hold.
The qualification matters. We must identify an actual symmetry of the model, specify allowed boundary terms, and use its dynamics. A pleasing visual pattern or an arbitrary change of variables is not enough.
statement: Continuous action symmetries lead to local conservation laws on physical solutions.

title: Symmetry, boundary term and on-shell current
body:
For a differentiable action, a continuous global transformation leaving the action invariant up to an allowed boundary term gives a current \(J^\mu\) satisfying
\[ \partial_\mu J^\mu=0 \]
on solutions of the equations of motion. “On shell” means precisely that those equations hold. In mechanics the corresponding statement is \(dQ/dt=0\).
The theorem concerns variational symmetries, not every symmetry of a picture. It is useful to distinguish this first theorem from identities associated with local gauge redundancy, treated by Noether's second theorem. Finite conserved totals also require suitable boundary behaviour.
statement: Noether’s first theorem associates a current with each continuous global variational symmetry, conserved on shell.

title: The symmetry is a symmetry of the action
body:
Two descriptions can have actions differing only by a boundary contribution. If that contribution is allowed by the problem, the transformation is still a variational symmetry.
For a fixed-coordinate internal transformation \(\delta\phi_a=\epsilon\Delta_a\), write its first-order density change as \(\delta\mathcal L=\epsilon\partial_\mu K^\mu\). This identity must describe the transformation of arbitrary allowed field configurations, not merely an accidental equality along one solution.
Time translations, spatial translations and rotations require including their coordinate or argument effects as well. The boundary term is part of constructing the current, not something to drop before the calculation begins.
statement: A symmetry may change \(\mathcal L\) by \(\partial_\mu K^\mu\), rather than leaving its written expression identical.

title: Continuous matters
body:
A continuous symmetry admits an infinitesimal parameter, allowing the variational calculation to isolate a current. A reflection is discrete, so it does not by itself supply a Noether current through this procedure.
A local gauge parameter is a different case again: it can encode redundancy and differential identities rather than one independent physical charge for every function. These distinctions prevent the slogan “every symmetry gives a conserved quantity” from being applied beyond its assumptions.
statement: Continuous global symmetry, discrete symmetry and local gauge redundancy have different consequences.

title: Deriving the current from the variational identity
body:
Let \(\Pi_a^\mu=\partial\mathcal L/\partial(\partial_\mu\phi_a)\) for a first-derivative field action. The chain rule and product rule give the general variation identity
\[ \delta\mathcal L=\left(\mathcal L_{\phi_a}-\partial_\mu\Pi_a^\mu\right)\delta\phi_a+\partial_\mu(\Pi_a^\mu\delta\phi_a). \]
The \cref{field Euler–Lagrange equation}{sr.field_equations.definition} sets the bracket to zero on physical solutions. For a constant infinitesimal parameter \(\epsilon\), suppose the variational symmetry has \(\delta\phi_a=\epsilon\Delta_a\) and \(\delta\mathcal L=\epsilon\partial_\mu K^\mu\). Comparing the two expressions yields
\[ \partial_\mu\left(\Pi_a^\mu\Delta_a-K^\mu\right)=0. \]
Thus \(J^\mu=\Pi_a^\mu\Delta_a-K^\mu\) is the current. The action supplies the derivative coefficient, symmetry supplies the special variation and boundary term, and the equations of motion turn the identity into conservation. All three inputs are needed.
statement: For \(\delta\phi_a=\epsilon\Delta_a\) and \(\delta\mathcal L=\epsilon\partial_\mu K^\mu\), \(J^\mu=\Pi_a^\mu\Delta_a-K^\mu\).

title: Mechanical examples
body:
If the full action has no preferred time origin, its time-translation symmetry gives conserved energy. Translating a complete experiment without changing the action gives spatial momentum conservation. Rotational invariance similarly gives angular momentum.
These claims refer to the full model, including relevant external structures. A particle in a fixed position-dependent external potential need not have spatial translation symmetry, even if the surrounding empty space is homogeneous. A smaller subsystem can exchange a conserved quantity with what the model has treated as external.
statement: Time, spatial and rotational symmetries produce energy, momentum and angular-momentum conservation under suitable assumptions.

title: A cyclic coordinate
body:
Suppose one coordinate \(q\) does not appear explicitly in \(L\), although its velocity may appear. A constant shift \(q\to q+\epsilon\) then leaves the Lagrangian unchanged.
The Euler–Lagrange equation gives
\[ \frac{dp}{dt}=\frac{\partial L}{\partial q}=0,\qquad p=\frac{\partial L}{\partial\dot q}. \]
This is the simplest Noether example: the shift symmetry gives the corresponding \cref{canonical momentum}{sr.canonical_momentum.definition}. If \(q\) is an angle, the conserved quantity has angular-momentum units. The symbol \(p\) need not mean ordinary linear momentum.
statement: If \(\partial L/\partial q=0\), Euler–Lagrange gives conserved \(p=\partial L/\partial\dot q\).

title: Field theory form
body:
A local current equation compares density change with flux. In coordinates \(x^0=ct\), a conserved total can be formed from the time component on a spatial slice, with the normalisation chosen for that current.
Integrating the divergence equation shows that the total changes only through boundary flux. For an isolated system with sufficiently decaying fields, that flux vanishes. Spacetime translations give four such currents, packaged as the \cref{energy–momentum tensor}{sr.energy_momentum_tensor.noether_origin}. This links local symmetry reasoning to global conservation without pretending every subsystem is isolated.
statement: A conserved current becomes a conserved total only when boundary flux is controlled.

title: Not a magic conservation generator
body:
One cannot infer a conserved quantity merely because an equation looks balanced or a diagram is symmetric. The transformation must be a variational symmetry of the model and must respect the allowed boundary setup.
The conservation equation holds on physical solutions. External forcing, explicit coordinate dependence, boundaries and gauge redundancy can change the conclusion or the interpretation of the current. These are hypotheses to check, not exceptions to ignore.
statement: The theorem uses an action symmetry and the equations of motion, not symmetry alone.

title: Noether resolves a relativity puzzle
body: Emmy Noether developed her 1918 theorems in Göttingen after Hilbert and Klein asked her to clarify conservation of energy in general relativity. Her first theorem linked continuous finite-dimensional symmetries to conserved currents; her second explained the identities associated with local gauge symmetries. The result transformed conservation laws from separately discovered facts into consequences of the symmetry of an action.
statement: Noether distinguished global conservation currents from identities tied to local gauge symmetry.

title: Using conservation to inspect a model
body:
The theorem provides a disciplined route from a specified action to its conserved currents. It can also guide diagnosis in reverse: when a previously conserved quantity changes, inspect which symmetry is broken or which boundary flux was omitted.
This is especially useful in field theory, where energy, momentum and charge can move between local regions. The invariant total and its local distribution are related by the current equation rather than by a separate bookkeeping rule.
statement: Conserved quantities reveal the continuous variational structure of the chosen model.

title: One number at each event
body:
A field describes a physical quantity throughout a region, rather than only along one particle's path. A scalar field is the simplest case: each event receives one value.
That value may change from place to place and time to time. “Scalar” tells us that different inertial observers agree on the value at the same event, even though their coordinate labels for that event differ. It does not mean the field is uniform or has no dynamics.
statement: A scalar field assigns one value to every event without a frame-dependent component direction.

title: The same value at the same event
body:
A scalar field \(\phi\) assigns one real value to each \cref{spacetime event}{sr.spacetime_event.definition} in its domain. For two \cref{Lorentz-related coordinate descriptions}{sr.lorentz_transformations.definition} of that event,
\[ \phi'(x')=\phi(x),\qquad x'=\Lambda x. \]
The prime labels a different coordinate representation, not a second physical field. The equality compares values at the same event. Comparing \(\phi'(x)\) and \(\phi(x)\) at the same numerical coordinates would generally compare different events.
A transformation rule specifies the kind of field. A field equation or action is additional information specifying its dynamics.
statement: A scalar field obeys \(\phi'(x')=\phi(x)\) at the same event.

title: Local value, not one global number
body:
Imagine a map colouring each point by one measured number. Changing the grid used to label the points does not recolour the map. It changes the coordinate formula used to find each value.
A temperature map in a room is a useful analogy for spatial variation. It is not a claim that every definition of temperature in relativistic thermodynamics is a Lorentz scalar. The lesson of the picture is the distinction between one value at each point and one constant value everywhere.
statement: A scalar value can vary over the domain while remaining independent of the coordinate description.

title: Same event, different coordinates
body:
The scalar transformation rule is \(\phi'(x')=\phi(x)\). Since \(x=\Lambda^{-1}x'\), another way to write it is \(\phi'(x')=\phi(\Lambda^{-1}x')\).
This shows why the coordinate formula can change. If one frame describes a pattern as stationary, a boosted observer can see that pattern moving through their coordinates. Agreement on the field value at an event does not imply agreement on which coordinate points carry which values at a chosen coordinate time.
statement: The functions \(\phi\) and \(\phi'\) can differ even though they describe the same scalar field.

title: Contrast with four-vectors
body:
A \cref{four-vector}{sr.four_vectors.definition} has time and spatial components that mix when the observer changes. A scalar field has no such component index to mix.
Both can still depend on all four spacetime coordinates. The distinction is about the value attached to each event, not whether the quantity varies through time or space. Scalar models are useful first examples because they retain the field's infinitely many degrees of freedom while avoiding extra component bookkeeping.
statement: Vector components mix under a boost; a scalar field value does not.

title: Examples and analogies
body:
A simple relativistic model takes a real-valued field \(\phi(x)\) with density \(\mathcal L=\tfrac12\partial_\mu\phi\partial^\mu\phi-V(\phi)\). The potential \(V\) and boundary or initial data determine the particular problem.
The formula illustrates a genuine dynamical scalar field; it is not the definition of scalar behaviour. Ordinary temperature maps or nonrelativistic density maps provide useful analogies for assigning numbers locally, but their physical transformation properties must be checked separately before calling them relativistic scalar fields.
statement: A real scalar model can use \(\phi(x)\) with kinetic term \(\tfrac12\partial_\mu\phi\partial^\mu\phi\).

title: Deriving the gradient’s transformation rule
body:
Given the scalar rule \(\phi'(x')=\phi(x)\), apply the chain rule:
\[ \partial'_\mu\phi'(x')=\frac{\partial x^\nu}{\partial x'^\mu}\partial_\nu\phi(x). \]
This is the covector transformation law. The derivative answers how the scalar changes in a chosen direction, so its directional information need not be scalar even though the original value is.
Contracting the gradient with the inverse metric gives the scalar \(\partial_\mu\phi\partial^\mu\phi\), a useful ingredient of an invariant field action. The \cref{covector readout}{math.cotangent_space.gradient_example} supplies the general geometric interpretation.
statement: The gradient \(\partial_\mu\phi\) transforms as a covector, although \(\phi\) is a scalar.

title: Scalar does not mean constant
body:
A scalar field may have a steep gradient or change rapidly in time. Its scalar character only means that observers agree on its value at one and the same event.
Constancy would be the extra condition that the value agree at different events as well. Do not confuse these two comparisons: changing observer and moving to another event are different operations.
statement: Scalar transformation behaviour does not imply spatial or temporal constancy.

title: Separating field type from field dynamics
body:
Once a scalar transformation rule is specified, we can choose a \cref{field Lagrangian}{sr.field_lagrangian.example_scalar} and derive its equation of motion. This separates the definition of the variable from the dynamics chosen for it.
Different potentials or derivative terms can give different equations for the same kind of scalar field. Studying these models helps us recognise which parts of a later electromagnetic calculation arise from variation in general and which depend specifically on vector and gauge structure.
statement: Scalar models let us study variation and propagation before introducing vector indices.

title: A vector at every event
body:
A vector field combines two ideas: values are assigned throughout spacetime, and each value has components that transform together as a four-vector.
The value at one event need not point in the same direction or have the same magnitude as the value next door. The transformation rule compares observers at the same event; derivatives compare values at nearby events. Keeping these comparisons separate makes field notation much easier to read.
statement: A relativistic vector field assigns a four-vector to each spacetime event.

title: The vector transformation law at every event
body:
A contravariant vector field assigns a four-vector \(V^\mu(x)\) to each event. Between inertial coordinate systems,
\[ V'^\mu(x')=\Lambda^\mu{}_\nu V^\nu(x). \]
Here \(x'\) and \(x\) label the same physical event, and the \cref{four-vector rule}{sr.four_vectors.definition} relates the components attached to it. The argument and the component index therefore have different jobs.
A covector field instead carries a lower index and the inverse transformation on that index. The metric relates vectors and covectors, but their transformation roles should not be blurred. We use \(V\) for a generic field, reserving \(A\) for the electromagnetic potential.
statement: At the same event, \(V'^\mu(x')=\Lambda^\mu{}_\nu V^\nu(x)\).

title: Local vectors, not one arrow
body:
Draw a small arrow at every point of a spatial slice. Nearby arrows may bend or change length; following those changes gives a first picture of a vector field.
A spacetime vector has a time component as well as spatial components, so the drawing only suggests the local assignment. It does not display every relativistic component. A field equation can constrain how these local values fit together without making them all copies of one global arrow.
statement: Think of a field as a collection of local arrows, not one arrow spanning the whole region.

title: Contrast with scalar fields
body:
One vector field has four component functions, but they mix under a boost. Four separate scalar fields would each retain their value at the event, with no such mixing of their labels.
The number of functions is therefore not enough to identify the field type. Compare the transformation law with the \cref{scalar rule}{sr.scalar_field.definition}. Both kinds of field depend on spacetime coordinates, while only the vector components acquire the Lorentz matrix.
statement: Four scalar functions and one four-vector field have different frame-change rules.

title: Both argument and components transform
body:
In \(V'^\mu(x')=\Lambda^\mu{}_\nu V^\nu(x)\), the argument change \(x\to x'\) and the component change \(V\to V'\) occur together.
If we want both functions expressed at the same coordinate argument, first use \(x=\Lambda^{-1}x'\). Otherwise we may accidentally compare vectors at different physical events. This is a bookkeeping warning, not an extra transformation law beyond the one in the definition.
statement: A frame change relabels the event and transforms the components attached to it.

title: The electromagnetic potential
body:
The \cref{electromagnetic potential}{sr.vector_potential.definition} provides an important example. In a chosen gauge its components form a four-potential over spacetime, conventionally written \(A^\mu=(\phi/c,\mathbf A)\) in SI units.
Its spacetime derivatives build the electromagnetic field tensor. Gauge-related potentials can describe the same field, so this example has additional redundancy beyond the definition of a generic vector field. Not every vector field is an electromagnetic potential.
statement: The electromagnetic four-potential is a vector-field example with gauge freedom.

title: What the two derivative indices mean
body:
A component derivative \(\partial_\mu V_
u\) records how the \(
u\)-component changes when the coordinates vary in the \(\mu\)-direction. Under constant Lorentz transformations, the chain rule transforms the derivative index and the covector rule transforms the field index.
This gives a rank-two covariant tensor in inertial Cartesian frames. Symmetric and antisymmetric combinations then provide different local constructions. For example, \(\partial_\mu A_
u-\partial_
u A_\mu\) builds electromagnetic field strength.
In general curvilinear coordinates, ordinary derivatives of vector components do not transform tensorially; a covariant derivative is needed. The simple statement here uses the inertial-coordinate setting.
statement: In inertial Cartesian coordinates, \(\partial_\mu V_\nu\) carries two covector indices.

title: Not four unrelated scalar fields
body:
It is possible to write one vector field as four functions, but the transformation law ties them together. A boost can mix its time component with the spatial component parallel to the boost.
Four scalar fields instead have four independently transforming scalar values. The two descriptions have the same number of written functions but different geometric meaning. This is why the transformation rule must accompany a component formula.
statement: The component index belongs to a Lorentz vector, not a label for four unrelated fields.

title: From local values to field models
body:
The event argument tells us where the field is evaluated. The vector index tells us how that local value is described by different observers. Derivatives add information about change between neighbouring events.
These ingredients provide the language for the four-potential and later tensor constructions. They specify how to build and transform quantities; an action or other dynamical principle is still needed to say which field configurations occur.
statement: Vector fields combine local spacetime dependence with a shared component transformation rule.

title: Action density for fields
body:
For particle mechanics, a trial history is a path. For a field, it is a whole assignment of field values throughout a spacetime region. We therefore need to add contributions over space as well as time.
The Lagrangian density supplies those contributions. Choosing it specifies a dynamical model, including derivative and interaction terms. Varying its integral then gives the local field equations. Locality and relativistic symmetry guide the choice without uniquely determining every possible model.
statement: A Lagrangian density supplies the local contribution to an action spread through spacetime.

title: Density and spacetime action
body:
A field Lagrangian density \(\mathcal L\) is a function of field values, their derivatives and possibly the event coordinates. For the first-derivative theories used here, define
\[ S[\phi]\coloneqq\int_\Omega d^4x\,\mathcal L(\phi_a,\partial_\mu\phi_a,x). \]
The label \(a\) distinguishes independent field components; \(\mu\) is a spacetime index. The \cref{action principle}{sr.action_principle.definition} is imposed on field variations with specified boundary behaviour.
Here the measure is written with \(x^0=ct\). Any constant factor of \(c\) needed to give \(S\) action units is included in the definition of \(\mathcal L\). Explicit examples using \(c=1\) will say so.
statement: A first-derivative field action has \(S=\int d^4x\,\mathcal L(\phi_a,\partial_\mu\phi_a,x)\).

title: Why a density
body:
Imagine dividing a spacetime region into small cells. A field history assigns values and rates of change within each cell. Multiplying its local density by the cell's four-volume gives one small contribution; adding them and taking a continuum limit gives the action.
This picture explains why the field version needs a density rather than just a single function of time. It does not mean the cells are physically independent: derivative terms connect how neighbouring field values fit together.
statement: A density lets each small spacetime cell contribute to the action.

title: Local building blocks
body:
The \cref{locality requirement}{sr.principle_of_locality.definition} says that the density at \(x\) is built from ingredients at \(x\), such as \(\phi(x)\) and \(\partial_\mu\phi(x)\). A derivative measures local change; it is not a direct dependence on a separately chosen distant event.
Restricting to first derivatives gives a useful, widely used class of models. Higher-derivative and nonlocal theories need additional treatment. Locality alone does not prove finite-speed propagation: the actual differential operator and its characteristic structure also matter.
statement: A local density uses fields and a finite number of derivatives evaluated at one event.

title: The action should be scalar
body:
For a Lorentz transformation, \(d^4x' = d^4x\), using the absolute Jacobian determinant. If \(\mathcal L'(x')=\mathcal L(x)\), the integral assigns the same action to the same physical field history.
This is why we contract indices rather than leaving an unpaired observer-dependent component in the action. For example, a scalar-field gradient is a covector, so \(\partial_\mu\phi\partial^\mu\phi\) is a scalar after using the metric.
Covariance constrains the form of the model; it does not fix the potential, coupling constants or every allowed interaction. The chosen action still carries physical input.
statement: Lorentz-scalar contractions and invariant four-volume make the flat-spacetime action frame-independent.

title: A scalar-field pattern
body:
Use a real \cref{scalar field}{sr.scalar_field.definition}, signature \(+---\), and natural units \(c=1\). Choose
\[ \mathcal L\coloneqq\tfrac12\partial_\mu\phi\partial^\mu\phi-V(\phi). \]
The contracted derivative term is Lorentz invariant. In components it is \(\tfrac12\dot\phi^2-\tfrac12|\nabla\phi|^2\), so it distinguishes temporal change from spatial gradients. The potential sets the local self-interaction.
For \(V=\tfrac12m^2\phi^2\) with \(\hbar=1\) as well, variation gives the Klein–Gordon equation. This is a chosen dynamical example, not a consequence of scalar transformation behaviour alone.
statement: With \(c=1\), \(\mathcal L=\tfrac12\partial_\mu\phi\partial^\mu\phi-V(\phi)\) is a simple scalar model.

title: Electromagnetic pattern
body:
In a rationalised natural-unit convention, \(c=1\) and \(\mu_0=1\), an electromagnetic example is
\[ \mathcal L=-	frac14F_{\mu
u}F^{\mu
u}-j^\mu A_\mu. \]
The potential \(A_\mu\) is the variable to vary, with \(F_{\mu
u}=\partial_\mu A_
u-\partial_
u A_\mu\). The first term describes the field; the second specifies its coupling to a prescribed current.
This example previews later electromagnetic structure. Its signs and normalisation must be kept together when deriving Maxwell's equations. It is not an energy-density formula, and the field-strength definition alone does not supply the dynamics.
statement: The electromagnetic action uses a field-strength contraction and a source-coupling term.

title: Variation gives equations
body:
Choose a smooth field variation \(\delta\phi_a\) that vanishes on the boundary of the region. Because the density depends on the field and its first derivatives, its variation contains both \(\delta\phi_a\) and \(\partial_\mu\delta\phi_a\).
Integration by parts moves the second derivative onto its coefficient. The boundary term then vanishes, leaving a coefficient multiplying each arbitrary interior \(\delta\phi_a\). Setting those coefficients to zero gives the \cref{field equations}{sr.field_equations.integration_by_parts}. This is the same logic as the particle calculation, now applied in four dimensions.
statement: Varying a local field action converts arbitrary interior field changes into local equations.

title: Not simply energy density
body:
The Lagrangian density is the input to a variational problem. Energy density is obtained from the time-translation generator or the energy–momentum tensor, so it has a different role.
For a scalar model in \(c=1\) units, \(\mathcal L=\tfrac12\dot\phi^2-\tfrac12|\nabla\phi|^2-V\). Its Hamiltonian density is \(\tfrac12\dot\phi^2+\tfrac12|\nabla\phi|^2+V\). The changed signs illustrate why one cannot read energy density by simply renaming \(\mathcal L\).
statement: The density used for variation is generally different from the density of physical energy.

title: From mechanics to field theory
body: The Lagrangian method began in mechanics, but nineteenth- and twentieth-century field theories made the density form central. Relativity sharpened the requirement that the action be expressible in a covariant way.
statement: The density formulation extended variational mechanics to spatially distributed fields.

title: One model, several connected consequences
body:
A field action keeps several modelling decisions in one place: which fields exist, which derivatives are used, how they interact and which transformations preserve the action.
Once those decisions are explicit, variation gives equations of motion and continuous symmetries give Noether currents. These outputs are connected consequences of the same model. Changing the density can change both its dynamics and its conservation structure, even while keeping the same transformation kind of field.
statement: The chosen density specifies local interactions; variation extracts their equations and symmetry consequences.

title: Local rules for fields
body:
A field configuration is a possible assignment of values throughout spacetime. A field equation distinguishes assignments that satisfy the chosen dynamics from those that do not.
For a local first-derivative action, the variational method gives local differential equations. These may contain both evolution equations and constraints on initial data. They are not simply one number measuring the total field over space.
statement: Field equations constrain the local values and derivatives of the dynamical fields.

title: The field Euler–Lagrange condition
body:
For \(S=\int d^4x\,\mathcal L(\phi_a,\partial_\mu\phi_a,x)\), stationary action gives
\[ \frac{\partial\mathcal L}{\partial\phi_a}-\partial_\mu\frac{\partial\mathcal L}{\partial(\partial_\mu\phi_a)}=0. \]
There is one equation for every independently varied field component. The \cref{density}{sr.field_lagrangian.definition} supplies the physical model, while the \cref{Euler–Lagrange method}{sr.euler_lagrange_equations.arbitrary_variation} supplies the variational reasoning.
These statements assume sufficient smoothness and suitable boundary variations. Gauge redundancy can make some equations dependent, so independent-looking component formulas need not all supply separate evolution laws.
statement: In Lagrangian field theory, the field equations are the Euler–Lagrange conditions on each field component.

title: From paths to fields
body:
In particle mechanics, \(q(t)\) is varied at interior times. For a field, \(\phi_a(x)\) is varied throughout a spacetime region, with \(\delta\phi_a\) vanishing on its boundary.
The coordinate \(x\) is now a label of the field's domain, not the particle position we are solving for. The unknown is the function assigning values at those coordinates. This change explains why ordinary time derivatives are replaced by spacetime partial derivatives in the variational calculation.
statement: A path variation becomes an independent variation of each field throughout a spacetime region.

title: Reading the equation as a balance
body:
Write \(P_a^\mu\coloneqq\partial\mathcal L/\partial(\partial_\mu\phi_a)\). The field Euler–Lagrange equation becomes
\[ \partial_\mu P_a^\mu=\frac{\partial\mathcal L}{\partial\phi_a}. \]
This is the spacetime analogue of \(d(\partial L/\partial\dot q)/dt=\partial L/\partial q\). It connects how the density depends on the local field value with how its derivative coefficient varies from event to event.
The formula is an instruction to differentiate the specified density, not a complete physical law without that input. For multiple fields the derivatives are taken for each independent component, with summation over the spacetime index.
statement: The field variational equation balances explicit field dependence against derivative dependence.

title: Deriving the field equation from the action
body:
Start with \(S=\int_\Omega d^4x\,\mathcal L(\phi_a,\partial_\mu\phi_a)\), and define \(P_a^\mu=\partial\mathcal L/\partial(\partial_\mu\phi_a)\). Varying the field and its derivatives gives
\[ \delta S=\int_\Omega d^4x\left(\mathcal L_{\phi_a}\delta\phi_a+P_a^\mu\partial_\mu\delta\phi_a\right). \]
Use the product rule to move the derivative:
\[ P_a^\mu\partial_\mu\delta\phi_a=\partial_\mu(P_a^\mu\delta\phi_a)-(\partial_\mu P_a^\mu)\delta\phi_a. \]
The first term integrates to a boundary contribution. It vanishes for variations zero on the boundary, leaving
\[ \delta S=\int_\Omega d^4x(\mathcal L_{\phi_a}-\partial_\mu P_a^\mu)\delta\phi_a. \]
Each smooth interior variation can be chosen independently. The same local reasoning as in the particle Euler–Lagrange proof therefore forces each coefficient to vanish. This combines the field action, its boundary conditions and the variational method into the field equation.
statement: The chain rule, spacetime integration by parts and arbitrary interior variations give the local field equation.

title: Local partial differential equations
body:
Imagine checking a proposed field configuration through a tiny spacetime window. The equation compares its values and derivatives there. If it fails at that location, agreement with a global average does not repair it.
This is the sense in which the equation is local. It does not automatically guarantee finite-speed propagation or a well-posed initial-value problem. Those properties depend on the differential operator and constraints of the actual model.
statement: A local differential equation constrains each small region, rather than prescribing instantaneous remote influence.

title: A scalar-field calculation producing the wave operator
body:
Choose the real scalar density \(\mathcal L=\tfrac12\partial_\mu\phi\partial^\mu\phi-V(\phi)\), with \(+---\) and \(c=1\) in this normalisation. Its derivatives are \(P^\mu=\partial^\mu\phi\) and \(\mathcal L_\phi=-V'(\phi)\). The field equation becomes
\[ \Box\phi+V'(\phi)=0. \]
Restoring the coordinate convention \(x^0=ct\), the operator is
\[ \Box=\frac{1}{c^2}\frac{\partial^2}{\partial t^2}-\nabla^2. \]
For zero potential derivative, this is the relativistic wave equation. The propagation property comes from this operator, not from the bare fact that an equation is differential.
statement: For \(\mathcal L=\tfrac12\partial_\mu\phi\partial^\mu\phi-V\), variation gives \(\Box\phi+V'(\phi)=0\).

title: Maxwell as the central example
body:
The electromagnetic example uses \(A_\mu\) as the field variable, with an action built from \(F_{\mu\nu}F^{\mu\nu}\) and source coupling. Varying \(A_\mu\) therefore yields equations for its derivatives rather than a particle trajectory.
The resulting \cref{Maxwell equations}{sr.maxwells_equations} provide the central vector-field example. Their sourced part is dynamical; the homogeneous part also reflects the antisymmetric potential construction. Distinguishing these origins will make the later derivation easier to follow.
statement: Varying the electromagnetic potential gives the sourced Maxwell equation.

title: Not just a global constraint
body:
An equality involving a spatial total can hide local imbalances. A field equation instead constrains the field and its derivatives at each event.
Integrating a local conservation equation can give a useful relation between a volume total and boundary flux. That is a consequence of the local rule, not a replacement for it. Boundary conditions and initial constraints remain necessary to determine a particular solution.
statement: A local field equation must hold event by event, even when it also implies integral conservation.

title: Field equations before relativity
body: Maxwell's nineteenth-century equations already had the character of local field equations. Special relativity later revealed their covariant spacetime structure and made such equations the model for modern field theory.
statement: Maxwell supplied local field dynamics before relativity revealed their spacetime covariance.

title: From a model to a particular field history
body:
The action and its variation provide the equations, but do not select one solution without further data. Initial conditions, boundary conditions and any constraints identify the physical problem being solved.
This distinction separates three tasks: choose the model, derive its equations, then solve them for the stated situation. It also helps us recognise when two different-looking formulations describe the same field dynamics.
statement: A chosen field model becomes a local differential problem with initial and boundary data.

title: The potential behind the field
body:
Electric and magnetic fields can be described together through a four-potential. Its derivatives build the field strength, while its components provide convenient variables for an action.
The potential description has redundancy: different potentials can produce the same physical field. This does not make the potential useless. It explains why we can choose convenient representations without changing the classical electric and magnetic forces.
statement: A four-potential describes electromagnetism through local derivatives, with gauge redundancy.

title: The four-potential and its component convention
body:
The electromagnetic four-potential is a \cref{vector field}{sr.vector_field.definition} whose derivatives represent the electromagnetic field. Use inertial coordinates \(x^0=ct\), signature \(+---\), and SI components
\[ A^\mu=(\phi/c,\mathbf A),\qquad A_\mu=(\phi/c,-\mathbf A). \]
Here \(\phi\) is the electric scalar potential and \(\mathbf A\) the spatial vector potential. The factor \(c\) makes the four entries have consistent units. Lowering spatial indices changes signs by the metric; it does not change observer.
Potentials related by a smooth gauge gradient represent the same local field strength. The transformation rule and this redundancy are separate parts of the description.
statement: In SI and \(+---\), \(A^\mu=(\phi/c,\mathbf A)\) and \(A_\mu=(\phi/c,-\mathbf A)\).

title: From potential to field strength
body:
Given a differentiable potential, construct
\[ F_{\mu\nu}\coloneqq\partial_\mu A_\nu-\partial_\nu A_\mu. \]
The derivative index describes a direction of change and the second index labels the potential component. Subtracting the reversed pair keeps the antisymmetric, curl-like part.
The resulting \cref{field tensor}{sr.field_tensor.definition} contains six independent components. This is a local construction and a convention for representing electromagnetic strength, not an equation determining which potential actually occurs. The dynamical equations come from a further physical model.
statement:
The local field strength is \(F_{\mu
u}=\partial_\mu A_
u-\partial_
u A_\mu\).

title: Why the antisymmetric derivative
body:
A gradient can change the potential without introducing local circulation. When we take derivatives in both orders and subtract, the mixed derivatives of that gradient cancel.
The antisymmetric combination therefore ignores precisely this redundant part of the potential. There are six independent pairs of distinct spacetime directions, matching the three electric and three magnetic components. This is a useful geometric reason for the construction; the physical field interpretation still belongs to electromagnetic theory.
statement: Antisymmetrising removes pure-gradient changes and leaves the curl-like content.

title: Gauge freedom
body:
For a smooth function \(\chi(x)\), let \(A'_\mu=A_\mu+\partial_\mu\chi\). The extra contribution to the antisymmetric derivative is zero because mixed partial derivatives commute. Thus different potentials can describe the same field.
With the SI convention used here, this means \(\phi'=\phi+\partial_t\chi\) and \(\mathbf A'=\mathbf A-\nabla\chi\). The minus sign in the spatial rule comes from lowering the spatial potential index. Using the opposite sign for the gauge function is equally valid if all its occurrences change together. The \cref{gauge cancellation}{sr.gauge_invariance.cancellation} spells out the argument.
statement: Adding \(\partial_\mu\chi\) to the potential leaves its field tensor unchanged.

title: Field variable in the action
body:
In the electromagnetic action, \(A_\mu\) is an independent field variable, while \(F_{\mu\nu}\) abbreviates its antisymmetric derivatives. Varying the potential therefore varies the field strength in a particular constrained way.
For the standard field-strength-square density and source coupling, this produces the sourced Maxwell equation. The \cref{field-action method}{sr.field_lagrangian.definition} explains the variational procedure; the electromagnetic density specifies the actual physics. It would be incorrect to say that a potential is produced simply by knowing what a Lagrangian is.
statement: The potential is varied in the electromagnetic action; it is not derived from the idea of an action.

title: Coupling to charge
body:
A point particle with signed charge \(q\) can couple through
\[ S_{\rm int}=-q\int A_\mu dx^\mu. \]
The contraction pairs the potential at an event with the displacement along the path. With \(A_\mu=(\phi/c,-\mathbf A)\), this is \(\int(q\mathbf A\cdot\mathbf v-q\phi)dt\).
This sign choice agrees with the usual force on a positive charge. It also makes a gauge change alter the action only by endpoint terms. The term is a physical coupling choice, developed in \cref{minimal coupling}{sr.minimal_coupling.worldline_term}, rather than a consequence of writing four components.
statement: The interaction \(S_{\rm int}=-q\int A_\mu dx^\mu\) is a scalar local coupling to a charged path.

title: Not simply the observed field
body:
The potential components are not simply alternative names for \(\mathbf E\) and \(\mathbf B\). Their derivatives enter the physical field strength, and many different component functions give the same strength.
In classical local electrodynamics, forces depend on gauge-invariant structure. This does not justify discarding potentials, especially in action and quantum formulations. It means that a change in a potential component must be interpreted together with its gauge transformation, not automatically as a physical disturbance.
statement: A gauge-dependent potential component is not the measured electric or magnetic field.

title: Potentials become central
body:
Potentials began as practical tools for solving classical electromagnetic problems. Their importance increased when actions made the potential the natural variable connecting field equations and charged-particle motion.
Later quantum theory gave gauge and phase structure an additional physical role. That development should not be confused with the elementary classical statement that smooth gradient changes leave the local field tensor unchanged.
statement: Potentials became central because they organise both field dynamics and coupling to matter.

title: One potential, field strength and charge coupling
body:
The potential gives us a common starting point for two constructions: its antisymmetric derivative produces field strength, and its contraction with a charged path produces an interaction action.
Both constructions handle gauge freedom coherently. This is why the four-potential is more than a trick for shortening formulas, even though its individual components are not unique physical observables.
statement: The potential supplies a convenient local description; gauge-invariant field strength carries its classical force content.

title: One tensor for electromagnetism
body:
The field tensor lets us describe electromagnetism before deciding which components to call electric and which to call magnetic. It is a tensorial object; each observer supplies a component description.
Choosing a time direction divides those six independent components into two groups of three. A boost changes that division, which explains why electric and magnetic fields must transform together rather than as separate relativistic objects.
statement: One antisymmetric tensor contains the electric and magnetic components seen in any inertial frame.

title: Field strength from a local potential
body:
For a local four-potential, define
\[ F_{\mu
u}\coloneqq\partial_\mu A_
u-\partial_
u A_\mu. \]
Use the \cref{potential convention}{sr.vector_potential.definition} \(x^0=ct\), \(+---\), \(A_\mu=(\phi/c,-\mathbf A)\). Swapping the two indices reverses the sign, so \(F_{\mu
u}=-F_{
u\mu}\).
The tensor transforms covariantly on both indices. Its local potential construction already imposes a differential identity, but does not supply the sourced dynamical Maxwell equation. On regions with nontrivial topology a single global potential need not exist, so the formula is stated locally.
statement:
\(F_{\mu
u}\coloneqq\partial_\mu A_
u-\partial_
u A_\mu\) is the antisymmetric electromagnetic field strength.

title: Counting the independent field components
body:
Set the indices equal: \(F_{\mu\mu}=-F_{\mu\mu}\), so each diagonal entry vanishes. For unequal indices, one entry determines its reversed partner.
The independent pairs are \(01,02,03,12,13,23\), giving \(4\times3/2=6\) components. There are no additional independent entries hidden in the other half of the matrix. This counting combines the four-dimensional domain with antisymmetry, without invoking any equations of motion.
statement: Antisymmetry leaves six independent components in four dimensions.

title: Why six is suggestive
body:
Picture an antisymmetric four-by-four table. Three independent entries join the time direction to a spatial direction; three join pairs of spatial directions.
An observer reads the first group as electric field and the second as magnetic field. The table organises the same six local measurements already familiar from classical electromagnetism. It adds a transformation law and a unified interpretation, not six new physical degrees of freedom.
statement: The six tensor components match three electric and three magnetic readings.

title: The explicit SI electric–magnetic split
body:
Using \(A_0=\phi/c\), \(A_i=-\mathbf A_i\), and \(\partial_0=c^{-1}\partial_t\), the potential definition gives
\[ F_{0i}=\frac{-\partial_t\mathbf A_i-\partial_i\phi}{c}=\frac{E_i}{c}. \]
For the spatial entries, \(F_{ij}=-\partial_i\mathbf A_j+\partial_j\mathbf A_i=-\epsilon_{ijk}B_k\), with \(\epsilon_{123}=+1\). Here boldface potential components are the usual three-vector components, not lowered spacetime components.
These identifications fix the electric/magnetic split used throughout this module. Keeping them explicit prevents a formula copied from the opposite signature or potential convention from silently changing a physical sign.
statement: With the stated SI convention, \(F_{0i}=E_i/c\) and \(F_{ij}=-\epsilon_{ijk}B_k\).

title: Index placement matters
body:
The \cref{metric}{sr.metric_tensor.lowering_indices} raises each field-tensor index separately. With diagonal entries \((1,-1,-1,-1)\), raising a time–space pair introduces one minus sign, whereas raising a spatial–spatial pair introduces two.
Thus \(F^{0i}=-F_{0i}=-E_i/c\), but \(F^{ij}=F_{ij}\). A mixed tensor such as \(F^\mu{}_{\nu}\) has only one index raised and must be formed accordingly.
These signs follow from index placement, not a new physical field or a change of observer. State the signature before comparing two tensor formulas.
statement: Raising indices gives \(F^{0i}=-E_i/c\), while \(F^{ij}=F_{ij}\) in \(+---\).

title: Why electric and magnetic mix
body:
A rank-two tensor transforms with a Lorentz matrix on each raised index, or the corresponding inverse factors on lower indices. A boost mixes the time direction with one spatial direction.
Consequently an entry that was read as purely magnetic in one frame can contribute to electric entries in another. The invariant object is the tensor itself; it is not correct to call every one of its components invariant. Particular scalar contractions, such as \(F_{\mu\nu}F^{\mu\nu}\), can be frame-independent.
statement: A tensor transformation mixes the observer’s time–space and space–space components.

title: Deriving the homogeneous cyclic identity
body:
Insert \(F_{\beta\gamma}=\partial_\beta A_\gamma-\partial_\gamma A_\beta\) into the cyclic sum of its derivatives. Each second derivative then occurs twice with opposite signs. For example, \(\partial_\alpha\partial_\beta A_\gamma\) cancels \(-\partial_\beta\partial_\alpha A_\gamma\).
For a twice-differentiable local potential, mixed partial derivatives commute, so the whole sum vanishes. This is the homogeneous field-strength identity. It supplies the no-monopole and Faraday-induction equations in the ordinary split, without deriving the sourced equations or choosing a particular solution.
statement: Commuting partial derivatives gives \(\partial_\alpha F_{\beta\gamma}+\partial_\beta F_{\gamma\alpha}+\partial_\gamma F_{\alpha\beta}=0\).

title: Not two unrelated fields
body:
In a fixed frame it is useful to discuss \(\mathbf E\) and \(\mathbf B\) separately because their contributions to forces look different. A boost need not preserve that separation.
The tensor viewpoint keeps their relationship explicit while retaining their operational meanings. It does not assert that electric and magnetic readings must be equal, or that one can always find a frame eliminating either one.
statement: Electric and magnetic fields are frame-dependent parts of one field-strength tensor.

title: Minkowski's electromagnetic form
body: After Einstein's special relativity, Minkowski's spacetime formulation made it natural to write electromagnetism with four-dimensional tensors. The field tensor is one of the cleanest examples of that reorganisation.
statement: Minkowski’s tensor formulation made the relativistic unity of electromagnetic components explicit.

title: What the tensor construction does—and does not—supply
body:
Starting with a potential, one antisymmetric derivative produces six field components and automatically satisfies a cyclic derivative identity. A chosen observer interprets these components as electric and magnetic fields.
The sourced dynamics still require Maxwell's physical field action or equivalent laws. Separating construction, transformation and dynamics makes it easier to see which part of an electromagnetic calculation establishes which result.
statement: Field strength unifies component measurements, transformation behaviour and the homogeneous identity.

title: The field seen by charges at rest
body:
A small positive test charge provides an operational way to recognise an electric field. At an instant when it is at rest relative to the chosen frame, its force per unit charge defines the electric field there.
Relativity adds a qualification: which charges count as at rest depends on the observer. The tensor formulation keeps track of how that electric reading is related to the magnetic reading of another observer.
statement: Electric field is the force-per-charge reading for a test charge instantaneously at rest in a chosen frame.

title: Force per unit resting test charge
body:
The electric field is a three-vector measured in a specified \cref{inertial frame}{sr.inertial_frames.definition} by the force on a sufficiently weak test charge instantaneously at rest. The test charge should not significantly disturb the source field.
In the stated SI tensor convention, \(E_i=cF_{0i}=cF^{i0}\). This connects the operational force definition with the time–space components of the \cref{field tensor}{sr.field_tensor.frame_split}.
The charge \(q\) is signed; a negative charge feels the opposite electric force. The field is a property of the physical situation in that frame, not of which sign of test charge we happen to use.
statement: In a chosen inertial frame, \(\mathbf E=\mathbf F/q\) for a test charge instantaneously at rest.

title: A chosen frame is part of the statement
body:
“Electric field at this event” includes a choice of time direction, and hence of which test charge is instantaneously at rest. Another moving observer uses a different time–space split of the same tensor.
The measured three-vector can therefore change without any physical disturbance of the field. Coordinate agreement is not required; the Lorentz transformation must relate the two descriptions consistently.
statement: Specifying the observer is part of specifying an electric-field measurement.

title: Reading electric components from the tensor
body:
An observer's time axis singles out the three pairs \(01,02,03\). The entries in those positions supply the electric reading:
\[ (E_x,E_y,E_z)=c(F_{01},F_{02},F_{03}). \]
If we raise both indices instead, the metric changes these entries' signs. Therefore a statement such as “the electric field is \(F^{0i}\)” is incomplete without its sign and unit convention. No physical ambiguity remains once the potential, signature and component definitions have been fixed.
statement: The three time–space components yield \(E_i=cF_{0i}\) in the adopted convention.

title: Deriving the electric potential formula
body:
Combine the \cref{potential components}{sr.vector_potential.definition} with \(F_{0i}=\partial_0A_i-\partial_iA_0\). Since \(A_i=-\mathbf A_i\), \(A_0=\phi/c\), and \(\partial_0=c^{-1}\partial_t\),
\[ \begin{aligned}F_{0i}&=-\frac{\partial_t\mathbf A_i}{c}-\frac{\partial_i\phi}{c},\\ E_i=cF_{0i}&=-\partial_i\phi-\partial_t\mathbf A_i.\end{aligned} \]
Assembling the spatial components gives \(\mathbf E=-\nabla\phi-\partial_t\mathbf A\). The first term survives in electrostatics; the second allows an electric field even when a spatial scalar-potential gradient alone cannot describe it.
statement: \(\mathbf E=-\nabla\phi-\partial_t\mathbf A\) follows from the time–space field tensor.

title: A uniform field from a linear potential
body:
Take a time-independent scalar potential \(\phi(x)=\phi_0-E_0x\) and a vector potential with no time derivative. Then \(E_x=-\partial_x\phi=E_0\), with the other components zero.
A positive test charge feels a force towards lower potential energy \(q\phi\); for \(E_0>0\), that is the positive \(x\)-direction. The arbitrary additive constant \(\phi_0\) disappears from the derivative, so it cannot affect this force.
statement: For \(\phi=\phi_0-E_0x\) and time-independent \(\mathbf A\), \(\mathbf E=E_0\hat{\mathbf x}\).

title: Force meaning
body:
Imagine placing a small positive test charge at an event and releasing it from rest in your laboratory frame. The initial electric force points along \(\mathbf E\); a negative charge responds oppositely.
This picture makes electric field concrete. As the charge moves, magnetic force may also enter, and a moving observer need not describe the same initial condition as rest. The complete motion is handled by the Lorentz force law rather than by treating this one frame's picture as absolute.
statement: A positive resting test charge begins accelerating along the electric field.

title: Not absolute by itself
body:
Two observers can measure different electric and magnetic fields at the same event while describing the same physical field tensor. The discrepancy is a frame change, not an inconsistency.
Calling the tensor the unified object does not mean its component numbers stay fixed under a boost. What is shared is the geometrical field and the transformation rule connecting those numbers.
statement: The electric three-vector is observer-dependent; the electromagnetic tensor transforms covariantly.

title: From electrostatics to field components
body: The electric field entered physics through electrostatic forces and Faraday's field picture. Special relativity later placed that familiar field inside a larger electromagnetic tensor.
statement: Force measurements and Faraday’s field picture preceded the relativistic tensor interpretation.

title: Connecting force, tensor and potential descriptions
body:
The force experiment supplies the physical meaning of \(\mathbf E\). The tensor split supplies its place in relativistic electromagnetism, and the potential derivative supplies a useful way to calculate it.
These are connected descriptions of the same quantity in one frame. None makes the electric field an observer-independent three-vector, and none permits us to forget the magnetic components when changing frame.
statement: The operational test-charge definition agrees with the tensor’s time–space component reading.

title: The field tied to motion and current
body:
In a laboratory frame, magnetic fields are recognised through their effects on moving charges and currents. They contribute a force perpendicular to a test charge's velocity.
Their relativistic meaning is more general than a list of source examples: the three magnetic components encode the tensor's spatial antisymmetric block. A different observer can mix those components with electric ones, so the source and force pictures must be tied to a specified frame.
statement: Magnetic field is the spatial antisymmetric part of the tensor, responsible for velocity-dependent deflection.

title: Magnetic components of field strength
body:
The magnetic field \(\mathbf B\) is the three-vector encoding the spatial antisymmetric components of the \cref{field tensor}{sr.field_tensor.frame_split} in a chosen inertial frame:
\[ F_{ij}=-\epsilon_{ijk}B_k. \]
Equivalently, \(B_k=-\tfrac12\epsilon_{kij}F_{ij}\). In SI units its operational force contribution is \(q\mathbf v\times\mathbf B\), where \(\mathbf v\) is the test charge's velocity in that same frame.
This definition fixes signs with \(+---\) and \(A_\mu=(\phi/c,-\mathbf A)\). It does not assert that every magnetic field must be produced by a steady current or be spatially uniform.
statement: With \(\epsilon_{123}=+1\), \(F_{ij}=-\epsilon_{ijk}B_k\) defines the magnetic tensor split.

title: Reading the spatial antisymmetric block
body:
A three-by-three antisymmetric spatial matrix has zero diagonal and three independent off-diagonal entries. With the adopted orientation,
\[ B_x=-F_{23},\quad B_y=-F_{31},\quad B_z=-F_{12}. \]
The reversed entries carry opposite signs. This packages a spatial antisymmetric two-index object as a three-component magnetic pseudovector. The packaging uses the orientation of three-dimensional space; the full spacetime tensor is the better object for general Lorentz transformations.
statement: The entries \(F_{23},F_{31},F_{12}\) give \(-B_x,-B_y,-B_z\).

title: Deriving the magnetic curl formula
body:
Use \(F_{ij}=\partial_iA_j-\partial_jA_i\), with \(A_i=-\mathbf A_i\). For example,
\[ \begin{aligned}F_{23}&=-\partial_y\mathbf A_z+\partial_z\mathbf A_y,\\ B_x=-F_{23}&=\partial_y\mathbf A_z-\partial_z\mathbf A_y.\end{aligned} \]
The two other cyclic choices give the remaining components of the curl, so \(\mathbf B=\nabla\times\mathbf A\). This combines the potential construction with the magnetic tensor split, rather than merely quoting a three-vector formula.
The argument is local and assumes a differentiable potential on the region. Global topology can require overlapping potential patches.
statement: \(\mathbf B=\nabla\times\mathbf A\) follows from the spatial potential derivatives.

title: Sideways force
body:
The cross product \(\mathbf v\times\mathbf B\) points perpendicular to velocity. A charge moving parallel to \(\mathbf B\) has no magnetic deflection; a transverse motion can bend into a curved path.
Since the force is perpendicular to \(\mathbf v\), its dot product with velocity is zero. In a purely magnetic external field, the point particle's speed and kinetic energy remain unchanged even while its direction changes. This statement concerns the ideal external-force law, not a full radiation-loss calculation.
statement: Magnetic force bends a charged path without doing instantaneous work on a point particle.

title: Current-carrying wire
body:
For a long straight wire carrying a steady current, symmetry and Maxwell's equations give magnetic field lines circling the wire. A moving test charge samples a local force according to its velocity and that circular field direction.
Changing to another inertial frame can alter both the source charge/current densities and the electric/magnetic split. It is not generally correct to say that the magnetic field simply disappears in a frame “moving with the current”: a wire can contain several charge populations with different velocities.
statement: A straight steady current produces circular magnetic field lines in the laboratory frame.

title: Frame-dependent split
body:
The distinction between electric and magnetic tensor entries uses one observer's time direction. A boost changes that direction, and therefore can change the magnetic components.
The magnetic field remains a useful, measurable three-vector in a specified frame. The caution is against treating it as a separate invariant substance, not against using ordinary magnetic calculations within that frame.
statement: A magnetic three-vector is not separately Lorentz invariant.

title: Why the local curl has zero divergence
body:
With \(\mathbf B=\nabla\times\mathbf A\), write \(B_i=\epsilon_{ijk}\partial_j\mathbf A_k\). Its divergence contracts the antisymmetric \(\epsilon_{ijk}\) with the symmetric pair of partial derivatives \(\partial_i\partial_j\), so it vanishes.
This explains the no-magnetic-source equation wherever the smooth local potential construction applies. It is not a proof that every imaginable theory forbids magnetic monopoles. Monopole models or nontrivial global configurations require revisiting the potential domain and patching assumptions.
statement:
A smooth local potential implies \(
abla\cdot\mathbf B=
abla\cdot(
abla	imes\mathbf A)=0\).

title: Not a separate substance
body:
Electric and magnetic forces can look quite different in one laboratory. The tensor transformation shows how these readings fit into a single interaction seen by different observers.
This unity does not mean one should identify \(\mathbf E\) with \(\mathbf B\) or ignore their different SI units. The factors of \(c\) and the frame choice are part of relating the components correctly.
statement: Magnetic and electric readings are related parts of one relativistic field.

title: From magnetism to electromagnetism
body: Magnetic effects were known long before relativity. Maxwell unified magnetism with electricity dynamically; special relativity then explained the electric/magnetic split as observer-dependent.
statement: Maxwell unified electric and magnetic dynamics; relativity clarified the observer-dependent split.

title: Connecting geometry with magnetic effects
body:
The spatial tensor entries tell us how magnetic components fit into spacetime geometry. The curl of a potential gives a convenient local calculation, and the velocity-dependent force states their operational effect.
Using all three views prevents common confusions: a drawn field line is not a particle trajectory, a magnetic component is not invariant, and a local potential identity is not the whole dynamical theory.
statement: The curl construction, tensor split and transverse force describe complementary aspects of magnetism.

title: One field, two frame faces
body:
Maxwell's theory relates electricity, magnetism and light. Relativistic notation makes their unity visible before choosing a laboratory frame: one field tensor supplies all six local components.
An observer's split into \(\mathbf E\) and \(\mathbf B\) is still physically useful, because it distinguishes force and power contributions in that frame. The unified description explains how those contributions change together when the observer changes.
statement: Electric and magnetic measurements are two observer-dependent descriptions of one electromagnetic field.

title: One strength tensor, several descriptions
body:
The electromagnetic field is the physical field represented covariantly by \(F_{\mu\nu}\). In a chosen inertial frame its six independent components are read as the \cref{electric field}{sr.electric_field.definition} and \cref{magnetic field}{sr.magnetic_field.definition}.
It is useful to distinguish this physical field from a particular potential representative. Gauge changes alter that representative without altering local field strength. A Lorentz transformation instead changes the observer's component description of the same strength. These are different operations.
statement: The physical electromagnetic strength is represented by one antisymmetric tensor and read as electric/magnetic components.

title: The six-component package
body:
The three time–space entries are proportional to \(\mathbf E\), and the three independent spatial entries encode \(\mathbf B\). They fill the antisymmetric \cref{field-strength table}{sr.field_tensor.frame_split} without introducing additional independent local components.
This is a reorganisation of the familiar fields, not a new equation of motion. Maxwell's equations constrain how those components vary and how they respond to sources. The tensor notation makes their transformation behaviour much easier to track.
statement: The tensor contains exactly the six electric and magnetic component readings in a fixed frame.

title: Observer-dependent decomposition
body:
Imagine marking which tensor entries involve your time axis. Those are the electric readings; the remaining spatial pairs give magnetic readings. A boosted observer draws a different time axis through spacetime.
Consequently the division of entries changes even though the field itself was not disturbed. This is a picture of changing description, rather than a process that physically converts an electric substance into a magnetic substance.
statement: Changing the observer changes the time–space split of the same field.

title: An explicit pair of electric–magnetic boost rules
body:
For \(S'\) moving along positive \(x\) at speed \(v\), the tensor boost rule gives, for example,
\[ \begin{aligned}E'_y&=\gamma(E_y-vB_z),\\ B'_z&=\gamma(B_z-vE_y/c^2).\end{aligned} \]
The factor \(c^2\) keeps the SI units consistent. These relations follow by transforming both indices of \(F\) and then reading its new electric and magnetic entries.
Thus a field that has only \(E_y\) in one frame generally has a magnetic component in the boosted frame. Not every field can be made purely electric or purely magnetic: invariant combinations of the components restrict such possibilities.
statement: A boost can produce \(E'_y=\gamma(E_y-vB_z)\) and \(B'_z=\gamma(B_z-vE_y/c^2)\).

title: A local physical field
body:
The field is assigned at each event. A charge responds to the field at its own location, while Maxwell's equations describe the connection between field variation and sources.
For the standard initial-value problem, disturbances propagate consistently with the light cone. This is a property of Maxwell dynamics and its allowed data, not a consequence of merely attaching a local value to every event. Static and instantaneous-looking solution formulas must still be interpreted with their assumptions and boundary conditions.
statement: Field strength and its local differential equations replace an instantaneous distant-force description.

title: The field participates in energy–momentum accounting
body:
A light pulse can deposit energy and push on an absorbing surface even where no material carrier travels with it. Static electric and magnetic configurations can also store energy.
The \cref{electromagnetic stress–energy tensor}{sr.em_stress_energy.definition} organises these facts into density, flow and stress. The field strength tells us about electromagnetic influence; a quadratic construction from that strength tells us about the field's own energy–momentum content.
statement: Fields carry energy and momentum as well as exerting forces on charges.

title: Not electricity plus magnetism glued together
body:
Electric and magnetic fields need not be thought of as two substances glued together. They are related component readings of one relativistic strength tensor.
Within one frame, distinguishing them is still useful: electric force can do work on a point charge and magnetic force gives a transverse contribution. The relativistic claim is that this division is not preserved independently under a change of observer.
statement: Unification relates the descriptions without erasing their frame-specific operational meanings.

title: Maxwell, Einstein, Minkowski
body: Maxwell unified electricity, magnetism, and light dynamically. Einstein's relativity and Minkowski's spacetime geometry then made the unity structurally explicit through covariant fields and tensors.
statement: Maxwell’s dynamical unification and the later spacetime reformulation answered different parts of the problem.

title: Choosing the representation for the task
body:
Tensor notation and three-vector language are complementary. The tensor keeps Lorentz transformations coherent; the electric and magnetic fields make laboratory forces and power transfer concrete.
A potential can help solve the equations, but gauge freedom means its components are not another set of uniquely measured field readings. Keeping field, components and representative distinct is the central organisational benefit of this formulation.
statement: Use the tensor to change observers and the electric/magnetic split to interpret measurements in one frame.
