title: Local laws of electromagnetism
body:
Charges and currents influence a local electromagnetic field, and the field can propagate even through source-free regions. Maxwell's equations specify those dynamics and constraints.
In potential language, the two halves have different origins. Varying the physical field action gives the sourced equation. The antisymmetric potential construction supplies the homogeneous identity. Understanding both makes the usual four three-vector equations feel like a connected system rather than a list.
statement: Maxwell’s equations combine sourced dynamics with the homogeneous field-strength identity.

title: The covariant vacuum equations with sources
body:
Use \(+---\), \(x^0=ct\), \(F_{0i}=E_i/c\), and \(j^\mu=(cho,\mathbf j)\). The equations are
\[ \partial_\mu F^{\mu
u}=\mu_0j^
u, \]
together with the vanishing cyclic sum of derivatives of \(F_{\mu
u}\). For a smooth local potential, that homogeneous condition follows from \(F_{\mu
u}=\partial_\mu A_
u-\partial_
u A_\mu\).
The sourced equation is a physical field law for the \cref{electromagnetic field}{sr.electromagnetic_field.definition}. The source is the \cref{four-current}{sr.four_current.definition}, which must be compatible with charge conservation. The pair does not determine a unique solution without appropriate initial and boundary data.
statement: In vacuum SI, Maxwell theory uses a sourced tensor equation and the cyclic derivative identity.

title: The physical source law
body:
For each value of \(\nu\), the sourced equation balances a derivative of field strength with one current component. Its four components include one electric-divergence condition and three equations involving magnetic curl and electric time variation.
The factor \(\mu_0\) fixes the SI normalisation; it is not a freely adjustable geometric factor. This equation supplies dynamics beyond the potential definition. A potential can define a perfectly antisymmetric tensor without that tensor satisfying the required source equation.
statement: \(\partial_\mu F^{\mu\nu}=\mu_0j^\nu\) relates local field derivatives to charge and current.

title: The homogeneous half in local potential form
body:
For a smooth local potential, the homogeneous relation is
\[  egin{aligned}\partial_\lambda F_{\mu
u}+\partial_\mu F_{
u\lambda}\ {}+\partial_
u F_{\lambda\mu}=0.\end{aligned} \]
The repeated cyclic pattern means that each choice of three distinct directions gives one condition. Splitting time and space produces \(
abla\cdot\mathbf B=0\) and \(
abla	imes\mathbf E=-\partial_t\mathbf B\).
There is no electric source term in this half. Its local identity follows from the potential representation; global topology or theories with magnetic sources require separate care.
statement: The cyclic derivative identity supplies zero magnetic divergence and Faraday induction.

title: Deriving the sourced equation by varying the action
body:
Choose the SI density
\[ \mathcal L=- rac{F_{\mu
u}F^{\mu
u}}{4\mu_0}-j^
u A_
u, \]
with prescribed current held fixed during the variation. A constant \(1/c\) multiplying \(\int d^4x\,\mathcal L\) supplies action units and cancels from stationarity. Since \(\delta F_{\mu
u}=\partial_\mu\delta A_
u-\partial_
u\delta A_\mu\), antisymmetry gives
\[ \delta\mathcal L=- rac{1}{\mu_0}F^{\mu
u}\partial_\mu\delta A_
u-j^
u\delta A_
u. \]
Apply the \cref{field variation method}{sr.field_equations.integration_by_parts}. Integration by parts moves the first derivative onto \(F\), and fixed boundary variations remove its surface term. Thus
\[ \delta S\propto\int d^4x\left( rac{\partial_\mu F^{\mu
u}}{\mu_0}-j^
uight)\delta A_
u. \]
Arbitrary interior \(\delta A_
u\) forces the bracket to vanish, giving \(\partial_\mu F^{\mu
u}=\mu_0j^
u\). The chosen density supplies the model and coefficient; the Euler–Lagrange reasoning supplies the local equation. This argument does not derive that physical choice of density from covariance alone.
statement: Varying the Maxwell density by the potential gives the sourced equation with its fixed coefficient.

title: Deriving the homogeneous identity from the potential
body:
Use the \cref{antisymmetric field construction}{sr.field_tensor.definition}. In the cyclic expression, \(\partial_\lambda F_{\mu
u}\) contributes \(\partial_\lambda\partial_\mu A_
u-\partial_\lambda\partial_
u A_\mu\), with analogous terms from the other two permutations.
The positive term involving \(A_
u\) cancels the negative \(\partial_\mu\partial_\lambda A_
u\); the pairs involving \(A_\mu\) and \(A_\lambda\) cancel in the same way. Smoothness lets the partial derivatives commute.
This establishes the homogeneous identity without using stationary action or the current. It is why the two halves of Maxwell's equations should not be presented as if they both came from the same algebraic step.
statement: Every second potential derivative cancels its reversed partner in the cyclic sum.

title: Recovering the four laboratory equations
body:
With the stated tensor components, the sourced equation gives
\[ \nabla\cdot\mathbf E=\rho/\epsilon_0,\qquad \nabla\times\mathbf B-\frac{\partial_t\mathbf E}{c^2}=\mu_0\mathbf j. \]
The homogeneous identity gives
\[ \nabla\cdot\mathbf B=0,\qquad \nabla\times\mathbf E+\partial_t\mathbf B=0. \]
The factors agree because \(\epsilon_0\mu_0c^2=1\). This split expresses the same tensor equations in laboratory language. It contains constraints as well as time-evolution relations; arbitrary initial electric and magnetic fields need not satisfy all four laws.
statement: The covariant pair yields Gauss’s two laws, Faraday induction and Ampère–Maxwell evolution.

title: Consistency with charge conservation
body:
Take \(\partial_
u\) of \(\partial_\mu F^{\mu
u}=\mu_0j^
u\). The left side contracts a symmetric pair of derivatives with an antisymmetric tensor, so it is zero:
\[ 0=\partial_
u\partial_\mu F^{\mu
u}=\mu_0\partial_
u j^
u. \]
Therefore any sufficiently smooth Maxwell solution requires \(\partial_
u j^
u=0\). This is a consistency consequence of the sourced field equation.
It does not mean that an arbitrary externally prescribed current becomes conserved merely because it is inserted into the equation. An incompatible current means that the intended Maxwell problem has no solution with those assumptions.
statement: The divergence of the sourced equation forces the current divergence to vanish.

title: Source-free waves
body:
Set \(j^\mu=0\) in a region. The equations still allow changing electric and magnetic fields linked by their curl relations, including propagating waves.
A wave may have been generated by sources elsewhere or by earlier initial data. Removing the local source term therefore does not require setting the solution to zero. The \cref{potential wave equation}{sr.wave_equation.maxwell_origin} and plane-wave examples develop these consequences.
statement: Source-free does not mean field-free: nonzero radiation can propagate through regions where current vanishes.

title: Not four unrelated formulas
body:
Gauss's laws and the two curl equations are not unrelated formulas with coincidentally matching constants. They are different components of the covariant source law and homogeneous field identity.
Their different roles still matter. The divergence conditions constrain admissible data, while the curl equations describe coupled time evolution. Treating them together helps keep charge conservation and wave propagation consistent.
statement: The laboratory equations belong to a single covariant dynamical and geometric structure.

title: Maxwell's synthesis
body: Maxwell combined experimental laws due to Coulomb, Ampere and Faraday with the displacement current needed for consistent charge flow. His 1865 theory predicted transverse electromagnetic waves travelling at a speed close to the measured speed of light, leading him to identify light as electromagnetic. The theory preceded special relativity, but its failure to fit Galilean transformations became one of relativity's central historical problems.
statement: Maxwell connected consistent charge flow with transverse electromagnetic waves and the measured speed of light.

title: From local equations to a physical solution
body:
The sourced law comes from the chosen electromagnetic action. The homogeneous law follows from the smooth local potential construction. Their component forms constrain the electric and magnetic data and link their subsequent evolution.
Conservation and wave propagation are then consequences to investigate, not extra disconnected facts. A particular solution still requires a compatible current and the relevant initial or boundary information.
statement: The field action and potential identity give a connected system for sources, constraints and propagating fields.

title: A covariant gauge choice
body:
Gauge freedom lets us choose a convenient representative of one electromagnetic field. Lorenz gauge uses a spacetime divergence, so the condition has the same form for all inertial observers.
It is particularly useful when solving the potential equations. That usefulness should not be confused with a new physical law: the gauge condition restricts the description, not which electric and magnetic field is present.
statement: Lorenz gauge restricts potential representatives by a Lorentz-scalar condition.

title: The covariant divergence condition
body:
Lorenz gauge imposes
\[ \partial_\mu A^\mu=0 \]
on a potential representative. With \(A^\mu=(\phi/c,\mathbf A)\) and \(x^0=ct\), this is \(\nabla\cdot\mathbf A+c^{-2}\partial_t\phi=0\).
The condition is compatible with \cref{gauge freedom}{sr.gauge_invariance.definition}: it chooses within a family of equivalent potentials. It is an example of gauge fixing, but does not necessarily fix the representative uniquely. Boundary and initial conditions must be considered alongside it.
statement: Lorenz gauge is \(\partial_\mu A^\mu=0\), or \(\nabla\cdot\mathbf A+c^{-2}\partial_t\phi=0\) in SI.

title: Why a gauge condition is allowed
body:
The physical field tensor is unchanged by \(A_\mu\to A_\mu+\partial_\mu\chi\). We can use that freedom to alter the divergence of the potential while keeping the electric and magnetic fields fixed.
A gauge condition is legitimate when an allowed gauge function reaches it for the region and boundary problem in question. It is not an independent restriction placed on a measured field strength. This distinction matters when solving initial-value problems or handling boundaries.
statement: Equivalent potentials permit a simplifying condition without changing local field strength.

title: Why this gauge is relativistic
body:
The derivative index and vector index are contracted in \(\partial_\mu A^\mu\). Under a constant Lorentz transformation, the inverse transformation on the derivative cancels the one on the vector component.
The result is a scalar. Therefore a potential satisfying zero divergence in one inertial frame satisfies it in every Lorentz-related frame. This explains why the condition is convenient for relativistic calculations without making it a physical observable.
statement: A zero scalar divergence remains zero after an inertial frame change.

title: Application: simplifying Maxwell’s potential equation
body:
As an application, suppose the sourced Maxwell equation \(\partial_\mu F^{\mu
u}=\mu_0j^
u\) is already given. Substituting the potential definition and commuting partial derivatives gives
\[ \Box A^
u-\partial^
u(\partial_\mu A^\mu)=\mu_0j^
u. \]
Lorenz gauge makes the second term vanish, leaving \(\Box A^
u=\mu_0j^
u\). Here \(\Box=c^{-2}\partial_t^2-
abla^2\).
This is an application of a chosen gauge to a supplied dynamical equation, not a derivation of the gauge choice from Maxwell's laws. The full wave-equation argument is developed later; we do not use that future result as a prerequisite for defining Lorenz gauge.
statement: Given the sourced Maxwell equation, Lorenz gauge removes the longitudinal derivative term.

title: It may not fix everything
body:
If \(\partial_\mu A^\mu=0\), a further change \(A'^\mu=A^\mu+\partial^\mu\chi\) has divergence \(\partial_\mu A'^\mu=\Box\chi\).
Consequently every allowed solution of the homogeneous equation \(\Box\chi=0\) preserves Lorenz gauge. Boundary conditions may remove some or all of this residual freedom. Zero divergence alone should therefore not be described as selecting one unique potential.
statement: A further gauge change preserves Lorenz gauge when \(\Box\chi=0\).

title: Not a new physical law
body:
A physical electromagnetic configuration can be described by many potentials. Lorenz gauge is a condition on those mathematical representatives, not an extra force or source.
The gauge-fixed potential must still solve the actual field equations and satisfy the problem's data. Conversely, satisfying zero divergence by itself says nothing about whether a proposed potential describes the required sources or radiation.
statement: The gauge condition changes the representative rather than adding electromagnetic dynamics.

title: Lorenz, not Lorentz
body: Ludvig Lorenz published the condition in 1867 while developing a retarded-potential account of electromagnetism. The nearly universal misspelling “Lorentz gauge” is tempting because Hendrik Lorentz worked on electrodynamics and the condition is Lorentz-covariant. The two physicists and the two names are nevertheless distinct.
statement: Ludvig Lorenz introduced the condition in 1867; he is distinct from Hendrik Lorentz.

title: Separate the gauge condition from the field law
body:
Lorenz gauge removes a redundant part of the potential description and retains Lorentz-covariant form. The electromagnetic action or Maxwell equations determine the physical dynamics.
Keeping these jobs separate avoids circular reasoning: we can define and reach the gauge without first proving a potential wave equation, then use it to simplify that equation when the dynamical input is available.
statement: Covariant gauge choice and dynamical field equations have different jobs.

title: Redundancy without physical change
body:
The same electric and magnetic field can have many potential descriptions. Gauge invariance identifies changes that alter this description without changing the local physical strength.
This redundancy is useful because it lets us simplify a calculation while preserving predictions. It is also a constraint: a proposed interaction must not turn a purely representational change into a different classical force.
statement: Smooth gradient changes of the potential leave local electromagnetic strength unchanged.

title: The local gauge equivalence of potentials
body:
Electromagnetic gauge invariance is the equivalence of potentials related by
\[ A'_\mu=A_\mu+\partial_\mu\chi. \]
For a sufficiently smooth function \(\chi\), these potentials have the same \cref{field tensor}{sr.field_tensor.definition}, hence the same local classical electric and magnetic fields in any chosen frame.
The transformation does not change spacetime coordinates or the inertial observer. Global boundary conditions and topology can restrict which gauge functions are allowed. The local statement here should not be silently extended beyond that setting.
statement: For smooth \(\chi\), \(A_\mu\mapsto A_\mu+\partial_\mu\chi\) leaves \(F_{\mu\nu}\) unchanged.

title: Deriving the unchanged field strength
body:
Start with the \cref{potential construction}{sr.field_tensor.definition} and replace \(A_\mu\) by \(A_\mu+\partial_\mu\chi\). The change is
\[  egin{aligned}F'_{\mu
u}-F_{\mu
u}&=\partial_\mu\partial_
u\chi\ &\quad-\partial_
u\partial_\mu\chi=0.\end{aligned} \]
The last equality uses commuting mixed partial derivatives for a smooth local gauge function. Thus the cancellation is a property of antisymmetric differentiation, not an additional Maxwell equation imposed on \(\chi\).
Field-strength terms in an action are therefore unchanged exactly. Couplings to charged matter require their own boundary or matter-transformation check; that does not follow solely by inspecting the free field term.
statement: The added Hessian is symmetric, so antisymmetrising it gives zero.

title: Many descriptions, one field
body:
Think of several labels attached to one physical configuration. Changing the label is not a disturbance sent through space; it is a different way to describe what is already there.
A gauge function makes this comparison local, since its gradient can vary from event to event. The analogy is about redundancy, not about declaring every change of a field variable unphysical. Only the specified gauge-related changes belong to the same equivalence class.
statement: Gauge-related potentials are different representatives of one local field.

title: Not every change in \(A_\mu\) is physical
body:
Adding a pure gradient can alter every potential component while leaving \(F\) unchanged. A detector responding to local electromagnetic forces does not register that as a new field.
Conversely, an arbitrary change of potential is not generally pure gauge and can change the field strength. Gauge invariance is a precise equivalence relation, not permission to change the model freely.
statement: A change in the written potential need not be a change in physical field strength.

title: Observable quantities
body:
The field tensor and its electric/magnetic readings determine local classical electromagnetic forces. Individual gauge-dependent potential components do not have this direct status.
Potentials remain important for solving the dynamics and describing coupling. Quantum interference can also depend on gauge-invariant phase or loop information; that is not a licence to call a single gauge-dependent component observable. State which invariant quantity is being predicted.
statement: Classical local force predictions depend on gauge-invariant structure.

title: Why gauge fixing exists
body:
If several potentials represent the same field, we can impose a useful extra condition on those representatives. This is \cref{gauge fixing}{sr.gauge_fixing.definition}, not another dynamical force law.
A legitimate condition must be reachable for the field and boundary problem under consideration. It can leave residual freedom. The aim is to remove redundant calculation, rather than to remove physical solutions or assume that every component is independently measurable.
statement: Gauge fixing restricts representatives without selecting a different electromagnetic field.

title: What gauge symmetry constrains—and what it does not
body:
For a charged worldline, the standard minimal interaction is \(-q\int A_\mu dx^\mu\). A gauge change makes its action change only by an endpoint term, so fixed-endpoint motion is unchanged.
This helps explain why the interaction is consistent. It does not prove that it is the only possible interaction: gauge-invariant terms involving field strength, spin or higher derivatives can be added in more general models. The \cref{minimal choice}{sr.minimal_coupling.why_minimal} deliberately excludes such extra structure.
statement: Gauge compatibility constrains interactions, but does not uniquely select minimal coupling.

title: From potential freedom to gauge theory
body:
The freedom to change electromagnetic potentials without changing the fields was already useful in classical calculations. Twentieth-century developments connected this freedom to transformations of charged matter and its quantum phase.
The modern organising principle is broader than the elementary cancellation shown here. Keeping the classical local argument explicit makes it possible to appreciate that extension without treating every later gauge-theory result as already proved.
statement: Classical potential redundancy became a broader principle for organising interactions.

title: Three distinct uses of the same freedom
body:
The local cancellation in \(F\) tells us which potential changes are redundant. Gauge fixing uses that redundancy to simplify representation, and coupling arguments must preserve it in physical predictions.
These are connected but different jobs. The existence of a redundancy neither proves a particular field equation nor uniquely chooses an interaction; those require an action and stated physical assumptions.
statement: Gauge invariance identifies redundant potential descriptions and tests the consistency of couplings.

title: Charge flow as a four-vector
body:
A frame measures both how much charge occupies a volume and how much crosses its boundary. Moving observers disagree about that volume and about which charges are moving.
The four-current packages these density and flow measurements into one object with a Lorentz transformation rule. Charge conservation is a further equation about this object, not something guaranteed merely by writing four components.
statement: Four-current joins local charge density with the rate and direction of charge flow.

title: Charge density and current density together
body:
The four-current is the relativistic source object
\[ j^\mu\coloneqq(c\rho,\mathbf j), \]
where \(\rho\) is signed charge per volume and \(\mathbf j\) is signed charge crossing unit area per unit time in the same frame. Its components transform as a \cref{four-vector}{sr.four_vectors.definition}.
For one population moving with velocity \(\mathbf v\), \(\mathbf j=\rho\mathbf v\). Several populations contribute additively, including their charge signs. The local continuity condition \(\partial_\mu j^\mu=0\) is a physical conservation requirement on the current, not part of counting its entries.
statement: In SI, \(j^\mu=(c\rho,\mathbf j)\) is the local charge four-current.

title: Why \(c\rho\)
body:
Charge density has SI units \(\mathrm{C\,m^{-3}}\). Multiplying by \(c\) gives \(\mathrm{C\,m^{-2}\,s^{-1}}\), the units of all three current-density components.
The same factor makes \(\partial_0j^0=\partial_t\rho\) when \(x^0=ct\). It therefore makes both the component dimensions and the continuity equation consistent. Setting \(c=1\) can hide this reasoning, so it is worth seeing the explicit conversion first.
statement: \(c\rho\) has the same units as current density and works with \(\partial_0=c^{-1}\partial_t\).

title: Charge density alone is not enough
body:
A neutral wire in one frame need not have zero charge density in every other frame. A boost changes simultaneous volume measurements and the motion assigned to each population of charges.
The invariant charge assigned to a given collection does not require its density to remain unchanged. Four-current provides the relation between the new density and current, rather than treating each as an unrelated observer disagreement.
statement: Density and current mix under a boost; charge density alone is not a Lorentz scalar.

title: Local charge flow
body:
A small spatial volume contains signed charge. Current through its boundary can increase or decrease that amount, just as a fluid flux changes the amount of fluid in a container.
The analogy concerns accounting, not a claim that every charge distribution is one continuous material fluid. Positive and negative carriers can move differently, and the field description can add their signed contributions. The four-current keeps the local density and flux together.
statement: Think of charge crossing the faces of a small spacetime cell.

title: Expanding the local conservation condition
body:
Use \(j^0=c\rho\), \(j^i=\mathbf j_i\) and \(\partial_0=c^{-1}\partial_t\). Expanding its four-divergence gives
\[ \partial_\mu j^\mu=\partial_t\rho+\nabla\cdot\mathbf j. \]
Setting this expression to zero is the local charge conservation law. The cancellation of \(c\) explains why it reproduces the familiar continuity equation.
This calculation translates a conservation condition; it does not prove conservation from the definition of a four-current. Maxwell consistency supplies one route to that physical condition in the electromagnetic model.
statement: If charge is locally conserved, \(\partial_\mu j^\mu=\partial_t\rho+\nabla\cdot\mathbf j=0\).

title: Source for the field
body:
In the stated SI convention, the local source equation is
\[ \partial_\mu F^{\mu\nu}=\mu_0j^\nu. \]
Its time component gives Gauss's electric law and its spatial components give the Ampère–Maxwell law. Thus density and current source related parts of one field equation.
The current must satisfy continuity for these equations to be consistent. Defining a formal four-component source with nonzero divergence would not produce a valid Maxwell solution.
statement: The sourced vacuum Maxwell equation is \(\partial_\mu F^{\mu\nu}=\mu_0j^\nu\).

title: Wire intuition
body:
Suppose a laboratory describes a wire by zero net charge density and current \(j_x\). For a frame moving along the wire at speed \(v\), four-vector transformation gives
\[ \rho'=\gamma(\rho-vj_x/c^2)=-\gamma vj_x/c^2. \]
This example shows directly how a current contribution becomes a density contribution. It does not create net charge from nothing: the two frames use different simultaneous slices and volume elements.
For a real wire, ions and electrons can be transformed separately and their currents then added. There is no single rest frame for all carriers in a current-carrying conductor.
statement: A wire with \(\rho=0\) and longitudinal current \(j_x\) has \(\rho'=-\gamma vj_x/c^2\) after a longitudinal boost.

title: Separate covariance from conservation
body:
The four-vector rule relates charge density and current measured by different inertial observers. The divergence equation states whether the resulting local flow conserves charge.
A source used in Maxwell dynamics must satisfy both the transformation meaning and the conservation condition. Keeping those jobs distinct prevents a definition of notation from being mistaken for a proof of a physical law.
statement: Source transformation and source conservation are separate requirements on the same local object.

title: The economical electromagnetic interaction
body:
To make a charged particle respond to an electromagnetic field, we must choose an interaction. The standard minimal choice couples its path directly to the four-potential.
This choice is local and Lorentz covariant, and changes by a boundary term under a gauge transformation. Those properties help justify it. They do not exclude all other allowed interactions, so “minimal” names a model choice rather than a theorem of gauge symmetry alone.
statement: Minimal coupling is a specified economical interaction, compatible with gauge freedom.

title: The minimally coupled particle action
body:
For a structureless massive particle of signed charge \(q\), the minimally coupled action is
\[ S=-mc^2\int d\tau-q\int A_\mu dx^\mu. \]
The first term is the free-particle model. The second samples the \cref{potential}{sr.vector_potential.definition} locally along the worldline. With \(+---\), it adds \(q\mathbf A\cdot\mathbf v-q\phi\) to the coordinate-time Lagrangian.
This definition specifies the coupling and sign used in the force derivation. It assumes a prescribed external field and omits extra spin, dipole and finite-size interactions. Gauge compatibility is a constraint on this model, not a unique derivation of it.
statement: The classical point-particle interaction is \(S_{\rm int}=-q\int A_\mu dx^\mu\) in the stated convention.

title: What minimal means
body:
The worldline term uses the charge and potential directly, without adding new response parameters. More elaborate models may couple dipole moments to field strength or contain finite-size and higher-derivative effects.
Such terms can also respect gauge invariance. Therefore symmetry alone does not force every charged object to obey the structureless minimal model. The economical choice is valuable because it describes a broad regime with few assumptions, and its predictions can be tested within that regime.
statement: Minimal excludes additional field-strength, derivative and internal-structure couplings.

title: Checking covariance and gauge compatibility
body:
The potential is a covector and \(dx^\mu\) a vector displacement, so \(A_\mu dx^\mu\) is a scalar. Under \(A_\mu\to A_\mu+\partial_\mu\chi\),
\[ \begin{aligned}\Delta S_{\rm int}&=-q\int\partial_\mu\chi\,dx^\mu\\ &=-q[\chi(x_2)-\chi(x_1)].\end{aligned} \]
The chain rule turns the added integrand into a derivative along the path. For fixed endpoint events, this change has zero path variation, so it leaves the equations of motion unchanged.
This combines the potential's gauge rule with the variational boundary condition. It establishes consistency of the chosen interaction without deriving its strength or excluding nonminimal alternatives.
statement: The contraction is Lorentz scalar and its gauge change is a fixed-endpoint boundary term.

title: Momentum replacement
body:
In a coordinate-time description, differentiating the interaction term \(q\mathbf A\cdot\mathbf v\) shifts the spatial canonical momentum. For a relativistic structureless particle,
\[ \mathbf p_{\rm can}=\gamma m\mathbf v+q\mathbf A. \]
Thus \(\mathbf p_{\rm can}-q\mathbf A\) is the mechanical momentum entering the free kinetic-energy relation. This explains the common “momentum replacement” language.
An unqualified expression \(p_\mu-qA_\mu\) can hide sign and definition changes between worldline, Hamiltonian and quantum conventions. Define the momentum and index placement before transferring that shorthand to a different formulation.
statement: For \(\mathbf p_{\rm can}=\mathbf p_{\rm mech}+q\mathbf A\), the mechanical combination is \(\mathbf p_{\rm can}-q\mathbf A\).

title: Gauge compatibility
body:
Two gauge-related potentials give different-looking interaction terms. Their difference is a contribution at the endpoints, so all allowed trial paths acquire the same variation-free shift.
The stationary path is therefore unchanged. The canonical momentum can shift with the representative, while the mechanical velocity need not. This is a concrete way to see why gauge dependence in an intermediate variable is compatible with gauge-independent motion.
statement: A gauge change adjusts the representative and canonical description without changing the path.

title: Canonical versus mechanical momentum
body:
Use
\[ L=-mc^2\sqrt{1-v^2/c^2}+q\mathbf A\cdot\mathbf v-q\phi. \]
Differentiating the free term gives \(\gamma m\mathbf v\); differentiating the linear velocity coupling gives \(q\mathbf A\). Hence
\[ \mathbf p_{\rm can}=\gamma m\mathbf v+q\mathbf A. \]
At low speed this reduces to the example in \cref{canonical momentum}{sr.canonical_momentum.velocity_dependent}. The potential term explains why canonical momentum can differ from the momentum inferred from mechanical motion.
statement: The minimal coordinate-time Lagrangian gives \(\mathbf p_{\rm can}=\gamma m\mathbf v+q\mathbf A\).

title: Why this coupling leads to the force law
body:
The interaction depends both on the potential sampled along the path and on the path displacement. Varying these two dependencies gives two potential-derivative terms.
After integration by parts they combine antisymmetrically into \(F_{\mu\nu}\). The \cref{charged-path derivation}{sr.lorentz_force_law.derivative_combination} shows the calculation. This is a consequence to be checked from the chosen action, not a force law used to define that same action in reverse.
statement: Varying the chosen charged action produces field-strength force, rather than requiring it as an input.

title: Not an arbitrary substitution trick
body:
The shorthand of replacing a momentum is useful only after the action, charge sign and relevant momentum have been identified. Applying it blindly can mix canonical and mechanical quantities or incompatible unit conventions.
Minimal coupling is supported by its covariance, gauge compatibility and successful physics. Those reasons are stronger than a mnemonic, but still leave room for additional interactions in models with more structure.
statement: The interaction is a physical model with a gauge-consistency check, not a universal substitution rule.

title: A bridge to modern gauge theory
body: The coupling of charged particles to electromagnetic potentials became a prototype for how interactions are introduced in gauge theories. Later quantum theory made this structural role even more prominent.
statement: Electromagnetic charge coupling became a prototype for the interaction structure of gauge theories.

title: The scope of the minimal model
body:
The minimal worldline term links charge to potential at each event and has a gauge change confined to fixed endpoints. This makes it a convenient interaction to combine with stationary action.
The resulting Lorentz-force model describes a structureless test particle in an external field. Self-force, dipole response and other corrections are separate modelling steps, rather than consequences silently contained in the word “minimal”.
statement: A local scalar coupling yields gauge-compatible point-particle motion within its stated approximation.

title: How fields move charges
body:
A field description becomes a particle prediction only when a dynamical coupling tells us how the charge responds. The Lorentz force is that response for the minimally coupled structureless test particle.
The covariant equation treats the interaction as one spacetime law. In one frame it splits into electric acceleration, magnetic deflection and an energy-transfer equation. The split is useful, but all these parts must agree with the same action convention.
statement: External electromagnetic strength changes a test particle’s four-momentum through its charge and motion.

title: The covariant external-field force
body:
The covariant external-field force law is
\[ \frac{dp^\mu}{d\tau}=qF^\mu{}_{\nu}U^\nu,\qquad p^\mu=mU^\mu. \]
Here \(q\) is signed charge, \(\tau\) the proper time, and \(m\) fixed invariant mass. The \cref{four-velocity}{sr.velocity_four_vector.definition} specifies the local motion and the \cref{field tensor}{sr.field_tensor.frame_split} supplies electromagnetic strength.
We use \(+---\) and the potential convention giving \(F_{0i}=E_i/c\). The law describes a prescribed external field and neglects self-force and internal structure. Those qualifications are part of its model, not optional sign conventions.
statement: For a fixed-mass charged test particle, \(dp^\mu/d\tau=qF^\mu{}_{\nu}U^\nu\).

title: Recovering the familiar spatial force
body:
Use \(U^\mu=\gamma(c,\mathbf v)\). With the stated field components, the spatial part of \(qF^\mu{}_{\nu}U^\nu\) is \(q\gamma(\mathbf E+\mathbf v\times\mathbf B)\).
Since \(dp^i/d\tau=\gamma\,dp^i/dt\), the same \(\gamma\) cancels on both sides:
\[ \frac{d\mathbf p}{dt}=q(\mathbf E+\mathbf v\times\mathbf B). \]
The momentum is relativistic mechanical momentum \(\gamma m\mathbf v\), not simply \(m\mathbf v\) at arbitrary speed. The cancellation explains how the familiar three-vector expression fits the covariant equation.
statement: Dividing the spatial proper-time equation by \(dt/d\tau=\gamma\) gives \(d\mathbf p/dt=q(\mathbf E+\mathbf v\times\mathbf B)\).

title: Setting up a valid charged-path variation
body:
Use the \cref{minimal action}{sr.minimal_coupling.definition} but describe the varied paths by one fixed parameter \(\lambda\). Let \(w=\sqrt{\eta_{\mu\nu}\dot x^\mu\dot x^\nu}\), with dots now meaning \(d/d\lambda\). The Lagrangian along this parameter is
\[ L_\lambda=-mcw-qA_\mu\dot x^\mu. \]
The identity \(w=c\,d\tau/d\lambda\) converts it back to the proper-time action. During the variation, the path and therefore \(d\tau\) can change; treating \(\tau\) as an unchanged external parameter would miss that variation.
Apply stationary action with fixed endpoint events. The resulting Euler–Lagrange equation uses derivatives with respect to \(x^\rho\) and \(\dot x^\rho\), calculated in the next combination argument.
statement: A fixed-parameter path variation avoids incorrectly holding proper time fixed during changes of the path.

The action principle supplies the stationarity condition; the chosen coupling supplies the two derivatives; antisymmetry combines them into field strength. The resulting law depends on \(F\), not a pure-gradient part of the potential.
statement: The two potential variations combine to give \(dp_\rho/d\tau=qF_{\rho\nu}U^\nu\).

title: Electric and magnetic roles
body:
In one laboratory frame, the magnetic contribution is perpendicular to the test charge's velocity. It can bend the path without directly changing the particle's energy through work. The electric contribution can point along the motion and transfer energy.
Another moving observer decomposes the same force differently. Thus these roles explain measurements within a frame; they are not a division into two independently invariant mechanisms.
statement: Electric force can change speed; magnetic force supplies a transverse deflection in the chosen frame.

title: Power delivered to the particle
body:
For fixed invariant mass, the \cref{work–energy relation}{sr.momentum_four_vector.work_energy} identifies \(dE/dt=\mathbf v\cdot d\mathbf p/dt\). Substitute the Lorentz force:
\[ \begin{aligned}\frac{dE}{dt}&=q\mathbf E\cdot\mathbf v\\ &\quad+q(\mathbf v\times\mathbf B)\cdot\mathbf v\\ &=q\mathbf E\cdot\mathbf v.\end{aligned} \]
The final step uses the perpendicularity of a cross product to its input vector. This is a statement about energy transfer to the ideal test particle in this frame. It does not say that time-dependent magnetic fields are irrelevant to energy transfer: Maxwell induction can generate an electric field, and self-radiation requires a larger energy balance.
statement: The work rate is \(dE/dt=q\mathbf E\cdot\mathbf v\); the magnetic cross product contributes zero.

title: Conventions matter
body:
The force sign cannot be checked independently of the potential and field-tensor definitions. Here a positive signed charge at rest has spatial force \(q\mathbf E\), because \(F^{i0}=E_i/c\).
If another source uses the opposite metric or defines \(F\) with the opposite derivative order, its written covariant formula may look different. Translate the whole set of conventions and verify the resting-charge limit. Do not repair a sign by changing only one isolated equation.
statement: Use \(+---\), \(x^0=ct\), \(F_{0i}=E_i/c\), and \(S_{\rm int}=-q\int A_\mu dx^\mu\) together.

title: Not the whole story for an emitting charge
body:
A charged particle creates a field as well as responding to one. The test-particle model treats the specified external field as given and neglects that back-reaction.
For a radiating charge, energy and momentum carried away must be accounted for by a consistent particle-plus-field treatment. Simply inserting the singular point-charge self-field into the external-force formula is not a completed self-force derivation.
statement: The prescribed external-field law omits the dynamical problem of the charge’s own field.

title: Lorentz's electron theory
body: The force formula emerged from late nineteenth-century attempts to describe charged matter inside Maxwell's field theory; closely related forms appeared before Lorentz's mature electron theory. Lorentz made the force on moving charged particles central to a systematic electrodynamics of electrons. Its modern covariant form shows more clearly than the historical three-vector expression that electric and magnetic forces are components of one interaction.
statement: Lorentz’s electron theory made forces on moving charges central to Maxwellian electrodynamics.

title: Checking the action, force and power together
body:
The action calculation produces the field tensor contracted with four-velocity. Splitting that result in a frame gives the three-force and its power transfer, with matching signs and units.
This coherence is a useful check on the model. Its limits—external field, fixed mass and neglected internal/self effects—must remain visible when comparing it with a real radiating or structured charged body.
statement: One covariant force law accounts for spatial deflection and energy transfer in every inertial frame.

title: Local bookkeeping
body:
A statement about a fixed total charge is useful, but local conservation says more. It specifies how charge can move between neighbouring regions through a current.
The continuity equation expresses that balance at each event. Integrating it recovers the relation between a volume's charge change and current crossing its surface, so local and global descriptions fit together.
statement: Charge in a region changes through boundary current rather than disappearing locally.

title: The local continuity law
body:
For \(j^\mu=(c\rho,\mathbf j)\) in coordinates \(x^0=ct\), charge conservation is
\[ \partial_\mu j^\mu=\partial_t\rho+\nabla\cdot\mathbf j=0. \]
The current is the \cref{local charge-flow object}{sr.four_current.definition}. Positive outward divergence means that the density must decrease, with the opposite sign for inward convergence.
This is a local physical condition, not just a definition of \(j\). In Maxwell theory it is also required by consistency of the sourced field equation. Global conserved charge additionally needs no net flux through the chosen system boundary.
statement: Local charge conservation is \(\partial_\mu j^\mu=0\), or \(\partial_t\rho+\nabla\cdot\mathbf j=0\).

title: What the equation says
body:
Imagine a very small box containing charge. If more signed charge leaves than enters, the charge inside decreases. In differential form, positive \(\nabla\cdot\mathbf j\) therefore requires negative \(\partial_t\rho\).
The accounting concerns signed charge: positive and negative carriers can contribute with different signs. It does not require the number of each species to be separately conserved, provided their total charge balance is respected.
statement: Outward current divergence reduces local density; inward convergence increases it.

title: From local to integral form
body:
Define \(Q_V(t)=\int_V\rho(t,\mathbf x)d^3x\) for a fixed spatial volume. Integrate the local continuity equation:
\[ \frac{dQ_V}{dt}=-\int_V\nabla\cdot\mathbf j\,d^3x. \]
The divergence theorem changes the right side to a boundary flux:
\[ \frac{dQ_V}{dt}=-\oint_{\partial V}\mathbf j\cdot d\mathbf a. \]
The area vector points outward, which explains the minus sign. If the net outward flux vanishes, the enclosed charge is constant. A moving boundary requires including the charge carried by that boundary motion; the fixed-volume formula should not be applied unchanged.
statement: For a fixed volume, \(dQ_V/dt=-\oint_{\partial V}\mathbf j\cdot d\mathbf a\).

title: Consistency of Maxwell's equations
body:
Use the \cref{sourced Maxwell equation}{sr.maxwells_equations.sourced_equation} \(\partial_\mu F^{\mu
u}=\mu_0j^
u\). Taking one more divergence gives
\[ C\coloneqq\partial_
u\partial_\mu F^{\mu
u}=\mu_0\partial_
u j^
u. \]
Swap the dummy indices and commute the partial derivatives. Antisymmetry of \(F\) then gives \(C=-C\), so \(C=0\). Since \(\mu_0
e0\), it follows that \(\partial_
u j^
u=0\).
The physical field law supplies the source relation and the tensor construction supplies its antisymmetry. Together they force continuity. This is a Maxwell consistency proof, not a general proof of every possible charge conservation principle from geometry alone.
statement: Antisymmetry of field strength and commuting derivatives enforce charge continuity in Maxwell theory.

title: Why antisymmetry matters
body:
Let \(C=\partial_\nu\partial_\mu F^{\mu\nu}\). Renaming the summed indices does not change the value, while reversing the field indices changes its sign.
For smooth fields the two partial derivatives commute. Consequently the renamed expression is \(-C\), so \(2C=0\). This argument explains the cancellation without assuming that each field component or each derivative separately vanishes.
statement: A symmetric double derivative contracts to zero with an antisymmetric field tensor.

title: Not just a global rule
body:
One could invent a rule in which charge vanishes in one region and appears far away at the same rate. The total might remain unchanged, but there would be no local flow accounting for the transfer.
The continuity equation rules out that unsupported local disappearance. It connects density change to a current through neighbouring boundaries. The global statement follows when the flux conditions are included, rather than replacing this stronger local information.
statement: A constant total does not alone specify the local current connecting charge changes.

title: Sources must be compatible
body:
If an external current is specified independently, check \(\partial_\mu j^\mu\) before trying to solve Maxwell's equations. A nonzero result contradicts the identically vanishing double divergence of antisymmetric field strength.
One may need to include omitted charge carriers or revise the source model. Imposing a gauge condition cannot repair a physically inconsistent source; gauge freedom changes the potential description, not its divergence consistency requirement.
statement: A prescribed Maxwell source must satisfy continuity; a nonconserved source is incompatible with the field equation.

title: From circuits to fields
body: Conservation of electric charge was first familiar from electrical and chemical phenomena. Field theory sharpens it into a local continuity equation tied to the structure of Maxwell's equations.
statement: Field theory sharpened charge conservation into a local density-and-flux law.

title: One law at local and regional scales
body:
The differential equation states the event-by-event balance. Its volume integral states how a selected region exchanges charge with its surroundings. Maxwell theory supplies a specific consistency route to the same local condition.
These are related views with different uses. Keeping the boundary and source assumptions visible prevents a conserved total from being mistaken for a complete description of transport.
statement: Continuity connects local transport, compatible sources and global charge totals.

title: Energy stored in fields
body:
A charged configuration can leave energy in the electric field between its sources. Magnetic fields and freely propagating radiation carry energy too.
Energy density asks how much of that field energy occupies a small volume in a specified frame. It is different from the flux describing how rapidly energy crosses the volume boundary, and both appear in the stress–energy description.
statement: Vacuum fields store local energy even in regions with no material particles.

title: Vacuum field energy per unit volume
body:
The vacuum electromagnetic energy density, measured in an inertial frame, is
\[ u=\frac12\epsilon_0|\mathbf E|^2+\frac{|\mathbf B|^2}{2\mu_0}. \]
It has units of joules per cubic metre. Both fields must be taken in the same frame; \(\epsilon_0\mu_0c^2=1\). In the symmetric physical stress–energy tensor, this is \(T^{00}\).
The formula includes static and radiative vacuum fields. Material media can store additional energy in their response, so the vacuum expression should not be silently used as the complete energy density of an arbitrary medium.
statement: In vacuum SI, \(u=\tfrac12\epsilon_0E^2+B^2/(2\mu_0)\).

title: Extracting and simplifying the time–time component
body:
Use the \cref{physical tensor formula}{sr.em_stress_energy.formula}, signature \(+---\), and \(F_{0i}=E_i/c\), \(F_{ij}=-\epsilon_{ijk}B_k\). The needed contractions are
\[ F_{\alpha\beta}F^{\alpha\beta}=2(B^2-E^2/c^2), \]
and \(F^{0\lambda}F^0{}_{\lambda}=-E^2/c^2\). Therefore
\[ \begin{aligned}T^{00}&=\frac{1}{\mu_0}\left(\frac{E^2}{c^2}+\frac12(B^2-E^2/c^2)\right)\\ &=\frac{\epsilon_0E^2}{2}+\frac{B^2}{2\mu_0}.\end{aligned} \]
The metric signs and the trace term work together to make both energy contributions positive. This calculation connects the tensor construction to the field reading, rather than merely asserting that \(T^{00}\) is energy.
statement: Substituting the electric and magnetic tensor components gives the positive squared-field energy density.

title: Why squared fields appear
body:
Imagine reversing the voltage on a capacitor with unchanged geometry. The electric field reverses, but the stored energy does not acquire a negative sign. A squared-field contribution has this behaviour.
The same reasoning motivates the magnetic square. It is an intuition for the form, not a way to determine the exact coefficients: those follow from the electromagnetic model and its physical normalisation. Doubling one field while holding the other fixed multiplies that contribution by four.
statement: Reversing a field leaves its vacuum stored energy unchanged; doubling it quadruples that contribution.

title: Energy beyond particles
body:
The field between capacitor plates can store energy that is later delivered to a circuit. A travelling light pulse transports energy through vacuum where no material medium carries it along.
These examples make local field energy physically useful. For a complete system, include the sources, supports and interactions as needed; the field contribution alone is not necessarily an isolated conserved total.
statement: Energy can reside in a field configuration, not only in the particles sourcing it.

title: Plane-wave balance
body:
A source-free travelling plane wave has \(E=cB\) and perpendicular electric and magnetic fields. Its magnetic energy density is
\[ \frac{B^2}{2\mu_0}=\frac{E^2}{2\mu_0c^2}=\frac12\epsilon_0E^2. \]
It therefore equals the electric contribution, giving \(u=\epsilon_0E^2\) instantaneously for a real plane travelling wave. Its Poynting magnitude is \(S=uc\).
This equality uses the plane-wave relation. It is not a general rule for static fields, near fields or arbitrary superpositions of waves.
statement: For a vacuum plane wave, \(E=cB\), so electric and magnetic energy contributions are equal.

title: Energy density is frame-dependent
body:
An observer measures field energy in a spatial volume defined by that frame. Another observer uses different electric/magnetic components and a different time–space split.
The resulting energy densities need not agree. They are related through transformation of the complete stress–energy tensor. A scalar contraction of that tensor is a different quantity from simply selecting \(T^{00}\).
statement: Energy density is the observer’s \(00\) component, not a Lorentz scalar.

title: Not just potential energy between charges
body:
In electrostatics, total field energy can be related to interaction energy among a specified set of sources. That useful connection should not be mistaken for a claim that fields never carry energy independently through a region.
Radiation makes the limitation clear: energy can leave the sources and later be absorbed elsewhere. Local density and flux describe its progress. A complete energy balance must avoid double-counting the same interaction energy in both source and field descriptions.
statement: The same field energy accounting applies to radiation as well as static source configurations.

title: Maxwell's field energy
body: The idea that electromagnetic fields themselves store energy was part of the shift from action-at-a-distance thinking to field theory. It became central once light was understood as an electromagnetic wave.
statement: Treating fields as energy-bearing replaced a purely distant-force picture with local accounting.

title: Using field energy without losing the physical setup
body:
The SI formula makes electric and magnetic storage explicit and allows comparison with experiments such as capacitors and radiation absorption. The tensor calculation explains how this familiar expression fits relativistic geometry.
To use it well, identify the observer, the system boundary and whether the region is vacuum or includes material response. Those qualifications carry physical information, rather than being optional notation.
statement: The squared-field expression is a frame-specific energy reading within a covariant tensor.

title: Energy in motion
body:
A field can transport energy across a surface and store momentum within a volume. The Poynting vector describes the first quantity; electromagnetic momentum density describes the second.
For a vacuum field in SI, they are related by \(\mathbf g=\mathbf S/c^2\). This relation is why they are discussed together here, but it does not make their units interchangeable. The stress–energy tensor shows how both fit one relativistic accounting object.
statement: Energy flux and electromagnetic momentum density are related, but have different units and roles.

title: Poynting flux and the associated momentum density
body:
The Poynting vector is electromagnetic energy flux:
\[ \mathbf S\coloneqq\frac{\mathbf E\times\mathbf B}{\mu_0}. \]
Its units are watts per square metre. The associated vacuum field momentum density is
\[ \mathbf g=\frac{\mathbf S}{c^2}=\epsilon_0\mathbf E\times\mathbf B. \]
Here \(\epsilon_0\mu_0c^2=1\). Momentum density has units of momentum per volume, not energy per area per time. The electric and magnetic fields are measured in the same inertial frame. Material-media bookkeeping needs additional matter-response terms; these formulas describe the vacuum electromagnetic contribution.
statement: In vacuum SI, \(\mathbf S=\mathbf E\times\mathbf B/\mu_0\) and \(\mathbf g=\mathbf S/c^2\).

title: Direction from a cross product
body:
Take a wave whose electric field points along \(y\) and magnetic field along \(z\). The right-hand rule gives \(\mathbf E\times\mathbf B\) along \(x\), the direction in which its energy travels.
For a general field, the vector still describes local energy flux, but its pattern need not be straight rays radiating outward. Static sources can support nonzero local field flux as well, so the plane-wave picture should not be imposed on every configuration.
statement: For a plane wave, the right-hand-rule direction of \(\mathbf E\times\mathbf B\) is the propagation direction.

title: Flux, not stored energy
body:
An oriented area element \(d\mathbf a\) samples a power \(\mathbf S\cdot d\mathbf a\). Integrating over a boundary gives net outward energy flow.
Energy density instead counts the energy already inside a small volume. An energy balance compares its rate of change with boundary flux and work done on matter. A large stored energy does not by itself specify a large outward flux, and a flux through a region need not accumulate energy there.
statement: The surface integral of \(\mathbf S\) is transported power; the volume integral of \(u\) is stored energy.

title: Extracting flux and momentum from the tensor
body:
Use the symmetric \cref{electromagnetic stress–energy tensor}{sr.em_stress_energy.formula}, with \(+---\) and the SI field split. Because \(\eta^{0i}=0\), its mixed component is
\[ T^{0i}=-\frac{1}{\mu_0}F^{0j}F^i{}_{j}. \]
Substituting \(F^{0j}=-E_j/c\) and \(F^i{}_{j}=\epsilon_{ijk}B_k\) gives
\[ T^{0i}=\frac{(\mathbf E\times\mathbf B)_i}{\mu_0c}=\frac{S_i}{c}. \]
The corresponding momentum-density reading is \(T^{i0}/c\). Symmetry of this physical tensor therefore yields \(g_i=S_i/c^2\). The factor of \(c\) in each component interpretation is essential in SI; it is hidden only after an explicit natural-unit choice.
statement: The mixed tensor components give \(T^{0i}=S_i/c\) and \(T^{i0}=cg_i\).

title: Why the momentum density is smaller by \(c^2\)
body:
From \(T^{0i}=S_i/c\), \(T^{i0}=cg_i\) and tensor symmetry, \(\mathbf g=\mathbf S/c^2\). In SI this is also \(\epsilon_0\mathbf E\times\mathbf B\).
For a plane wave, \(S=uc\), so the momentum density has magnitude \(u/c\). A pulse with energy \(E\) travelling in one direction consequently carries momentum \(E/c\). This joins field accounting with the massless energy–momentum relation, without identifying energy flux with a literal particle velocity field.
statement: Dividing the energy flux by \(c^2\) gives the vacuum field momentum per volume.

title: Radiation pressure
body:
Let \(I\) be the incoming energy per area per time for a normally incident vacuum plane beam. Its incoming momentum flux is \(I/c\). A surface that absorbs the beam receives that momentum, so its pressure is \(I/c\), neglecting other emissions.
For ideal specular reflection, the outgoing momentum reverses direction with the same magnitude. The transfer doubles, giving \(2I/c\). The surface response and incidence assumptions matter: these expressions are not a general pressure formula for every electromagnetic configuration.
statement: At normal incidence, a steady plane beam gives pressure \(I/c\) on an absorber and \(2I/c\) on an ideal reflector.

title: Unit conventions
body:
In SI, \(S\) has units \(\mathrm{J\,m^{-2}\,s^{-1}}\), while \(g\) has units \(\mathrm{kg\,m^{-2}\,s^{-1}}\). Dividing by \(c^2\) converts the first to the second.
Expressions such as \(\mathbf S=\mathbf E\times\mathbf B\) suppress the electromagnetic unit normalisation. They should not be compared directly with SI formulas unless the constants and field units have been translated consistently.
statement: Keep the SI flux, density and tensor-component factors distinct.

title: Not a stream of little arrows
body:
The arrow \(\mathbf S\) gives the direction and rate of local energy transport in the classical field description. Drawing it does not establish that identifiable particles follow every flux line.
For radiation, a photon description can reproduce the energy and momentum accounting in its range of validity. For near fields or static configurations, interpreting every flux arrow as an outgoing light ray can be misleading.
statement: A local flux arrow represents field energy transport, not necessarily a material stream or particle path.

title: Poynting makes energy flow local
body: In 1884 John Henry Poynting derived a local balance law for electromagnetic energy and identified the vector now bearing his name. Energy could be followed through the field surrounding a circuit rather than imagined as jumping directly from source to receiver. This local flux picture later became indispensable for radiation, momentum transfer and relativistic stress-energy.
statement: Poynting’s 1884 balance law made electromagnetic energy flow a local quantity.

title: One cross product, two distinct accounting roles
body:
The cross product gives an oriented flow quantity built from electric and magnetic fields in one frame. The stress–energy tensor connects its flux interpretation to momentum density and stress.
This makes surface energy balances and radiation-pressure calculations parts of one local conservation picture. The geometry is shared, but the SI units and the distinction between volume density and surface flow remain necessary.
statement: The same field cross product enters energy flow and vacuum momentum density, with different conversion factors.

title: The field's accounting tensor
body:
Knowing the force on a test charge is not yet a complete account of the field. Fields can store and transport energy and momentum themselves.
The stress–energy tensor keeps these quantities together so that their frame dependence and local exchange with matter can be treated consistently. It is constructed from field strength and the metric, not added as another independent electromagnetic degree of freedom.
statement: The electromagnetic stress–energy tensor organises stored energy, energy flux, momentum and stress.

title: The physical electromagnetic accounting tensor
body:
The electromagnetic stress–energy tensor \(T^{\mu\nu}_{\rm EM}\) describes the vacuum field contribution to local energy and momentum accounting. In one inertial frame,
\[ T^{00}=u,\quad T^{0i}=S_i/c,\quad T^{i0}=cg_i. \]
The spatial components record momentum flux and stress. This is the electromagnetic case of the general \cref{energy–momentum tensor}{sr.energy_momentum_tensor.definition}.
We use the symmetric, gauge-invariant physical tensor. Canonical tensors and their improvements are related constructions, not automatically identical component formulas. For an interacting field alone, divergence need not vanish: energy and momentum can be transferred to matter.
statement: The symmetric electromagnetic tensor gives the vacuum field’s local energy–momentum density and flow.

title: Constructing the physical tensor from the Maxwell density
body:
Use the SI field density \(\mathcal L=-F_{\alpha eta}F^{\alpha eta}/(4\mu_0)\). A useful construction defines stress–energy through the response to the measuring metric, temporarily replacing \(\eta\) by an auxiliary \(g\), then returning to flat space. Hold \(F_{\mu
u}\) fixed with lower indices.
Let \(X=F_{\alpha eta}F^{\alpha eta}\). Differentiating its two inverse-metric contractions gives \(\partial X/\partial g^{\mu
u}=2F_{\mu\lambda}F_
u{}^\lambda\). Including the volume-factor response, the physical metric tensor is
\[ T_{\mu
u}=2 rac{\partial\mathcal L}{\partial g^{\mu
u}}-g_{\mu
u}\mathcal L. \]
Substitution and raising both indices give
\[  egin{aligned}T^{\mu
u}&= rac{1}{\mu_0}\left(-F^{\mu\lambda}F^
u{}_{\lambda}ight.\ &\qquad\left.+ rac14\eta^{\mu
u}Xight).\end{aligned} \]
This is a metric-response construction of the physical tensor from the chosen field action, not a derivation from Lorentz symmetry alone. No gravitational field equation is assumed. Its \(00\) and \(0i\) components reproduce field energy and flux; the coefficient is fixed by the Maxwell action normalisation.
statement: Metric response of the Maxwell action gives a quadratic, symmetric tensor with fixed normalisation.

title: Why it is quadratic
body:
If every electromagnetic field component changes sign, a physically stored energy should not simply turn negative. A quadratic expression in field strength has the needed even behaviour.
Two uncontracted indices allow the same object to carry directional flow and stress information. This motivates the kind of construction, but does not uniquely derive its coefficient or every possible term. The chosen field action supplies the precise expression.
statement: Quadratic field strength permits energy to remain unchanged when the entire field reverses sign.

title: Interpreting the components with SI factors
body:
For this symmetric physical tensor, \(T^{00}=u\) is energy density, \(cT^{i0}=S_i\) is energy flow, and \(T^{0i}/c=g_i\) is momentum density. Symmetry makes these agree with the alternative mixed-component readings.
The spatial entry \(T^{ij}\) is the flux of \(j\)-momentum through a surface normal to direction \(i\). It is related by a sign to one common definition of the Maxwell mechanical stress matrix, so check the stress convention before comparing formulas.
The component roles refer to a chosen observer. Their covariant organisation allows another observer to make a different, consistent split.
statement: The tensor’s first index labels the flux direction and the second the energy–momentum component.

title: Stress and pressure
body:
Light incident on a surface carries momentum towards it. Absorption or reflection changes that momentum, giving a mechanical push described by the spatial stress–energy components.
Static fields can exert stresses too, as electric fields in a capacitor pull on its plates. “Stress” therefore includes more than radiation travelling away. It accounts for directional momentum transfer in the field, including configurations whose energy density is not changing in time.
statement: Electromagnetic stress describes momentum crossing a surface and exerting pressure or tension.

title: Observer-dependent split
body:
An observer identifies time and spatial directions before naming tensor entries as density or flux. A boost changes that identification.
The values of \(u\), \(\mathbf S\) and the spatial stresses can consequently differ between observers. This does not destroy local conservation or change the underlying field; it means those quantities are parts of a tensor rather than separate invariant scalars.
statement: Energy density, flow and stress mix when the inertial observer changes.

title: Not a new electromagnetic field
body:
Once \(F\), the metric and the Maxwell model normalisation are specified, the physical electromagnetic stress–energy tensor follows from the construction. Its entries are not additional freely adjustable fields.
It answers a different physical question from \(F\): how much energy and momentum the field stores, transports and exchanges. The same field data can therefore support several useful descriptions without introducing new degrees of freedom.
statement: Stress–energy is constructed from electromagnetic strength, not a new independent electromagnetic variable.

title: Electromagnetic momentum made local
body:
Classical work on electromagnetic energy transfer and radiation pressure made it clear that fields participate in momentum accounting, rather than merely transmitting forces between particles.
Relativistic tensor methods then placed energy density, flux and stress into one framework. Later distinctions between canonical, improved and metric tensors clarified why different-looking local formulas can encode the same integrated conserved quantities under suitable boundary conditions.
statement: Energy flow, radiation pressure and field momentum motivated a relativistic local accounting tensor.

title: Field accounting is part of total system accounting
body:
The quadratic tensor links stored energy, transported energy, momentum density and directional stress. Its component normalisation can be checked against the familiar SI field-energy and Poynting expressions.
For an isolated complete system, field and matter transfers cancel in total energy–momentum conservation. For the field subsystem alone, a nonzero divergence can record work and force delivered to matter; it is not automatically a violation of conservation.
statement: The physical tensor turns field strength into a coherent account of energy–momentum and its exchange with matter.

title: Local energy-momentum bookkeeping
body:
Energy and momentum can be stored in matter or fields and can cross surfaces. A local description therefore needs more than a total energy or a single force vector.
The energy–momentum tensor packages four currents, one for each energy–momentum component. It relates density change to directional flux and stress, while allowing those readings to transform together between observers.
statement: A rank-two current organises local energy–momentum densities and directional transport.

title: Energy–momentum density and flux conventions
body:
With the convention \(\partial_\mu T^{\mu\nu}=0\) for a conserved total, the index \(\mu\) labels the spacetime flux direction and \(\nu\) the energy–momentum component. In SI,
\[ T^{00}=u,\qquad cT^{i0}=S_i,\qquad T^{0i}/c=g_i. \]
Spatial entries \(T^{ij}\) describe flux of \(j\)-momentum across surfaces normal to \(i\). For a translation-invariant closed model on its equations of motion, the total tensor is divergence-free.
An interacting subsystem may have nonzero divergence because it exchanges energy and momentum with the rest. Canonical, improved and physical metric tensors need not have identical local formulas; identify the representative before using its component interpretation.
statement: The first tensor index gives flux direction; the second labels the transported energy–momentum component.

title: Reading the tensor as four local currents
body:
In a small volume, \(T^{00}\) counts stored energy. The entries \(T^{i0}\) give its flow in spatial direction \(i\), with the SI factor \(c\). The entries \(T^{0j}\) count momentum density, with the inverse factor \(c\).
A spatial pair \(T^{ij}\) records momentum transport through a surface. This is why pressure and shear belong in the same accounting object as energy density. For a symmetric physical tensor, mixed entries connect energy flux to momentum density; a canonical tensor is not automatically symmetric.
statement: Time components record densities and energy transport; spatial pairs record momentum flux and stress.

title: Deriving the canonical translation current
body:
Take a first-derivative density with no explicit coordinate dependence. A constant translation of the field argument has \(\delta\phi_a=\epsilon^
u\partial_
u\phi_a\). The chain rule gives \(\delta\mathcal L=\epsilon^
u\partial_
u\mathcal L\), a total derivative with \(K^\mu=\epsilon^
u\delta^\mu{}_{
u}\mathcal L\).
Insert these into the \cref{Noether current formula}{sr.noether_theorem.derivation_sketch}, with \(\Pi_a^\mu=\partial\mathcal L/\partial(\partial_\mu\phi_a)\):
\[ J^\mu=\epsilon^
u\left(\Pi_a^\mu\partial_
u\phi_a-\delta^\mu{}_{
u}\mathcal Light). \]
Each of the four constant parameters can be chosen independently, so its coefficient defines one conserved current:
\[ T^\mu{}_{
u}=\Pi_a^\mu\partial_
u\phi_a-\delta^\mu{}_{
u}\mathcal L. \]
On shell, \(\partial_\mu T^\mu{}_{
u}=0\). Translation symmetry supplies the special variation; the field action supplies the derivative coefficients; Noether's argument supplies conservation. An explicit external coordinate dependence would spoil the assumed symmetry.

title: Using the canonical formula for a chosen model
body:
For \(\mathcal L(\phi_a,\partial_\mu\phi_a)\), define \(\Pi_a^\mu=\partial\mathcal L/\partial(\partial_\mu\phi_a)\). The canonical expression is
\[ T^\mu{}_{
u}=\Pi_a^\mu\partial_
u\phi_a-\delta^\mu{}_{
u}\mathcal L. \]
For a real scalar model in \(c=1\) units, this gives \(T^{00}=	frac12\dot\phi^2+	frac12|
abla\phi|^2+V(\phi)\), rather than the Lagrangian density itself.
The formula depends on the chosen action and its variables. Calling it canonical identifies the construction; it does not assert gauge invariance or symmetry for every model.
statement: The canonical tensor is the translation current of the specified field Lagrangian.

title: Conservation as flow
body:
For each energy–momentum component, a zero divergence says that local loss is accounted for by transport through neighbouring surfaces. A volume integral converts this into a boundary balance.
For matter and electromagnetic field separately, forces can transfer energy and momentum between them. Their divergences then contain opposite exchange terms. Adding the complete contributions removes that internal transfer, so total conservation can hold even when neither subsystem is divergence-free on its own.
statement: Density change is balanced by flux, with exchange terms for an interacting subsystem.

title: Canonical is not always final
body:
A canonical tensor can fail to be symmetric or gauge-invariant. One may add a term \(\partial_\lambda B^{\lambda\mu\nu}\), with \(B\) antisymmetric in \(\lambda,\mu\), whose further divergence vanishes identically for smooth fields.
This preserves the conservation equation. Integrated charges are unchanged only when the associated boundary contribution vanishes or is included consistently. Improvement is therefore a controlled freedom in representation, not permission to ignore boundaries or arbitrary local terms.
statement: Improvement terms can change local tensor form while preserving totals under suitable boundary conditions.

title: Electromagnetic example
body:
The \cref{electromagnetic tensor construction}{sr.em_stress_energy.formula} uses field strength and the metric to produce a useful physical representative. Its \(00\) component is the vacuum squared-field energy density and its mixed components give Poynting flow and momentum density.
With sources, the field subsystem transfers force density \(f^
u=F^{
u\lambda}j_\lambda\) to matter, so \(\partial_\mu T_{m EM}^{\mu
u}=-f^
u\). Adding the corresponding matter contribution restores the closed-system balance. This example illustrates why a physical representative and a complete system definition matter.
statement: The physical electromagnetic representative is symmetric and gauge-invariant, with field–matter exchange when sources act.

title: Not just energy density
body:
Knowing \(T^{00}\) does not tell us where energy flows or how momentum crosses a surface. Two configurations can have equal energy density and different flux or stress.
The remaining components supply that missing directional information. A frame change mixes the readings, which is why retaining the complete tensor is more informative than treating energy density as the whole covariant story.
statement: The tensor contains directional flux and stress, not only the energy density entry.

title: From conservation laws to tensors
body: The tensor form grew from nineteenth-century conservation laws and twentieth-century field theory. In relativity, energy and momentum cannot be separated cleanly, so their densities and fluxes naturally become one spacetime object.
statement: Relativity combined energy and momentum currents that classical field theory had studied separately.

title: What to specify before using a tensor balance
body:
Noether translation currents explain the canonical construction. Improved or metric tensors can make other physical properties clearer without changing appropriate integrated totals.
To use any of them, identify the model and whether the chosen contribution is a closed total or an exchanging subsystem. This keeps local energy and momentum accounting consistent across particle, field and relativistic descriptions.
statement: Specify the model, tensor representative and system boundary before applying local conservation.

title: Light as a field disturbance
body:
A travelling electromagnetic wave contains changing electric and magnetic fields, but they are not independent oscillations to be chosen separately. Maxwell's equations link their directions, magnitudes and rates of change.
A plane wave is a particularly clear example. It shows transversality and propagation speed explicitly, while reminding us that more complicated radiation is built from compatible field configurations, not arbitrary pairs of waves.
statement: Vacuum radiation is one propagating electromagnetic disturbance with linked electric and magnetic components.

title: Propagating Maxwell fields in vacuum
body:
Electromagnetic waves are propagating disturbances of the physical field satisfying the source-free Maxwell equations in vacuum. In a chosen inertial frame they appear as related electric and magnetic components.
For a travelling plane wave, both fields are transverse to the propagation direction and \(\mathbf B=\hat{\mathbf k}\times\mathbf E/c\). General superpositions need not resemble one globally oriented plane wave. Source-free refers to the region of propagation; sources can have generated the radiation elsewhere or earlier.
statement: A vacuum electromagnetic wave is a propagating source-free Maxwell solution, with speed \(c\).

title: Deriving the plane-wave constraints and field relation
body:
In a source-free region, the \cref{wave-equation route}{sr.wave_equation.maxwell_origin} and Maxwell's curl/divergence equations constrain the radiation. Try complex amplitudes \(\mathbf E_0,\mathbf B_0\) with common phase \(\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf x-\omega t\).
The wave equation gives \(\omega^2=c^2k^2\), where \(k=|\mathbf k|\). The Maxwell divergences give
\[ \mathbf k\cdot\mathbf E_0=0,\qquad \mathbf k\cdot\mathbf B_0=0. \]
Faraday's curl equation gives \(\mathbf k\times\mathbf E_0=\omega\mathbf B_0\). For positive frequency \(\omega=ck\), this becomes
\[ \mathbf B_0=\frac{\hat{\mathbf k}\times\mathbf E_0}{c}. \]
Thus the operator fixes the dispersion, while the Maxwell constraints and curl law fix polarisation and the linked magnetic amplitude. Four arbitrary scalar wave solutions would not automatically satisfy these electromagnetic requirements.
statement: Plane-wave substitution combines the wave equation with Maxwell constraints to fix dispersion and the field relation.

title: Why the plane-wave fields are transverse
body:
For a plane wave, a spatial derivative of its phase brings down \(i\mathbf k\). Therefore \(\nabla\cdot\mathbf E=0\) becomes \(i\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf E_0=0\), and similarly for \(\mathbf B\).
Both field amplitudes lie in the plane perpendicular to propagation. This conclusion uses the vacuum source-free Maxwell constraints, not the scalar wave equation alone. Near sources and in material media, other longitudinal components can occur, so the plane-wave statement should not be promoted to an unqualified claim about every electromagnetic field.
statement: The source-free divergences require \(\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf E_0=\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf B_0=0\) for a plane wave.

title: The wave triad
body:
Choose \(\hat{\mathbf k}\) along \(x\) and electric field along \(y\). The plane-wave relation then puts magnetic field along \(z\), so the right-hand rule gives \(\mathbf E\times\mathbf B\) in the direction of propagation.
The two fields share one travelling pattern and have linked amplitudes, with \(E=cB\) in SI. This picture is useful for polarisation and energy flow. A superposition can have a more complicated local pattern, so the triad is a model of a single travelling plane wave.
statement: For one travelling plane wave, the electric field, magnetic field and energy-flow direction form a right-handed triad.

title: What the vacuum dispersion says about speed
body:
The nonzero plane-wave solution satisfies \(\omega=ck\) for positive frequency and \(k>0\). Its phase speed is \(\omega/k=c\), while the group speed for a narrow packet is \(d\omega/dk=c\).
The same speed is fixed by vacuum electromagnetic constants through \(c^{-2}=\epsilon_0\mu_0\) and fits the light-cone structure of SR. This is not a disturbance travelling through an ether-like material. Material dispersion changes the propagation problem and cannot be inferred by reusing the vacuum relation unchanged.
statement: Vacuum dispersion \(\omega=ck\) gives phase and wave-packet group speeds \(c\).

title: Energy and momentum
body:
For a real travelling vacuum plane wave, \(\mathbf E\perp\mathbf B\) and \(E=cB\). Its electric and magnetic energy contributions are equal, giving \(u=\epsilon_0E^2\).
The Poynting expression therefore gives \(\mathbf S=uc\hat{\mathbf k}\), and vacuum momentum density is \(\mathbf g=\mathbf S/c^2=u\hat{\mathbf k}/c\). A pulse can consequently heat an absorber and push on it.
These relations are a field calculation of the energy–momentum carried by radiation. They do not require material particles travelling along the wave, and they apply instantaneously to this ideal plane-wave pattern.
statement: A travelling plane wave carries energy flux \(\mathbf S=uc\hat{\mathbf k}\) and momentum density \(\mathbf g=u\hat{\mathbf k}/c\).

title: Not two separate waves
body:
Two arbitrary sinusoidal electric and magnetic fields may each solve a wave equation and still fail Maxwell's curl relations. A physical vacuum plane wave must satisfy the transversality and amplitude relations as well.
It is therefore better to think of one electromagnetic solution with two linked component readings, rather than an electric wave and a separate magnetic wave that happen to travel together.
statement: The magnetic amplitude and polarisation cannot be selected independently of the electric plane wave.

title: Maxwell identifies light
body: Maxwell found that disturbances of his electromagnetic field obeyed a wave equation whose speed, calculated from electrical measurements, agreed with the known speed of light. In 1865 he argued that light itself is an electromagnetic disturbance. This was more than a new theory of light: it united optics with electricity and magnetism and placed finite-speed propagation at the heart of field physics.
