statement: Maxwell’s calculated wave speed linked light with electrical and magnetic measurements.

title: Combining propagation, constraints and transport
body:
The source-free operator explains the dispersion relation. The divergence and curl equations determine which amplitudes represent transverse electromagnetic radiation and how electric and magnetic parts fit together.
Energy–momentum accounting then explains absorption and pressure. Keeping all three steps visible is more informative than stopping at four component wave equations or simply quoting the speed of light.
statement: The wave operator supplies propagation; Maxwell structure supplies the electromagnetic constraints.

title: Finite-speed propagation
body:
A disturbance governed by a wave equation has a spatial pattern whose changes propagate rather than simply oscillate independently at every point. In flat relativistic spacetime, the relevant operator combines time and space derivatives with speed \(c\).
The generic mathematical equation is useful for scalar components. For electromagnetic potentials it arises from Maxwell dynamics plus a gauge choice, and its solutions must still obey the associated constraints.
statement: The relativistic wave operator connects temporal and spatial change along the vacuum light-cone structure.

title: The operator and its generic wave equation
body:
In inertial coordinates \(x^0=ct\) and signature \(+---\), define
\[ \Box\coloneqq\partial_\mu\partial^\mu=\frac{1}{c^2}\frac{\partial^2}{\partial t^2}-\nabla^2. \]
The source-free relativistic wave equation is \(\Box\psi=0\). A source replaces zero by a specified driving term.
For an electromagnetic potential, each component obeys such an equation in Lorenz gauge, but the components are not arbitrary independent scalar fields. The gauge condition and Maxwell constraints restrict the physically allowed solution. Initial and boundary data are required to choose a particular wave history.
statement: The flat source-free wave equation is \(\Box\psi=0\), with \(\Box=c^{-2}\partial_t^2-\nabla^2\).

title: Metric structure
body:
The contracted derivatives use the Minkowski metric: one positive time term and three negative spatial terms in \(+---\). Those signs distinguish the wave operator from an ordinary Euclidean Laplacian.
This operator has finite propagation speed for its standard well-posed initial-value problem. The same conclusion does not follow from locality alone or from every equation containing derivatives. For electromagnetic applications, this sign structure is already encoded in the covariant Maxwell equations and the flat-spacetime derivative convention.
statement: Opposite time and spatial signs give the hyperbolic operator associated with the Minkowski light cone.

title: Deriving the Lorenz-gauge potential equation
body:
Take the \cref{sourced Maxwell equation}{sr.maxwells_equations.sourced_equation}, and insert \(F^{\mu
u}=\partial^\mu A^
u-\partial^
u A^\mu\). Commuting flat partial derivatives gives
\[ \partial_\mu F^{\mu
u}=\Box A^
u-\partial^
u(\partial_\mu A^\mu). \]
The \cref{Lorenz condition}{sr.lorenz_gauge.definition} makes the divergence in the second term zero. Consequently
\[ \Box A^
u=\mu_0j^
u. \]
The field law supplies the source term, the potential construction supplies the derivative combination, and the gauge choice removes its longitudinal part. Dropping that term without stating the gauge would miss an assumption. The resulting component equations remain coupled through the condition on the potential and the admissible current.
statement: Expanding sourced Maxwell in potentials and applying Lorenz gauge gives \(\Box A^\nu=\mu_0j^\nu\).

title: Source-free region
body:
If \(j^\mu=0\) in a region, the Lorenz-gauge potential equations reduce to \(\Box A^\mu=0\). Nonzero wave solutions are permitted.
They must also satisfy \(\partial_\mu A^\mu=0\) and any boundary or initial constraints. A pure-gauge potential can solve these equations while representing no field; conversely nonzero field radiation can propagate with no local charge source. Potential components alone do not decide which case we have.
statement: Zero current gives homogeneous potential equations, not an absence of electromagnetic field.

title: Plane-wave test
body:
Use a complex exponential as a calculation device, taking its real part for a real physical field. Time differentiation twice gives \(-\omega^2\psi\), and the spatial Laplacian gives \(-|\mathbf k|^2\psi\).
Substitution into \(\Box\psi=0\) gives
\[ \left(-\frac{\omega^2}{c^2}+|\mathbf k|^2\right)\psi=0. \]
A nonzero amplitude therefore requires \(\omega^2=c^2|\mathbf k|^2\). On the positive-frequency branch, \(\omega=c|\mathbf k|\), so phase speed is \(c\). A plane wave is an idealised infinite pattern, not a finite pulse with a specified source history.
statement: For \(\psi=e^{i(\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf x-\omega t)}\), the equation gives \(\omega^2=c^2|\mathbf k|^2\).

title: Sources change the equation
body:
A nonzero right-hand side describes how local charges and currents drive the potential. A particular sourced solution can be combined with homogeneous solutions representing other allowed radiation.
Boundary conditions distinguish choices such as outgoing retarded response from incoming radiation. The differential equation alone does not pick that physical history. In electromagnetic theory the source must also obey continuity, consistently with Lorenz gauge.
statement: A sourced equation needs compatible currents and data; the homogeneous part still carries independent radiation.

title: Not every oscillation is a wave equation
body:
A pendulum or a single field value can oscillate without specifying how neighbouring locations affect one another. A wave equation couples temporal change to spatial derivatives throughout a region.
To infer propagation, examine that spatial coupling, its characteristic speed and the allowed data. Merely inserting a sinusoid into a time-only equation does not derive relativistic wave behaviour.
statement: An oscillator at one point does not establish a spatial wave equation or a propagation speed.

title: Reading the wave equation as part of a field problem
body:
The compact component equation is useful because it exposes propagation structure and permits familiar wave techniques. It is not a substitute for the electromagnetic meaning of the potential.
Check the gauge, compatible source and initial or boundary data before interpreting a mathematical solution as a physical field. These steps distinguish a real disturbance from a redundant potential representation.
statement: The wave operator, gauge condition, source and data together define the electromagnetic potential problem.

title: When the charge feels its own radiation
body:
An accelerating charge can emit electromagnetic radiation. If its motion were calculated without accounting for that energy and momentum, the particle-only result could miss part of the physical balance.
Radiation reaction is the associated back-effect of the charge's own field. It is subtle because the near field can also store and return energy, and the ideal point-charge self-field is singular. A useful account must state its approximation rather than treating the effect as an automatic friction term.
statement: A consistent particle–field model must account for energy and momentum carried into radiation.

title: Back-reaction in a specified particle–field model
body:
Radiation reaction is the correction to charged-body motion required by its own electromagnetic field, including the energy–momentum carried into outgoing radiation. It supplements the \cref{external-field Lorentz model}{sr.lorentz_force_law.definition}.
A complete treatment must separate particle, near-field and radiative contributions consistently. For a point particle, this requires handling the singular self-field and the meaning of the physical mass. The concept is not a universal extra force obtained merely by subtracting a far-zone radiated power from mechanical energy at each instant.
statement: Radiation reaction is self-field back-reaction beyond a prescribed external Lorentz force.

title: Deriving the necessary energy-balance structure
body:
Start with local conservation of the complete \cref{energy–momentum tensor}{sr.energy_momentum_tensor.definition}. Integrating its energy component over a region converts the divergence into surface flux. For a finite charged-body model, or a consistently regularised point-charge description, separate the retained energy into particle and bound near-field parts.
With the outward radiative flux written as \(P_{\rm rad}\), the energy balance has the form
\[ P_{\rm ext}=\frac{dE_{\rm particle}}{dt}+\frac{dE_{\rm bound}}{dt}+P_{\rm rad}. \]
The terms must be evaluated in one frame with a consistent region and radiation-flux convention. Momentum obeys a corresponding vector balance.
The outgoing waves account for one part of the field's energy. A changing bound field supplies another, so the instantaneous particle-energy loss need not equal the radiated power. This derives a necessary balance, not a unique self-force law: a charge model, field solution and regularisation or controlled approximation are further inputs.
statement: External work balances changes of particle and near-field energy plus outgoing radiative flux.

title: External force versus self-effect
body:
A prescribed external field is an input to the ordinary test-particle force calculation. The particle's influence on that field and on its own near field has been neglected.
A self-consistent treatment changes this division: the moving charge generates fields that carry energy and momentum, and those fields affect the particle. Raw substitution of a point charge's divergent self-field is not a solution. One must specify a finite-size model or a mathematically controlled point-particle approximation.
statement: The external-field test-particle approximation omits the field’s response to the charge’s own motion.

title: Radiative damping
body:
Imagine driving a small charged oscillator. Over many cycles, some supplied work can leave as outgoing waves. Less is available to build the mechanical oscillation, giving a damping-like effect.
The averaged picture is useful, but not the whole instantaneous story. The bound field can store and return energy during a cycle. Calling the effect damping does not mean that a single local friction coefficient always captures the self-force.
statement: A driven charged oscillator can lose supplied work to radiation rather than storing it all mechanically.

title: Not ordinary friction
body:
Radiation can carry energy through vacuum, so no surrounding fluid or ether is needed to slow an emitting charged system. The relevant exchange is between the body and its electromagnetic field.
A simple friction law depends only on local velocity and dissipates mechanical energy monotonically. Self-field effects can depend on acceleration history or derivatives and on near-field energy changes. A damping analogy is therefore helpful only within a stated approximation or averaged regime.
statement: Radiation reaction does not require a material medium and is not generally a force proportional to minus velocity.

title: Runaways and pre-acceleration
body:
The nonrelativistic Abraham–Lorentz model has the schematic form
\[ m\mathbf a=\mathbf F_{\rm ext}+m\tau_0\dot{\mathbf a},\qquad \tau_0>0. \]
With zero external force, it admits \(\dot{\mathbf a}=\mathbf a/\tau_0\), hence exponentially growing acceleration. These runaway solutions are not ordinary damping. Imposing a future no-runaway condition on the unreduced equation can instead yield apparent response before the external force acts.
This illustrates why the singular point-charge idealisation and its extra initial-data requirements need care. The formula is a limited nonrelativistic model, not a universal equation to solve literally at every time scale.
statement: Higher-order point-charge equations admit runaway solutions; removing them can introduce pre-acceleration issues.

title: Why a controlled reduced-order description is useful
body:
Suppose radiation reaction is small over the time scale of external-force variation. In the nonrelativistic model \(m\mathbf a=\mathbf F_{\rm ext}+m\tau_0\dot{\mathbf a}\), use the leading motion \(m\mathbf a\simeq\mathbf F_{\rm ext}\) inside the already small correction. This gives
\[ m\mathbf a\simeq\mathbf F_{\rm ext}+\tau_0\frac{d\mathbf F_{\rm ext}}{dt}, \]
with the derivative evaluated along the leading trajectory. This is a simple illustration of reduction of order; the relativistic Landau–Lifshitz treatment keeps the appropriate covariant terms.
The approximation should not be extrapolated to rapid variation or regimes where self-force is no longer a small correction. Nor does classical modelling settle regimes where quantum recoil or internal structure becomes important.
statement: Reduction of order uses lower-order motion inside a small self-force correction.

title: The classical electron confronts its own field
body: Around 1900 Abraham and Lorentz tried to account for the inertia and radiation of an electron through its electromagnetic field. A charge acting on itself exposed divergences, dependence on the assumed charge model and equations with unwanted solutions. Radiation reaction therefore became an early warning that classical point particles and classical fields do not combine as innocently as their separate equations suggest.
statement: Early electron models exposed divergences and unwanted solutions when a charge acted on its own field.

title: What the balance argument establishes
body:
Outgoing radiation cannot be ignored in a complete energy–momentum balance. The bound near field and the particle contribution must be treated consistently as well.
This explains both the need for radiation reaction and the limits of a purely qualitative argument. A trustworthy calculation states its particle model, regularisation or effective approximation, boundary conditions and range of validity. Balance alone does not supply all of that missing dynamics.
statement: Energy balance motivates self-force, while a controlled charge model determines its usable form.

title: A symmetry requirement on physical laws
body:
Lorentz invariance turns the claim that no inertial frame is privileged into a symmetry requirement on physical laws. We describe the same situation in Lorentz-related frames and ask whether the complete law still applies.
The component numbers need not stay fixed. What matters is that they transform consistently, so that changing inertial frame does not change the physical relationship the law asserts.
statement: Changing inertial frame must preserve the physical content of a Lorentz-invariant law.

title: Same physical law in Lorentz-related frames
body:
Lorentz invariance is a physical symmetry requirement: laws retain their physical content when descriptions or physical configurations are related by \cref{Lorentz transformations}{sr.lorentz_transformations}.
There are two related ideas to distinguish. An invariant scalar has the same value in different inertial descriptions. Vector and tensor components generally change, but a covariant equation transforms consistently on both sides, so it remains valid.
Tensor notation helps us express and check this consistency. It does not, by itself, prove that a proposed law is physically true, or that every fixed structure included in that law respects the symmetry. We must examine the whole law, rather than just the appearance of its symbols.
statement: Lorentz invariance requires consistent frame changes of the full physical law, not identical component values.

title: Relativity expressed with Lorentz transformations
body:
The \cref{relativity postulate}{sr.principle_of_relativity} gives inertial laboratories equal physical standing. Combining it with common vacuum light speed, homogeneity and isotropy leads to their \cref{Lorentz coordinate changes}{sr.lorentz_transformations}.
We can then test a candidate SR law: describe the complete experiment in another such frame and transform all its ingredients. Energy or field components may take different values, but the relationship predicting the experiment must not require a preferred laboratory.
This is how physical inertial equivalence motivates the symmetry test. Remember that the comparison changes frame while keeping the physical situation fixed. A conservation claim asks a different question—how a quantity behaves as the system evolves.
statement: The relativity postulate becomes a Lorentz-symmetry requirement once the inertial frame changes are established.

title: Invariant scalar products
body:
In Cartesian inertial coordinates with signature \(+---\), let \(\eta=\mathrm{diag}(1,-1,-1,-1)\). The \cref{matrix preservation condition}{sr.lorentz_transformations.matrix_form} for a Lorentz transformation \(\Lambda\) is \(\Lambda^T\eta\Lambda=\eta\).
Now describe the same two vectors in another frame, using \(V'=\Lambda V\) and \(W'=\Lambda W\),
\[\begin{aligned}
V'^T\eta W'
 &=V^T\Lambda^T\eta\Lambda W\\
 &=V^T\eta W.
\end{aligned}\]
This is the scalar product written as \(V^\mu W_\mu\). The factors representing the component changes cancel through the metric-preservation identity. That is why the scalar product has the same value even though the separate components change.
So this is an example of an invariant scalar, not a claim that each component of every tensor stays fixed. The distinction is between the combined result and the components used to calculate it.
statement: Metric preservation makes \(V^\mu W_\mu\) agree in Lorentz-related inertial frames.

title: Matching transformation laws on both sides
body:
Suppose both sides of an equation are genuine tensors of the same type, and all their ingredients obey the stated Lorentz transformation rules. Then changing frame acts on both sides in the same way. This is what allows the equality to survive even though its component numbers change.
The \cref{matching-transformation argument}{sr.lorentz_invariance.covariance_argument} makes this explicit. For example, let two component columns transform as \(V'=\Lambda V\) and \(W'=\Lambda W\). If \(V=W\), applying the same matrix gives \(V'=W'\). Since the matrix is invertible, we can also work backwards: the equality holds in one frame if and only if it holds in the other.
Matching free indices is therefore a useful check, but adding indices to a symbol does not establish its transformation behaviour. We must check every ingredient, including any fixed background structures or coefficients, before concluding that the complete law meets the physical symmetry requirement.
statement: An equation remains covariant when its complete ingredients transform with matching tensor laws.

title: Covariant objects used throughout SR
body:
\cref{Four-vectors}{sr.four_vectors}, the \cref{Field tensor}{sr.field_tensor} and the \cref{Energy--momentum tensor}{sr.energy_momentum_tensor} provide standard ways to organise quantities that transform consistently under Lorentz changes.
Their components are not generally identical in different frames. Their usefulness is that we know how those components change, so we can write relationships between them that remain valid without choosing a preferred inertial frame. This is how covariant objects help express mechanics and electromagnetism in a common relativistic language.
statement: Four-vectors and field tensors carry changing components while supporting frame-independent physical laws.

title: Scalars versus covariant component equations
body:
An invariant scalar keeps its value when we change inertial frame. A vector or tensor, by contrast, generally has a different list of components in the new frame.
A covariant equation remains valid because its ingredients transform consistently, not because every component remains the same. Thus Lorentz invariance of a physical law should not be read as a demand for identical numerical component lists.
statement: An invariant scalar keeps its value; a covariant equation keeps its validity as components change.

title: One electromagnetic field, different splits
body:
An observer splits the \cref{electromagnetic field tensor}{sr.field_tensor} into electric and magnetic components. After a boost, another observer generally makes a different split: quantities called \(\mathbf E\) and \(\mathbf B\) mix with one another.
This might seem to threaten agreement about electromagnetism. But Maxwell's equations relate more than an isolated component: the field, current and spacetime derivatives all transform together. Their transformed relationship can therefore keep the same form even when the separately measured fields change.
So observer agreement concerns the complete law connecting fields and sources. Requiring equal electric and magnetic component lists would be a stronger condition, and generally the wrong one.
statement: Electric and magnetic components can mix while Maxwell's tensor equations retain their form.

title: A physical constraint, not typographical style
body:
Lorentz symmetry constrains the physical content of a candidate SR law, rather than just the way we print it. If a law treats two otherwise equivalent inertial laboratories differently, adding indices cannot remove that difference.
To check the symmetry, we must know how every quantity and fixed structure in the law transforms. Tensor notation is useful because it makes consistent transformation rules visible. The notation alone does not establish that those rules apply, or that the underlying physical law agrees with experiment.
statement: Tensor notation cannot make an unsupported preferred-frame law physically Lorentz-invariant.

title: From covariance to spacetime symmetry
body:
Lorentz developed transformations that preserved the form of key electromagnetic equations, and Poincaré recognised that the transformations form a group. Einstein's treatment gave equivalence between inertial frames a direct physical meaning, rather than using transformed quantities to conceal motion through an ether.
Minkowski then connected Lorentz invariance with the geometry of the invariant spacetime interval. This made symmetry more than a feature of particular electromagnetic formulae: it became an organising constraint on how relativistic physical laws should be expressed.
statement: Lorentz symmetry grew from electrodynamics into a general constraint on physical laws.

title: The symmetry test for a proposed law
body:
To test Lorentz invariance, compare the complete law in Lorentz-related inertial frames. Invariant contractions give the same scalar values, while covariant tensor equations remain valid as their components change.
These are complementary ways of expressing the same demand: changing the inertial description must not introduce a preferred frame into the physics. The check concerns the whole relationship, not the numerical constancy of every symbol appearing in it.
statement: Compare the whole law under frame changes, distinguishing invariant values from changing components.

title: Choosing one description from many
body:
If many potentials represent one field, a calculation can contain more freedom than the physical problem needs. Gauge fixing imposes an extra condition to organise that freedom.
The aim is a convenient representation of the same field, not a new physical restriction. A good choice simplifies the equations while respecting the boundary problem and making any residual freedom explicit.
statement: Gauge fixing selects a useful potential description within an equivalence class.

title: Restricting a redundant description
body:
Gauge fixing imposes a condition on a potential to reduce redundancy under \cref{gauge equivalence}{sr.gauge_invariance.definition}. It is a choice of representative, or a restricted family of representatives, for the same physical field.
The condition must be reachable using gauge functions allowed by the region and its boundary data. It may leave further transformations that preserve it. Complete uniqueness requires additional information, not merely the word “fixed”.
statement: A gauge condition restricts potential representatives without changing gauge-invariant predictions.

title: Why it is needed
body:
Without a gauge condition, equivalent potentials can be added to a solution and produce the same physical result. That freedom may leave equations looking underdetermined or introduce redundant terms into intermediate calculations.
A suitable condition can remove the troublesome part while preserving the field strength. It is especially useful for writing evolution equations or identifying physical modes, but does not replace the actual dynamical equations or their initial data.
statement: Removing representational freedom can make solving the potential equations better determined.

title: Representative, not new physics
body:
An equivalence class contains descriptions that differ on paper but give the same physical field. A gauge condition acts like a rule for choosing which descriptions we will work with.
The choice can make a problem easier or harder, much as a coordinate choice can. The important question is not which potential is “really there”, but whether the chosen representative satisfies the problem and yields invariant predictions.
statement: Choose a convenient member of a family, rather than a different physical electromagnetic field.

title: Lorenz gauge example
body:
The \cref{Lorenz condition}{sr.lorenz_gauge.definition} sets the potential divergence to zero. Because the divergence is a Lorentz scalar, the condition retains the same form across inertial frames.
When Maxwell dynamics are supplied, it also simplifies the potential equation. A further gauge function satisfying the homogeneous wave equation preserves it, so additional boundary or initial requirements can still be needed. The simplification is an advantage of the choice, not a proof that it removes all redundancy.
statement: Lorenz gauge uses \(\partial_\mu A^\mu=0\), leaving residual functions with \(\Box\chi=0\).

title: Residual freedom can remain
body:
After imposing a condition, substitute another allowed gauge change and ask when the condition still holds. For Lorenz gauge, the answer is \(\Box\chi=0\).
Such residual transformations describe the same physical field and may still alter potential components. Boundary conditions and the intended physical class of solutions decide which are permitted. A residual freedom is not automatically a physical mode or an inconsistency.
statement: A condition can leave transformations that preserve it, so gauge fixing need not mean unique representation.

title: Keep observables gauge-invariant
body:
A calculation may be easiest in one gauge, but its physical predictions must remain unchanged under allowed changes of representative. Field strength, particle trajectories and properly defined transferred energies provide useful checks.
A canonical momentum or a potential component can change without changing those predictions. If an alleged observable depends on residual gauge freedom, inspect what it measures and whether additional terms or definitions are missing.
statement: Fixing a gauge does not turn every potential-dependent intermediate expression into an observable.

title: Coordinate analogy and its limit
body:
Choosing axes can simplify the description of a physical vector without rotating the vector itself. Gauge fixing similarly simplifies potential data without changing field strength.
The analogy has a limit. A coordinate transformation relabels events or changes component bases, whereas the electromagnetic gauge change adds a gradient to the potential at the same event. Confusing them can hide which transformation is responsible for a component or field change.
statement: Gauge and coordinate choices both organise descriptions, but act on different variables.

title: Not an extra law of nature
body:
A gauge condition should not add a force, remove a physical source or change the electromagnetic tensor. Its role is to restrict equivalent potential descriptions.
It still has to be implemented consistently. An incompatible boundary condition or an unjustified uniqueness claim can remove legitimate solutions even though the intended purpose was only to remove redundancy.
statement: Gauge fixing is a representational choice, not an additional force equation.

title: A disciplined sequence for using a gauge
body:
Choose a condition suited to the problem, check that an allowed transformation reaches it, and identify transformations that still preserve it. Then solve the dynamical equations with the required data.
Physical predictions should agree with those obtained from any other allowed representative. This sequence keeps gauge fixing a practical tool rather than letting it masquerade as another dynamical law.
statement: A useful gauge choice simplifies calculation while keeping equivalence, boundary conditions and residual freedom visible.

title: From Galileo's ship to inertial systems
body:
Galileo's ship argument asked which features of motion could be detected without looking outside the ship. It separated smooth, uniform motion from motion that produces detectable effects inside the laboratory.
Newton later formulated mechanics relative to what he called absolute space. Nineteenth-century mechanics increasingly identified inertial frames operationally: they are the frames in which free bodies move uniformly. Special relativity kept this distinguished class of frames, but denied that any one of them could be singled out as absolutely at rest. So the useful idea of an inertial frame survived, while absolute rest did not.
statement: The relativity of uniform motion survived the abandonment of absolute rest.

title: From wave transformations to Lorentz symmetry
body:
The transformation grew out of attempts to reconcile wave theory and electrodynamics with motion. Woldemar Voigt wrote a related transformation in 1887 while studying waves, although it did not have exactly the form or physical role used today.
Lorentz developed the transformation for the electrodynamics of moving bodies. In 1905, Poincaré identified its group structure and named it for Lorentz. So the familiar mathematics had a history before it was understood as the coordinate relation between equally valid inertial observers; it did not first appear fully formed from Einstein's postulates.
statement: Wave theory and electrodynamics supplied predecessors to the modern Lorentz transformation.

title: From ether device to spacetime symmetry
body:
Lorentz retained an ether and initially understood local time and length contraction as features of matter moving through it. On that account, the ether still supplied an underlying preferred rest frame.
Einstein's 1905 formulation changed the interpretation: the transformation related equally valid inertial frames, with no observable ether frame. Minkowski's spacetime geometry then recast these transformations as the analogues of rotations in a four-dimensional geometry with an invariant interval. The geometry is not Euclidean, but the comparison helps explain why changing coordinates can preserve a common measuring rule.
statement: Einstein reinterpreted the frame changes physically; Minkowski expressed their invariant geometry.

title: Minkowski's invariant geometry
body:
Poincaré recognised the invariant quadratic form associated with Lorentz transformations. Minkowski then made it the organising geometry of relativity in his 1908 lecture “Space and Time”.
This changed the emphasis: rather than seeking separate observer-independent spatial distances and elapsed times, one could work with a combined spacetime separation. Its interval is shared by inertial observers even when they divide that separation into space and time differently.
statement: Minkowski made invariant spacetime separation an organising geometric principle.

title: Minkowski's light cone
body:
Minkowski's spacetime picture turned the light paths through one event into a geometric boundary. This made it possible to see the distinction between causal possibilities and spacelike separation on one diagram, rather than infer it separately from coordinate formulae.
Changing inertial frame tilts the coordinate axes, but cannot move a fixed event across that boundary. The cone therefore displays an observer-independent causal structure even while the coordinates used to describe it change.
statement: Minkowski's geometry made observer-independent causal separation visible.

title: A geometry designed for relativity
body:
Minkowski's 1908 spacetime formulation supplied a geometric language in which Lorentz transformations, simultaneity and causal order could be considered together. What appeared as separate coordinate effects could be understood as features of one spacetime geometry.
The familiar teaching diagram is a simplified descendant of that approach. It suppresses spatial dimensions so that worldlines and light cones fit on a page, while retaining the relationships needed to reason about inertial observers.
statement: Today's spacetime diagrams simplify Minkowski's geometric way of expressing relativity.

title: From local time to moving clocks
body:
Lorentz introduced a transformed “local time” while retaining an underlying ether time. Einstein's 1905 treatment gave the transformed time a direct operational meaning: it was the time assigned by clocks synchronised using exchanged light signals.
With that interpretation, the slower accumulation of time by a moving clock was not a defect measured against a hidden universal clock. It followed from how equally valid inertial frames assign space and time coordinates to the clock's events.
statement: Einstein gave transformed time an operational clock meaning rather than an underlying ether-time interpretation.

title: The FitzGerald-Lorentz contraction
body:
George FitzGerald and Hendrik Lorentz independently proposed that matter moving through the ether might contract enough to explain null ether-drift experiments. That proposal treated contraction as a physical response to motion relative to the ether.
Einstein's 1905 theory removed the need for that mechanism. Length contraction followed instead from the coordinate comparison: each frame measures endpoint positions simultaneously according to its own clocks, and the frames disagree about which events are simultaneous.
statement: Einstein replaced an ether-contraction mechanism with a difference in simultaneity-based measurements.

title: Minkowski's four-dimensional calculus
body:
Minkowski's 1908 spacetime formulation brought time and space into a common four-dimensional geometry. Position, velocity, momentum and current could then be treated through their transformation properties, rather than as separate collections of formulas for each observer.
The mathematical reorganisation mattered because it exposed invariant relations that lengthy component calculations could hide. Four-vector methods became a practical language for expressing relativistic laws and identifying which parts of a calculation depend on the frame.
statement: Minkowski organised relativistic quantities into objects whose invariant relations survive frame changes.

title: From Maxwell's system to four equations
body: Maxwell's 1865 theory used a larger collection of component equations and a mechanical ether model. Oliver Heaviside, in parallel with Gibbs's development of vector analysis, helped recast the theory in the compact vector form now taught as four Maxwell equations. The later tensor form is another reorganisation: it reveals their Lorentz-covariant structure rather than changing their empirical content.
statement: Heaviside’s vector reformulation and the later tensor form reorganised Maxwell’s theory without replacing its empirical content.

title: How gauge became a principle
body: Hermann Weyl introduced the word “gauge” in 1918 for a proposed local change of length scale; that gravitational-electromagnetic theory was not viable. After quantum mechanics, Weyl reinterpreted the freedom as a local change of wavefunction phase linked to the electromagnetic potential. This shifted gauge freedom from a calculational ambiguity toward a general principle for constructing interactions.
statement: Weyl’s unsuccessful scale gauge became, after quantum mechanics, a phase-based electromagnetic principle.

title: Hertz makes the waves visible
body: Maxwell inferred that electromagnetic disturbances should propagate at the measured speed of light. In the late 1880s Heinrich Hertz generated and detected radio waves, observing reflection, refraction, interference and polarisation. His experiments gave striking laboratory support to Maxwell's identification of light with electromagnetic waves.
statement: Hertz’s generated radio waves provided laboratory evidence for Maxwell’s wave prediction.

title: Dirac and Landau-Lifshitz
body: Early electron models due to Abraham and Lorentz produced a self-force but also severe conceptual difficulties. Dirac derived a relativistic point-charge equation in 1938; its runaway and pre-acceleration solutions made the problem especially stark. Landau and Lifshitz later advocated a reduced-order equation that is widely used when radiation reaction is a small correction to the external force.
statement: Dirac’s point-charge equation and later reduced-order approaches clarified different aspects of the self-force problem.

title: Why matching transformations preserve an equation
body:
We can see why matching transformations preserve an equation with a simple component example. Consider \(V=W\). Suppose that a \cref{Lorentz change}{sr.lorentz_transformations.definition} acts on both sides by the same invertible matrix: \(V'=\Lambda V\), \(W'=\Lambda W\). Subtracting the transformed sides and factoring out the common matrix gives
\[V'-W'=\Lambda(V-W).\]
If the equation is true in the first frame, \(V-W=0\). Multiplying zero by \(\Lambda\) still gives zero, so the transformed equation is true too. Because \(\Lambda\) is invertible, the same reasoning works backwards.
Tensor equations extend this reasoning: each matching index slot contributes matching transformation factors. We must still check that derivatives, sources and every other ingredient really have the required transformation behaviour.
Thus we have shown consistency under the stated transformation rules. We have not proved the proposed physical law from kinematics: that remains a separate physical question. A tensor-looking expression is only helpful once the complete law has been checked.
statement: An invertible common transformation preserves equality without preserving each component value.

title: Straight tracks at equal times
body:
The dots mark the positions of a free test particle at equal coordinate-time steps. Since both the direction and the spacing stay the same, the track represents constant velocity.
A curved or uneven track would need investigation: the particle might be interacting with something, or the grid itself might be non-inertial. The drawing therefore illustrates what to test, rather than deciding between those possibilities on its own.
statement: Equal position increments at equal times depict free motion in an inertial frame.

title: One vacuum speed in every direction
body:
The expanding rings picture a flash using one inertial clock network. Another standard inertial frame also measures speed c, although it assigns its own times to the distant wavefront events.
So the drawing is a reminder of the common vacuum speed. It should not be read as one simultaneous shell that all observers agree on point by point; simultaneity itself changes between the frames.
statement: The lightfront motif represents the common vacuum speed, not a preferred stationary observer.

title: Two equally valid laboratories
body:
The paired laboratories have equal physical standing: neither is drawn as the fundamental stationary one. Their matching internal experiments illustrate why uniform motion alone cannot identify absolute rest.
They can nevertheless report different coordinates and measured components. The agreement is about the physical laws, not about every number in their records.
statement: The paired laboratories represent equal physical laws despite relative uniform motion.

title: One event on a coordinate plot
body:
The red point represents one spacetime occurrence. Its projections onto the axes show the values of x and ct assigned in the displayed frame.
Changing the frame would change those labels, not the occurrence. Also, because the drawing shows an isolated event rather than a sequence, the point should not be read as an entire particle history.
statement: The point is one occurrence; the projections show its chosen frame coordinates.

title: Local dependence at one event
body:
The highlighted neighbourhood represents field values and their limiting variation near one event. The short arrows indicate the information entering a local differential law; the isolated distant point is not added as a separate instantaneous input.
The arrows do not establish a propagation speed. To decide whether a disturbance stays within a light cone, we must also examine the field dynamics and its causal conditions.
statement: The short arrows represent inputs to a local law, rather than a proof of its propagation speed.

title: Time and space in one measuring rule
body:
The motif represents the Minkowski bilinear rule in the +--- convention. The time entry contributes with one sign and the three spatial entries with the opposite sign, so they can cancel in a scalar product.
This is why the rule should not be read as an ordinary four-dimensional Euclidean length: even a nonzero displacement can have zero Minkowski square.
statement: The metric combines components with opposite time and space signs.

title: Three types of event separation
body:
The examples show timelike, null and spacelike separations in +--- signature. Compare how the time contribution balances the spatial one: their difference determines the sign and hence the causal type.
Observers may report different coordinate components for the same event pair, but cannot change that classification. Each drawn segment illustrates an event separation; it does not represent the proper time accumulated along every possible clock path between its endpoints.
statement: The sign of a fixed event pair’s interval distinguishes its causal type.

title: Two coordinate grids for one event
body:
The black and blue axes belong to relatively moving inertial frames sharing an origin. Each set of projections assigns time and space coordinates to the same event, so the point need not move when its labels change.
Take care with the tilted axes: ordinary page lengths along them are not automatically correctly calibrated Lorentz coordinate intervals. Their coordinate ticks must follow the transformation, not a Euclidean ruler laid along the drawing.
statement: The tilted axes relabel the event without moving it.

title: Two paths of the same internal pulse
body:
The drawings compare the same transverse light clock in its rest frame and in a lab where it moves. In both descriptions, departure and return occur on the same lower mirror.
The lab path slopes because the apparatus moves while the pulse travels. It is still the pulse's path inside the clock, not the route of a signal sent to a remote camera. This keeps the time-dilation argument separate from signal-arrival effects.
statement: The moving mirrors lengthen the lab light path while its speed remains c.

title: Two simultaneity slices through a rod
body:
The two coordinate descriptions choose different simultaneous slices through the same rod history. In the rod's rest frame, its endpoints are stationary and their separation gives the rest length. The lab instead uses endpoint events simultaneous according to its own clocks.
So the shorter moving length reflects a different measurement slice, rather than a drawing of the material being crushed.
statement: Length is an endpoint separation on the measuring frame’s simultaneous slice.

title: The null boundary and causal regions
body:
The null rays mark light propagation through the vertex event. Inside the boundary, slower-than-light causal histories are possible; outside it, the separation from the vertex is spacelike.
The familiar 45-degree slopes come from using equal scales for x and ct. A stretched drawing would change those angles without changing which physical paths are null.
statement: The cone boundary marks zero interval; its interior is timelike.

title: Events and worldlines on spacetime axes
body:
The points mark events and the curves trace histories through them. With equal scales for x and ct, a vertical history is stationary in the plotted frame, while null histories lie at 45 degrees.
A different inertial frame assigns different coordinate slopes to these histories. The physical events remain the same, so the change is in their description rather than in which occurrences form the history.
statement: One plot distinguishes stationary, moving and null histories.

title: One law described by two inertial frames
body:
The two inertial-coordinate descriptions feed into the same physical relationship. Their component values can differ, but a consistently transformed equation remains true in either description.
The emphasis is on preserving the law, not every number. Nor does the motif imply that any expression with indices automatically has the required physical symmetry; its transformation rules must be established first.
statement: The unchanged law is the focus, rather than unchanged component values.

title: How a boost mixes energy and momentum
body:
Let frame \(S'\) move at speed \(v\) along the positive \(x\)-axis of \(S\), and define \(\beta=v/c\). Four-momentum obeys the same boost rule as a spacetime vector. With \(p^0=E/c\), its time component transforms as
\[ \begin{aligned}\frac{E'}{c}&=\gamma\left(\frac{E}{c}-\beta p_x\right),\\ E'&=\gamma(E-vp_x).\end{aligned} \]
Its longitudinal momentum correspondingly becomes \(p'_x=\gamma(p_x-vE/c^2)\). So energy and momentum must transform together; neither is an invariant by itself.
For two equal light pulses of energy \(L/2\) travelling oppositely along \(x\), use \(p_x=\pm L/(2c)\). Their transformed energies add to \(\gamma L\), since the two terms linear in \(v\) cancel. This supplies the radiation energy transformation used in the light-emission argument. It assumes the physical four-vector description of light's energy–momentum, not a rest-energy formula for the emitter.
statement: For a boost along \(x\), \(E'=\gamma(E-vp_x)\).

title: A box of light can have mass
body:
Imagine a reflecting box containing light travelling in opposite directions. The box is at rest as a whole. Each light pulse has zero individual invariant mass, but it still carries energy and momentum. Opposite momenta can cancel; the energies do not cancel.
The rest frame belongs to the complete box-plus-radiation system, not to a photon. Retaining extra radiation raises that system's rest energy and therefore its mass. A useful limiting calculation takes two opposite equal pulses, each with energy \(\epsilon\). Together they have total momentum zero and energy \(2\epsilon\), so their system mass is \(2\epsilon/c^2\), despite neither pulse having rest mass.
This is an interpretation of the energy–momentum relation, not an independent proof. It helps break the intuition that mass must count pieces of massive material: even internal motion and radiation contribute. In a real reflecting box, include the walls and their changed state as part of the complete system.
statement: Opposite light momenta can cancel while their energies add, contributing to a system's rest mass.

title: One vector, different frame components
body: A four-vector is one spacetime object with linked components; Lorentz transformations reshuffle the components without changing the underlying object.
statement: One spacetime arrow and a component column represent a single four-vector.

title: Rest energy in the momentum geometry
body: Rest mass is stored energy: in the rest frame, the invariant four-momentum relation becomes E=mc^2.
statement: The iconic equation marks rest energy as mass times c squared.

title: Energy and momentum components
body: Four-momentum p^mu packages energy and spatial momentum together; for a massive particle it points with the four-velocity u^mu.
statement: The four-momentum arrow combines energy and spatial momentum.

title: An event relative to the origin
body: The position four-vector x^mu packages the coordinates of event P relative to origin O, making event location a spacetime vector.
statement: The position four-vector points from the origin event O to event P.

title: The clock follows the path
body: Proper time is the time carried by a clock along its own timelike path; coordinate time is a frame-dependent comparison.
statement: Ticks along a timelike worldline represent accumulated proper time tau.

title: The timelike tangent
body: Four-velocity u^mu is tangent to a timelike worldline and measures change of position four-vector per unit proper time.
statement: A green tangent vector at a worldline event represents four-velocity.

title: Action principle — visual model
body: The physical path is the one whose action is stationary: small fixed-endpoint variations make no first-order change in S.
statement: A highlighted path between fixed endpoints is compared with nearby variations.

title: Canonical momentum — visual model
body: Canonical momentum p is paired with coordinate q because it comes from how the Lagrangian depends on q's velocity.
statement: The coordinate q is paired with a conjugate momentum p.

title: Euler-Lagrange equations — visual model
body: Fixed-endpoint variations of the path impose delta S = 0, which turns the action principle into the Euler-Lagrange equations.
statement: A varied path leads to an Euler-Lagrange equation tile.

title: Field equations — visual model
body: Field equations are local update rules: neighbouring field values and derivatives determine how the field changes and propagates.
statement: Neighbouring field values feed a local field-equation tile.

title: Field Lagrangian — visual model
body: Field action integrates a Lagrangian density over a spacetime region, replacing a particle path with local field values everywhere.
statement: An irregular spacetime region integrates Lagrangian density into the action S.

title: Hamiltonian formalism — visual model
body: Hamiltonian mechanics describes dynamics as flow in q-p phase space, where H generates time evolution of coordinates and momenta.
statement: A curve in q-p phase space is generated by H.

title: Lagrangian — visual model
body: The Lagrangian is the local rule assigned along a history; adding it up through time gives the action S.
statement: Local Lagrangian tiles accumulate into the action S.

title: Scalar field — visual model
body: A scalar field assigns one number phi(x) to every spacetime point; the value can vary from point to point but has no direction.
statement: Different-sized discs show one scalar value at each spacetime point.

title: Vector field — visual model
body: A vector field assigns a vector such as A_mu(x) at each event, so both size and direction can vary across spacetime.
statement: Anchored arrows show a vector attached to each spacetime point.

title: Reaching the divergence condition
body:
Given a potential and its smooth gauge freedom, set \(A'^\mu=A^\mu+\partial^\mu\chi\). Take the divergence:
\[ \partial_\mu A'^\mu=\partial_\mu A^\mu+\Box\chi, \]
where \(\Box\coloneqq\partial_\mu\partial^\mu=c^{-2}\partial_t^2-\nabla^2\). To make the left-hand side zero, solve
\[ \Box\chi=-\partial_\mu A^\mu. \]
When this equation admits a sufficiently smooth solution compatible with the chosen boundary and initial conditions, the new potential is in Lorenz gauge and has unchanged field strength. The right-hand side is a known function of the original potential, not a new physical source. This construction explains the reachability condition; global or boundary obstructions must be checked rather than assumed away.
statement: A gauge function satisfying \(\Box\chi=-\partial_\mu A^\mu\) brings the potential to Lorenz gauge.

title: Electric field — visual model
body: The electric field tells a stationary positive test charge which direction it would be pushed at each point.
statement: Radial E arrows show the electric field of a positive charge.

title: Electromagnetic field — visual model
body: The electromagnetic field is the single tensor F_mu_nu; electric and magnetic fields are frame-dependent views of that object.
statement: One F object gives rise to E and B component views.

title: Energy density of EM field — visual model
body: Electromagnetic energy density is stored locally in the field; stronger E and B values mean more energy in that spacetime cell.
statement: A field cell stores energy density u in E and B.

title: Stress-energy of EM field — visual model
body: The electromagnetic stress-energy tensor collects field energy density, momentum flow, and stresses into one object that can be conserved and transported.
statement: A T_EM block combines field glyphs with face arrows.

title: Field tensor \(F_{\mu\nu}\) — visual model
body: The field tensor F_mu_nu packages electric and magnetic components into one relativistic object rather than two unrelated fields.
statement: An F tensor badge contains electric and magnetic component cues.

title: Gauge fixing — visual model
body: Gauge fixing chooses one representative potential from many equivalent descriptions, simplifying calculation while leaving the physical field F unchanged.
statement: Many gauge-equivalent potentials pass through a selector to one A.

title: Gauge invariance — visual model
body: Gauge invariance means different potentials, such as A_mu and A_mu + partial_mu Lambda, can describe the same electromagnetic field.
statement: Two gauge-related potentials point to the same F.

title: Lorentz force law — visual model
body: The Lorentz force law uses charge, field tensor, and four-velocity to determine the particle's momentum change dp^mu/dtau.
statement: A particle with velocity u in field F receives a momentum change dp.

title: Lorenz gauge — visual model
body: Lorenz gauge is a convenient condition, partial_mu A^mu = 0, selecting one potential description without changing the physical field.
statement: Potential representatives pass through a Lorenz gauge selector.

title: Magnetic field — visual model
body: Magnetic fields are tied to motion: currents or moving charges create circular B patterns, and moving test charges feel sideways forces.
statement: Circular B arrows wrap around a moving charge or current.

title: Minimal coupling — visual model
body: Minimal coupling introduces electromagnetism by replacing free momentum with p_mu - e A_mu, so motion responds to the vector potential.
statement: Free momentum p enters an A-dependent coupling rule.

title: Momentum density (Poynting vector) — visual model
body: The Poynting vector S points in the direction electromagnetic energy and momentum flow, set by the combined E and B fields.
statement: Crossed E and B arrows produce a Poynting vector S.

title: Vector potential \(A_\mu\) — visual model
body: The vector potential A_mu is not the field itself; local derivatives of A_mu combine to form the electromagnetic tensor F_mu_nu.
statement: A vector-potential field feeds a derivative operation to produce F.

title: Boosting density and current together
body:
Take a boost along positive \(x\) with speed \(v\), \(\beta=v/c\). Apply the four-vector rule to \(j^0=c\rho\) and \(j^1=j_x\):
\[ \begin{aligned}c\rho'&=\gamma(c\rho-\beta j_x),\\ j'_x&=\gamma(j_x-\beta c\rho).\end{aligned} \]
Divide the first equation by \(c\) to obtain \(\rho'=\gamma(\rho-vj_x/c^2)\); the second is \(j'_x=\gamma(j_x-v\rho)\). Transverse components are unchanged for this standard boost.
The derivation uses the physical identification of charge flow as a four-vector, with charge an invariant scalar. It does not infer that identification solely from matching units. It explains how the assumed geometric source description connects measurements across frames.
statement: A longitudinal boost gives \(\rho'=\gamma(\rho-vj_x/c^2)\) and \(j'_x=\gamma(j_x-v\rho)\).

title: Charge conservation — visual model
body: Charge conservation is local bookkeeping: changes of charge inside a volume must be balanced by current crossing its boundary.
statement: Charge dots leave a local box only through current arrows.

title: Electromagnetic waves — visual model
body: Electromagnetic waves are coupled E and B oscillations that sustain each other, propagate at c, and carry energy-momentum.
statement: Coupled E and B waves propagate in the c direction.

title: Energy--momentum tensor — visual model
body: The energy-momentum tensor records local density and flux of energy and momentum; zero divergence means local conservation.
statement: A T^munu tile highlights density and flux cells.

title: Four-current — visual model
body: The four-current J^mu packages charge density and current flow into one relativistic source for the electromagnetic field.
statement: A J^mu badge combines charge density and current.

title: Maxwell's equations — visual model
body: Maxwell's equations are local rules linking charge-current sources J to electromagnetic fields and explaining how disturbances propagate as waves.
statement: A source J feeds a field F, with outgoing wave marks.

title: Noether's theorem — visual model
body: Noether's theorem links symmetry to conservation: if a smooth transformation leaves S unchanged, a corresponding quantity Q is conserved.
statement: A continuous symmetry of S points to a conserved Q.

title: Radiation reaction — visual model
body: Radiation reaction is self-back-reaction: an accelerating charge emits waves that carry energy-momentum away, altering the charge's later motion.
statement: An accelerating charge emits waves and recoils.

title: Wave equation — visual model
body: A wave equation is a local propagation rule: sources can create disturbances, while source-free regions support travelling wave solutions.
statement: A wave operator acting on A produces a propagating wave.
